structured_extraction.program_name: Baltimore City Free COVID-19 Vaccination Program
structured_extraction.program_description: The Baltimore City Health Department provides free COVID-19 vaccinations to residents ages 6 months and older, including walk-up clinics and at-home vaccinations for those who cannot travel.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Free COVID-19 vaccines (Moderna, Pfizer, or Novavax) are provided at walk-up vaccination clinics or at home for residents who cannot travel. The 2024-25 updated vaccine targets the most widespread current COVID strain. At-home vaccination can be scheduled by calling (443)-216-9511.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Baltimore City residents ages 6 months and older, especially those 65 or older, at high risk for severe COVID-19, or never previously vaccinated.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Free COVID-19 vaccination to protect against severe disease, hospitalization, and death.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available to residents of Baltimore City.
requirements_list: Must be a Baltimore City resident
Must be at least 6 months old
At-home vaccination requires scheduling by phone
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Visit a walk-up vaccination clinic (see weekly clinic schedule on the Baltimore City website) or call (443)-216-9511 to schedule an at-home vaccination.

structured_extraction.program_name: Baltimore City Housing Department LIGHT Program
structured_extraction.program_description: LIGHT (Living In Green and Healthy Together) helps Baltimore City residents get free or low-cost services to make their homes safer, healthier, and more comfortable. It serves as a single point of access for services from Baltimore's Housing and Community Development Department's Division of Housing Property and Preservation, providing access to three grant and loan programs plus 60+ additional programs and benefits from public and nonprofit agencies. LIGHT Coordinators talk with residents to find out what they need, then connect them with programs that can help — including home repairs, energy efficiency improvements, lead hazard reduction, and addressing high water bills. The program also provides case management to help applicants access and coordinate eligible services.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Free or low-cost home services coordinated by LIGHT Coordinators who assess resident needs and connect them with appropriate programs. Assistance includes grants and loans (forgivable loans forgiven after 5 years if primary residence maintained; deferred loans due upon home sale from sale proceeds). Programs cover: climatization/energy efficiency improvements (attic insulation, air sealing, weather stripping, heating system maintenance/repair, pipe wrapping, light bulbs), lead risk reduction (remediation for eligible owners and tenants in occupied properties), and home rehabilitation (roof repair, water/sewer line repair, water heater replacement, electrical repair, accessibility modifications, pipe repair, plumbing, HVAC, disability accessibility modifications). Eligible tenants may qualify for lead remediation. Residents can apply through a housing counselor, a Community Action Center, or online.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Baltimore City homeowners and residents who need help making their homes safer, healthier, and more comfortable, including those experiencing high water bills or energy efficiency issues; eligible tenants (for lead remediation); pregnant women or families with children under 6 (for lead remediation); and persons with disabilities (for accessibility improvements)
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Home repairs and improvements including disability accessibility modifications, electrical work, energy efficiency improvements (attic insulation, air sealing/caulking, weather stripping, heating system maintenance/repair, pipe wrapping, light bulbs), HVAC, lead paint hazard reduction and remediation (paint treatment, window/door replacement, floor treatment, paint removal and repainting), plumbing, roof repair, sewer line and water line repairs, water heater replacement, and pipe repairs
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Baltimore City, Maryland residents only (417 East Fayette Street, Suite 1125, Baltimore, MD 21202)
requirements_list: Pre-application submission required
Household income documentation needed
For homeowners: deed verification, mortgage status, judgment/bankruptcy history, foreclosure status, homeowner's insurance, ground rent/property tax status
For renters: lease documentation and landlord contact information
Lead-based paint disclosure required for homes built before 1978
Basic home condition assessment (electricity, water, heating, roof)
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Apply online through the Neighborly Software portal, download and mail a pre-application form to 417 East Fayette Street, Suite 1125, Baltimore, MD 21202, email dhcd.light@baltimorecity.gov, or apply through a housing counselor or a Community Action Center.

structured_extraction.program_name: Baltimore City Intergenerational Initiative For Trauma And Youth (B-CIITY) Supported By ReCAST
structured_extraction.program_description: B-CIITY is a community coalition program funded by SAMHSA's Resiliency in Communities After Stress and Trauma (ReCAST) grant. It reduces the impact of trauma and builds resilience in Central West Baltimore communities affected by the April 2015 unrest. The program empowers community organizations to deliver trauma-informed, resilience-based services to youth ages 14–24 and their families, supporting school completion, healthy relationships, and financial stability.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: SAMHSA awarded a five-year, $5 million grant to BCHD. B-CIITY sub-grants funding to community organizations that implement trauma-informed and resilience-based initiatives. Applicants must focus on up to three of seven defined community results and track at least two indicators of success.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Community organizations and residents in Central West Baltimore (Sandtown/Winchester, Upton/Druid Heights, Penn North) serving youth ages 14–24 and their families experiencing trauma.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Implementing high-quality, trauma-informed services to promote connectedness and resilience in youth; leadership, education and workforce development; mental, physical, and spiritual health support; family, community, and cultural connectedness initiatives.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Limited to Central West Baltimore communities in the 21217 zip code area, specifically Sandtown/Winchester, Upton/Druid Heights, and Penn North.
requirements_list: Must serve youth ages 14–24 and their families in Central West Baltimore
Must implement trauma-informed and resilience-based services
Must choose no more than three of the seven B-CIITY results to focus on
Must match chosen results with at least two indicators of success
Must have community experience in the target neighborhoods
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Organizations apply for sub-grant funding through the B-CIITY Community Board, which serves in a leadership and advisory capacity and oversees the grant funding process.

structured_extraction.program_description: The Mayor's Office of Employment Development and the Department of Human Resources, in partnership with the Annie E. Casey Foundation, connect Baltimore City residents with paid apprenticeship opportunities across City agencies, contractors, and unions. The program creates a coordinated apprenticeship ecosystem that aligns capital contracts with apprenticeship utilization goals and provides clear entry points through pre-apprenticeship and training programs. Apprentices receive on-the-job training and related instruction in industries such as healthcare, plumbing, HVAC, construction, technology, transportation, and telecommunications while earning wages and scheduled pay increases tied to skills and service. Apprentices also earn credentials to boost career opportunities. Pre-apprenticeship support including resume building and skills assessments is also available.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Paid apprenticeships providing at least 2,000 hours per year of on-the-job training at a worksite under skilled journeyworkers, plus at least 144 hours of related instruction per year, with scheduled pay increases tied to skills and service. Apprentices earn credentials to boost career opportunities. The program also coordinates a citywide apprenticeship ecosystem aligning capital contracts with apprenticeship utilization goals and provides clear entry points through pre-apprenticeship and training programs. Pre-apprenticeship support including resume building and skills assessments is available.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Baltimore City residents 18 years or older seeking paid apprenticeship and workforce development opportunities with City agencies, contractors, and unions
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Paid on-the-job training and instruction in skilled trades and other industries; apprentice wages with scheduled pay increases; credential attainment; workforce development and apprenticeship placement
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Applicants must live in Baltimore City
requirements_list: Must be 18 years or older
Must be a Baltimore City resident
Employers must provide minimum 2,000 hours per year of on-the-job training
Training under direction of highly skilled journeyworker
Minimum 144 hours of related instruction per year
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Fill out the Apprenticeship Form at https://bit.ly/bmoreapp and the office will follow up by email. Pre-apprenticeship support available including resume building and skills assessment. Contact apprenticeships@baltimorecity.gov or call 410-396-1910 for additional information.

structured_extraction.program_name: Baltimore City Live Near Your Work Program
structured_extraction.program_description: A partnership between participating employers and the City of Baltimore designed to encourage homeownership near an employee's place of employment. Employees of participating employers (who must be first-time homebuyers) can receive a matching grant from the City of Baltimore toward down payment and closing costs when purchasing a home in Baltimore City near their workplace. The City matches the employer's contribution — each contributing a minimum of $1,000 — for a total grant of at least $2,000, and up to $5,000 or more depending on the employer's contribution (employer contributions range from $1,000 to $2,500, with the City matching up to $2,500). The grant is forgivable at 20% per year over 5 years and does not require repayment as long as the buyer maintains the property as their primary residence. There are no annual income limits.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: A minimum $2,000 grant split between the City of Baltimore ($1,000 minimum) and the participating employer ($1,000 minimum), with employer contributions ranging up to $2,500 and the City matching up to $2,500, for a total of up to $5,000 or more. Funds are used toward down payment and closing costs. No annual income limits. The grant is forgivable at 20% per year over 5 years. The buyer must contribute at least $1,000 of personal funds toward the purchase and must use the property as their primary residence.
structured_extraction.application_deadline_string: Funding available on a first-come, first-served basis per fiscal year (July 1 – June 30); 93 incentives remaining as of 4/6/2026
structured_extraction.program_audience: Employees of participating employers who are first-time homebuyers seeking to purchase a home near their workplace in Baltimore City
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Down payment and closing cost assistance for purchase of a primary residence in Baltimore City near the buyer's place of employment
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Must purchase a home in Baltimore City near the participating employer's location. Individual employers may also restrict eligible neighborhoods.
requirements_list: Must work for a participating employer
Must be a first-time homebuyer
Must purchase a home in Baltimore City near place of employment
Must use the property as the primary residence
Must contribute at least $1,000 of personal funds toward the purchase
Must complete a homeownership counseling class from a City-approved agency within one year before applying
Settlement date must be at least 30 days after application submission
Must provide the Title Company's EIN in the application
Individual employers may add additional eligibility requirements
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Register and submit an application through the Neighborly Applicant Portal at portal.neighborlysoftware.com/baltimoremd/Participant at least 30 days before closing. Check livebaltimore.com/live-near-your-work for a list of participating employers. For general information, contact Debra Braxton at Baltimore Housing's Office of Homeownership at 417 E. Fayette Street, Suite 1125, Baltimore, MD 21202, or email DHCD.Homeownership@baltimorecity.gov. Additional information is also available at Healthy Neighborhoods, Inc. (healthyneighborhoods.org/baltimore-city-live-near-your-work-program/).

structured_extraction.program_description: Law requiring vendors, contractors, and sub-contractors doing business with Baltimore City to hire local residents for city-funded contracts, effective December 23, 2013. The Mayor's Office of Employment Development (MOED) supports compliance by providing free recruitment, pre-screening, interview space, and tax credit information to businesses awarded city contracts. Requires employment analysis and 51% residency requirement for new hires on covered contracts.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: MOED provides free employer services to businesses with city contracts, including: sharing job postings citywide at no cost, pre-screening applicants, and offering free interview space. MOED also connects businesses to tax credits, recruitment help, and training reimbursement. Vendors manage compliance through the B2Gnow platform for employment analyses, monthly reports, and new hire data entry. Applies to city-awarded contracts over $300,000 and city-subsidized projects over $5,000,000. All industries are covered except emergency services and some federally-funded contracts; professional services are not exempt.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Vendors, contractors, and sub-contractors awarded Baltimore City contracts over $300,000 or city-subsidized projects over $5,000,000.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Recruitment support, pre-screening, interview space, and connections to tax credits and training reimbursement for businesses hiring Baltimore City residents. This is primarily a hiring compliance requirement rather than a funding program.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Baltimore City contracts only. Work must be performed on Baltimore City contracts.
requirements_list: Meet with MOED within 2 weeks after contract award to complete an Employment Analysis
Post new jobs with MOED only for a period of seven days
Utilize MOED's recruitment services for new hires
51% of all new hires for city-funded contracts must be Baltimore City residents
Submit monthly employment reports on current workers, new workers, and Baltimore City residents on the project by the first business day of each month
Complete employment analysis once per contract via B2Gnow platform
Report total employees on payroll and project workers needed for company-performed and subcontractor work

Enter new hire data into B2Gnow system including employee information (name, SSN last 4 digits, position, date started, pay rate), local hiring details (referral source, education level, benefits offered, hours/week), and home address
Assign employees to specific contracts in B2Gnow system
Manage subcontractors/subgrantees/subrecipients on contract profile
Apply for waiver from Local Hiring Review Committee if unable to meet requirements (e.g., union collective bargaining agreements)
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: After a city contract is awarded, the city agency submits a Vendor Contact Form to MOED. The business or vendor then meets with MOED Employer Services staff within two weeks to complete an Employment Analysis and discuss staffing needs and available services. When ready to hire, the business sends job postings to MOED. MOED shares listings, pre-screens applicants, and provides interview space. Vendors manage ongoing compliance through the B2Gnow platform: access vendor and contract profiles, update business information, add employees, complete employment analyses, and submit monthly employment reports each month for prior month's activity. A local hiring coordinator is available for guidance.

structured_extraction.program_name: Baltimore City Opioid Restitution Fund (ORF) Community Grant
structured_extraction.program_description: Baltimore City established the Opioid Restitution Fund (ORF) using approximately $579.9 million recovered from lawsuits against pharmaceutical manufacturers and distributors for their role in the opioid epidemic. Established by Mayor Brandon Scott's August 2024 Executive Order, the fund supports programs, interventions, and services to address the opioid and overdose crisis in Baltimore City, including substance use prevention, treatment, recovery, harm reduction, and programs addressing social determinants of health related to the opioid epidemic. The fund is designed to sustain impact for at least 15 years. The Mayor's Office of Recovery Programs (MORP) coordinates fiscal management and oversight for all grants, ensuring funds are used responsibly and in compliance with grant terms. The ORF Community Grant specifically supports nonprofit organizations in Baltimore City leading community-driven efforts to address the opioid and overdose crisis, with $2 million available for Round 1 (Fiscal Year 2026). Three funding tiers are available: Tier 1 (up to $50,000 for low-barrier social support services), Tier 2 (up to $250,000 for harm reduction services), and Tier 3 (up to $500,000 for mobile treatment services with robust harm reduction).
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Grants funded by approximately $579.9 million in settlements and awards recovered from pharmaceutical companies. For the ORF Community Grant (Round 1, FY2026), a total of $2 million is available, with proposed project funding spreadable across up to two years. Three funding tiers: Tier 1 - up to $50,000 (approximately 3-6 awards) for low-barrier social support services (housing, transportation, food, education, employment); Tier 2 - up to $250,000 (approximately 2-4 awards) for a full array of harm reduction services (naloxone distribution, drug checking, syringe service programs, wound care, evidence-based strategies); Tier 3 - up to $500,000 (approximately 2-3 awards) for low-barrier mobile treatment services in areas disproportionately affected by overdose, must include robust harm reduction services. Final number of awards depends on approved applications received per tier and total available funding; awarded amounts may differ from proposed budgets based on scope of work and available funding. Indirect/overhead costs capped at 15% of grant award. MORP serves as the lead contract administrator and monitors grantee compliance with grant terms.
structured_extraction.application_deadline_string: Proposals due November 23 by 11:59 p.m. EST; Applications due January 25 by 11:59 p.m. EST
structured_extraction.program_audience: Nonprofit organizations in Baltimore City leading community-driven efforts to address substance use prevention, treatment, recovery, harm reduction, and social determinants of health related to the opioid and overdose crisis. Includes organizations serving people who use drugs, people with substance use disorders, individuals at risk, families, youth/adolescents, and communities affected by the opioid crisis.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Overdose prevention, treatment access, harm reduction, and recovery services related to the opioid crisis, as well as programs addressing social determinants of health related to the opioid epidemic. Allowable uses include: salaries and staffing, contracts and services, materials and supplies, equipment, harm reduction services (naloxone, drug checking, syringe programs), social services (housing, transportation, food, education, employment), clinical treatment services, medication-assisted treatment (MOUD including buprenorphine and methadone), peer support and peer navigation, case management, behavioral health counseling, substance use disorder screening, program-specific evaluation and data collection, organization-wide trainings (when essential, up to 15% overhead cap), clinical/support software (proportionally allocated), and vehicle/van purchases if correlating to specific tier activities. Unallowable uses include: law enforcement salaries/equipment, drug-related arrests, drug courts, mandatory treatment, coercive services, abstinence-only programs, stigmatizing materials, capital campaigns, large-scale construction, real estate purchases, and fundraising costs.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Baltimore City only. Available to programs serving Baltimore City residents.
requirements_list: All grants must align with the City's approved uses to address overdose and substance use disorder, including prevention, treatment, recovery, harm reduction, and social determinants of health.
Must be a nonprofit organization (501(c)(3) status required for Tier 2 and Tier 3 applicants; nonstock corporation registered with Maryland Department of Assessments & Taxation for Tier 1).
For-profit companies are NOT eligible.
Must not be a quasi-City entity or affiliate/subsidiary of one that can be or is funded by the City through the annual budgeting process.
Must have a valid Employer Identification Number (EIN) and be in good financial standing.
Must be in good standing with the State of Maryland and the City of Baltimore.
Must have an existing office in the City of Baltimore and proven direct service experience serving identified populations in Baltimore City.
Must have more than 5 years of proven experience serving identified populations in Baltimore City (for additional scoring points).
Must meet eligibility criteria outlined in the Instructions for Proposals document.
Must register and create an account in the Grant Lifecycle Manager portal.
Must comply with financial policies and reporting requirements, including reviewing expenditures and invoices against approved budgets.
Self-assess project eligibility before submission.
Provide accurate, honest, and timely information.
Comply with all laws, contractual requirements, guidelines, and agreements.
Complete projects per approved scope of work and timeline.
Retain final reports for future audits.
Reconcile all funds and return unused funding.
Overhead costs capped at 15% of grant award.
Software and training costs must be proportionally allocated if shared across multiple programs.
Services/supplies must not duplicate existing State Settlement funding.
Services must not be law enforcement or carceral in nature, coercive, or abstinence-only.
Marketing/materials must not use stigmatizing messaging.
Organizations must track and report standard performance measures across categories: General, Prevention, Treatment, Recovery, Harm Reduction, and Social Determinants of Health.
Activities must be implementable with measurable impact within two-year grant period.
Must align with the City's Comprehensive Needs Assessment and Overdose Response Strategic Plan.
Must have compassionate, supportive, nonjudgmental mission and hiring practices toward individuals with substance use experience.
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Organizations submit proposals through the Mayor's Office of Recovery Programs Application Portal (Grant Lifecycle Manager). The process includes: (1) Create a new online account with organization, user, and executive officer information and confirm email address; (2) Complete initial proposal/LOI stage (proposals due November 23 by 11:59 p.m. EST); (3) If deemed eligible, complete full application form (applications due January 25 by 11:59 p.m. EST); (4) Applications reviewed and scored by the Restitution Advisory Board using criteria outlined in Appendices C and D (maximum 110+ points); (5) View decision status on dashboard; (6) Complete sequential follow-up reports if approved. A recorded orientation training is available to guide applicants through the process. Applicants should also monitor the City's website for funding announcements and notices of funding availability.

structured_extraction.program_name: Baltimore City Opioid-Associated Disease Prevention and Outreach Program (OADPOP)
structured_extraction.program_description: The OADPOP (formerly the Baltimore City Syringe Service Program) works to reduce HIV, Hepatitis C, and other infections by reducing the circulation of used syringes. The program connects people with substance use disorders to drug treatment services, provides HIV and syphilis counseling and testing, and offers opioid overdose response training. Needle exchange services are available at 11 locations across Baltimore City.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Free and confidential harm reduction services including syringe exchange, HIV and syphilis counseling and testing, referrals to drug treatment, and opioid overdose response training. Services are provided through mobile outreach at 11 locations during 18 weekly time slots throughout Baltimore City.
structured_extraction.program_audience: High-risk individuals and the general public in Baltimore City, particularly those with substance use disorders.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Syringe exchange, HIV/syphilis testing and counseling, drug treatment referrals, and opioid overdose response training.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Baltimore City and surrounding jurisdictions.
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: No formal application required. Services are available at mobile sites throughout Baltimore City during scheduled hours. See the locations and hours table on the program page.

structured_extraction.program_name: Baltimore City Strategic Investment – Rapid Re-housing
structured_extraction.program_description: This program uses American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) funding to support rapid re-housing for individuals and families experiencing homelessness in Baltimore City. Using a Housing First approach, the Mayor's Office of Homeless Services (MOHS) awards grants to qualified non-profit organizations and city government agencies to provide housing placement, time-limited rental assistance (4-24 months), and support services. The program aims to rapidly connect individuals and families to permanent housing, reduce time spent homeless, reduce unsheltered homelessness and encampments, advance racial equity, and support person-centered approaches.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: MOHS received $5,663,850 in ARPA funding to award to multiple non-profit and city government providers to implement and operate Rapid Re-housing projects in Baltimore City. Average annual award is $500,000-$800,000. The program has three main components: (1) Housing Identification, (2) Rental Assistance Administration (security deposits, moving expenses, utilities, and rent subsidies for 4-24 months using FY2022 FMR data), and (3) Case Management and Supportive Services (up to 24 months, can extend beyond rental subsidy end date). Uses progressive engagement approach with declining subsidy, fixed percentage, or fixed subsidy models. Joint applications are allowed with a lead agency and subrecipient structure.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Non-profit organizations and city government agencies with capacity to implement and operate Rapid Re-housing programs for individuals and families experiencing homelessness in Baltimore City. Program participants include individuals and families experiencing Category 1 or 4 homelessness with income under 30% of Area Median Income, prioritized through Baltimore City's Coordinated Access System, with special focus on the most vulnerable households including individuals of color, seniors, those with multiple health conditions, pregnant or parenting individuals, LGBTQ individuals, domestic violence survivors, human trafficking survivors, and veterans.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Housing identification and securing permanent housing; rental assistance payments (short- and medium-term subsidies, 4-24 months); security deposits; moving expenses; utilities; case management and supportive services; employment and workforce development referrals; health, mental health, and behavioral health service connections; landlord incentives; personnel costs for full-time or part-time positions.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Baltimore City only.
requirements_list: Must be a qualified non-profit 501(c)(3) tax-exempt organization or city government agency
Must demonstrate experience and capacity to provide housing placement and support services
Must utilize Housing First approach
Must meet the scope of work outlined in the RFP
Must submit application by the deadline
Complete application in PDF with required signatures
Budget Workbook & Narrative
MOHS Fair Housing Policy Statement and Agreement
MOHS Housing First Policy Agreement
Conflict of Interest Questionnaire
Federal Tax-Exempt Determination Letter
Articles of Incorporation & Bylaws
Current Certificate of Good Standing from Maryland (within 30 days)
Current Board of Directors list
Agency Organizational Chart
Project Organizational Chart
2 years of financial audits or board-approved financial statements
Cannot screen out clients for: insufficient income, substance abuse history, criminal record, or domestic violence history
Cannot terminate clients for: non-participation in services, lack of progress, income loss, or domestic violence victimization
Serve approximately 155 households over the program period
Joint applications allowed with designated lead agency and subrecipient structure
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Applicants submit a project proposal including a Project Application and Project Budget Workbook. MOHS reviews and scores proposals, issues conditional funding letters, and begins contracting. Authorized representative must complete and sign Housing First compliance agreement. Projects start October 1, 2022.

structured_extraction.program_description: The Baltimore City Health Department provides free tuberculosis (TB) services, including case management, testing, treatment, and medication for people with active TB or latent TB infection (LTBI). The program serves Baltimore City residents and anyone referred by a health care provider who needs TB consultation, evaluation, or treatment support.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: All TB services are provided free of charge. Services include nurse case management, expert medical TB management (lab work, sputum collection, imaging), TB medications for LTBI, and daily Directly Observed Therapy (DOT) for active TB. Referrals to outside services and providers are also available. Contact investigations are conducted for all infectious active TB cases. Diagnostic testing is limited to chest X-rays, sputum AFB smear, and sputum mycobacterial culture.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Individuals with active TB disease, latent TB infection (LTBI), or those at high risk (e.g., HIV-positive, immunocompromised, recently incarcerated, homeless, recent immigrants, contacts of active TB cases) who need TB evaluation, treatment, or medication and may lack insurance or face other barriers to care.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: TB case management, lab work, imaging, TB medications, and Directly Observed Therapy (DOT).
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Baltimore City. Services are provided at the Eastern Chest Clinic, 1200 E. Fayette Street, Baltimore, MD 21202.
requirements_list: Individuals must have confirmed or clinically diagnosed active TB, presumptive TB, or diagnosed LTBI
Complete diagnostic evaluation must be completed prior to referral
Identified clinical provider for future evaluation/care
Referrals for LTBI must involve one of the following: no insurance to pay for TB medications, barriers to evaluation, high-risk status, or recent immigration from a TB-endemic country
Active TB cases must be referred immediately to the Baltimore City Health Department
Appointments required — no walk-ins accepted
Pre-employment TB screening (skin test/PPD, chest X-rays) is not provided
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Health care providers or individuals can refer a patient by completing the TB Referral Form and either faxing it to 410-396-9403 (with relevant radiology reports, lab reports, and narrative notes) or submitting it electronically via the Qualtrics TB referral portal. For TB consultation services, call 410-396-9413.

structured_extraction.program_description: The City of Baltimore offers a variety of property tax credits to eligible property owners. A tax credit is an amount of money that taxpayers can subtract directly from the taxes they owe.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Property tax credits are subtracted directly from the property taxes owed by eligible property owners in Baltimore City.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Eligible property owners in Baltimore City
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Reduction of property tax liability
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Baltimore City only
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Apply through the Online Tax Credit Application System at https://propertytaxcredits.baltimorecity.gov/PropertyTaxCredits/

structured_extraction.program_name: Baltimore Clean Air Act Air Monitoring Contractor Certification
structured_extraction.program_description: The Baltimore City Health Department certifies entities to serve as Air Monitoring Contractors under the Baltimore Clean Air Act. Certified contractors are authorized to be hired by regulated Commercial Solid Waste Incinerators in Baltimore City to design, install, operate, and maintain continuous emissions monitoring systems (CEMS), report emissions data and violations, display and archive data on a public website, and conduct periodic inspections.
eligible_industries: Administrative and Support and Waste Management and Remediation Services
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Certification to operate as an Air Monitoring Contractor in Baltimore City, authorizing the entity to be hired by regulated Commercial Solid Waste Incinerators and comparable facilities. Certified contractors design, install, operate, and maintain CEMS, manage public environmental data reporting, and conduct periodic inspections. Applicants may be a single contractor, a single contractor with subcontractors, or a partnership of co-applicants. An application fee was pending Board of Estimates approval as of September 5, 2019.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Entities capable of designing, installing, operating, and maintaining continuous emissions monitoring systems (CEMS) and providing related air quality monitoring and reporting services for commercial solid waste incinerators, medical waste incinerators, and comparable facilities in Baltimore City.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Not applicable — this is a certification program, not a funding program. Certified contractors provide CEMS installation, operation, maintenance, emissions reporting, public data dissemination, and periodic inspections for regulated incinerators.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Baltimore City only. Contractors must serve regulated Commercial Solid Waste Incinerators located within Baltimore City. Applicant inspection staff must be reasonably close in proximity to Baltimore City.
requirements_list: Must be capable of providing all required services including CEMS design, installation, operation, and maintenance
Must be capable of performing regular inspections to identify tampering and ensure proper operation
Must be able to develop software to capture and disseminate CEMS and stack test data (historical and current)
Must not have a conflict of interest as defined in § 8-124(b) of the Baltimore City Health Code
May apply as a single contractor, single contractor with subcontractors, or a partnership of co-applicants
Maryland Workers' Compensation Certificate of Compliance or insurance policy/binder number
Experience with data feeds to off-site locations
Web design and data management capability
Access to equipment for monitoring specified pollutants (dioxins/furans, CO2, CO, HCl, HF, NOx, SO2, PM, VOCs, PAHs, metals)
Staff availability for inspections when needed
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Submit an application using the Air Monitoring Contractor Application form available on the Baltimore City website. The Baltimore City Health Department reviews applications and certifies qualifying entities.

structured_extraction.program_description: Offers grants, zero-interest loans, and small business support to small businesses in Baltimore.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Grants, zero-interest loans, and small business support services for small businesses in Baltimore.

structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Small business startup and growth

structured_extraction.program_description: The Baltimore Financial Empowerment Center provides free, one-on-one financial counseling and coaching to Baltimore City residents of any income level. Professionally trained and certified counselors help residents manage money, pay down debt, increase savings, build credit, access affordable banking products, and plan for their legacy including wills, Power of Attorney, and probate.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Free in-person and remote one-on-one financial counseling sessions. structured_extraction.program_name: Baltimore's Homelessness and Housing Initiative – Housing Accelerator Fund and HOME-ARP (ARPA-Funded)
structured_extraction.program_description: A joint funding initiative led by the Mayor's Office of Homeless Services (MOHS), Baltimore City Department of Housing & Community Development (DHCD), and the Mayor's Office of Recovery Programs (MORP) using American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) and HUD HOME-ARP federal funding to reduce homelessness and expand affordable housing in Baltimore City. The Housing Accelerator Fund provides grants to construct permanent supportive housing (PSH) that combines affordable housing, health care, and supportive services, helping individuals and families who are homeless, formerly homeless, or otherwise unable to maintain housing stability. The Housing Accelerator Fund and HOME-ARP Notice of Funding Availability invests nearly $30 million — $15.2 million in State and Local Fiscal Recovery Funds (SLFRF) and $14.7 million in HOME-ARP funds — to support the creation of permanent supportive housing and traditional affordable housing for people experiencing homelessness or in need of extra support services. Total combined ARPA and HOME-ARP funding for the Housing Accelerator Fund is approximately $32.5 million. The broader initiative also includes projects for non-congregate emergency housing, housing navigation, and shelter demobilization, with nearly $200 million in total ARPA funding. Grant awards totaling $29.8 million were announced on March 11, 2024.
eligible_industries: Real Estate and Rental and Leasing
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Nearly $200 million in total ARPA funding and $15.4 million in HUD HOME-ARP funding support multiple projects: $42.3 million for non-congregate emergency housing for people experiencing homelessness; $7.6 million for housing navigation and landlord recruitment support; $5.5 million for shelter demobilization; and approximately $29.8–$32.5 million combined ARPA and HOME-ARP for the Housing Accelerator Fund to create permanent supportive housing and traditional affordable housing. Housing Accelerator Fund awards include up to $250,000 per unit for permanent supportive housing construction, up to $100,000 per unit for traditional affordable housing construction, and up to $500,000 for predevelopment costs associated with funded units. Affordability restrictions: 15 years at 30% AMI (Housing Accelerator); 20 years for new construction/rehab (HOME-ARP). Grant awards were announced on March 11, 2024.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Baltimore City residents experiencing homelessness or housing insecurity, as well as developers, nonprofit organizations, government entities, and service providers seeking to build permanent supportive housing or traditional affordable housing in Baltimore City.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Emergency non-congregate housing, housing navigation and landlord recruitment, shelter demobilization, and construction of permanent supportive housing and traditional affordable housing, including predevelopment costs associated with funded units, as well as creating homes with support services for people who need extra support. Eligible costs include architectural and engineering fees, environmental assessment and testing, market analysis, carrying costs, legal fees, acquisition, rehabilitation, new construction, demolition, personnel and consultant costs, and construction costs (including prevailing wage, Davis Bacon, Section 3 requirements). Housing must integrate affordable housing, health care, and supportive services.

Provide evidence of insurance prior to commitment letter (Directors and Officers Liability, Commercial General Liability, E&O, Blanket Crime Coverage, Automobile, Payment and Performance Bonds)
Meet MORP reporting requirements
Subject to final underwriting by DHCD and Board of Estimates approval
Identify confidential/proprietary information per Maryland Public Information Act
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: A Notice of Funding Availability (NOFA) was announced beginning September 6, 2023, by DHCD and MOHS for the construction of permanent supportive housing. For the Housing Accelerator Fund and HOME-ARP NOFA, applications were submitted through the Neighborly application portal (portal.neighborlysoftware.com/baltimoremd); the portal opened October 20, 2023 and the deadline was November 20, 2023. Applications are available on the DHCD website; revisions and addenda are posted on the DHCD website periodically. Award amounts are determined by the Housing Commissioner and final awards are subject to underwriting and Board of Estimates approval. Grant awards totaling $29.8 million were announced on March 11, 2024. A PSH Hotel Conversion application round has already selected an awardee (Sojourner Place at the Falls). Other projects (e.g., PSH Hotel Conversion) have separate competitive application processes. See MOHS and DHCD websites for details on individual funding opportunities.

structured_extraction.program_name: CFY 2027 Transportation Services Request for Proposals (RFP)
structured_extraction.program_description: A recurring grant program from Baltimore City's Mayor's Office of Homeless Services (MOHS) that funds organizations providing free transportation services to individuals and families experiencing homelessness in Baltimore City during City Fiscal Year 2027 (July 1, 2026 – June 30, 2027). Both new and renewal proposals are accepted. Providers transport homeless people to 8-10 designated city-funded shelters and other community service locations within the Baltimore Continuum of Care, with pick-up and drop-off services at 11-15 designated stops throughout the day. Service hours are 6:45 AM – 11:00 AM and 3:00 PM – 9:00 PM, with additional services during Code Blue and Code Red declarations. Priority is given based on vulnerability and severity of need. Services must be available during both the winter shelter period (October 15 through March 31) and the non-winter shelter period (April 1 through October 14). Funding is awarded through a competitive Request for Proposals process using Baltimore City General Funds, with an estimated $400,000 available for CFY 2027.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Competitive grant funding through a Request for Proposals process, funded by Baltimore City General Funds. Estimated $400,000 available for CFY 2027 (July 1, 2026 – June 30, 2027). Payments are structured as a flat monthly rate inclusive of service and operating costs. Covers transportation services for homeless individuals and families traveling to 8-10 designated shelters and other homeless service program locations within the Baltimore Continuum of Care. Minimum vehicle requirements: 2-3 vehicles during non-Code Blue periods; minimum 4 vehicles during Code Blue with 2 replacements on standby. Vehicles must have minimum 12-seat capacity.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Non-profit 501(c)(3) organizations, eligible for-profit business entities, city agencies, and other organizations (new and renewal applicants) that can provide transportation services to homeless individuals and families in Baltimore City. Includes religious organizations (with restrictions). End beneficiaries are single adults and families experiencing homelessness, including older adults and persons with mobility issues.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Providing free transportation services to homeless individuals and families to shelters and other homeless service locations within the Baltimore Continuum of Care during City Fiscal Year 2027. Allowable costs include: vehicle operations and coordination (minimum 2-3 vehicles during non-Code Blue; minimum 4 vehicles during Code Blue with 2 replacements); personnel costs (staff, drivers); vehicle maintenance, fuel, and repairs; equipment and supplies (2-way radios, mobile devices, cleaning products); training programs; administrative costs; and insurance and liability coverage.

structured_extraction.program_name: CHAP Historic Restoration & Rehabilitation Tax Credit
structured_extraction.program_description: Baltimore City's Historic Tax Credit, administered by the Commission for Historical and Architectural Preservation (CHAP), provides a 10-year property tax credit to owners who rehabilitate historically designated properties in Baltimore City. Eligible properties must be located within one of Baltimore City's 38 designated local historic districts, be a designated Baltimore City Landmark (200+ landmark properties), individually listed on the National Register, or contribute to a recognized historic district or the Baltimore National Heritage Area. The project must invest at least 25% of the property's full cash value in qualifying rehabilitation work that meets CHAP Design Guidelines. The credit is computed on the increased assessed property value resulting from qualifying rehabilitation work, is calculated once and applied for the entire 10-year period, and is fully transferable to a new owner for the remaining life of the credit. Both residential and commercial properties are eligible. For projects with costs exceeding $3.5 million, applicants must submit specific appraisal, verification, and economic impact forms, and projects must also be reviewed and approved by the Baltimore City Department of Finance. The credit cannot be combined with any other Baltimore City property tax credit, but can be combined with Maryland Historic Revitalization Tax Credits and Federal Historic Preservation Tax Incentives.
eligible_industries: Real Estate and Rental and Leasing
structured_extraction.assistance_description: A 10-year property tax credit (listed as a 'Special Credit' on the tax bill) equal to the increased assessed property value resulting from qualifying historic rehabilitation or restoration work. For projects with construction costs of $5.0 million or less: 100% credit for Years 1-10. For projects with construction costs exceeding $5.0 million: 80% (Years 1-5), 70% (Year 6), 60% (Year 7), 50% (Year 8), 40% (Year 9), 30% (Year 10). The credit cannot reduce tax liability below the baseline established at preliminary approval. The credit appears on the next issued tax bill after CHAP issues final certification. The credit is fully transferable to a new owner for the remaining life of the credit. Projects under $3.5 million have two years to complete rehabilitation (with a one-time two-year extension available). Projects over $3.5 million have three years (with a one-time three-year extension). A $50 non-refundable review fee is required at application. For projects with costs exceeding $3.5 million, applicants must submit an Appraisal Narrative, Appraisal Spreadsheet, Enterprise Zone Verification Form, Affidavit of Vacancy Status, and Projected Economic Impact form via email to Tax.Credits@baltimorecity.gov, and the project must be reviewed and approved by the Baltimore City Department of Finance. The credit cannot be combined with any other Baltimore City property tax credit, but can be combined with Maryland Historic Revitalization Tax Credits and the Federal Historic Preservation Tax Incentives.
structured_extraction.application_deadline_string: No new applications for the tax credit may be filed after August 28, 2024
structured_extraction.program_audience: Owners of historically designated properties in Baltimore City who plan to rehabilitate those properties, including homeowners, businesses, developers, residential, commercial, and mixed-use building owners located within Baltimore City's 38 designated local historic districts or among its 200+ designated landmark properties.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Rehabilitation of historically designated properties in Baltimore City, including interior and exterior work that meets CHAP Design Guidelines. Eligible costs include materials, labor, and architect/engineering/design fees. Property acquisition costs, utility bills, property tax bills, and other holding costs are not eligible.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Must be located within Baltimore City. The property must be historically designated as a Baltimore City Landmark, individually listed on the National Register, contributing to one of Baltimore City's 38 designated local historic districts, contributing to a National Register Historic District, or contributing to the Baltimore National Heritage Area. Eligible areas encompass approximately 20% of Baltimore's land area, spanning 38 of Baltimore's 55 Community Statistical Areas (CSAs).

structured_extraction.application_process_overview: 1. Read the Tax Credit FAQ and Program Rules and Regulations. 2. Review the CHAP Design Guidelines. 3. Apply online at the CHAP Historic Tax Credit Application portal (paper applications are not accepted). Submit all required materials including color high-resolution photographs, plans, detailed scope of work, proof of ownership, appraisal, and pay the $50 non-refundable review fee online. 4. CHAP staff will review and issue approval in writing via email before any work begins. Preliminary certification must be received within 180 days of requesting it or the application expires. 5. For projects over $3.5 million, complete and email the required forms — Appraisal Narrative, Appraisal Spreadsheet, Enterprise Zone Verification Form, Affidavit of Vacancy Status, and Projected Economic Impact — to Tax.Credits@baltimorecity.gov, and ensure review and approval by the Baltimore City Department of Finance. 6. Upon project completion, submit final certification materials through the online system including completion photos, copies of permits, notarized cost documentation, and a final appraisal. After CHAP issues final certification, the credit will appear on the next property tax bill. Send questions to historictaxcredit@baltimorecity.gov or apply online through the Baltimore City Property Tax Credits portal at propertytaxcredits.baltimorecity.gov.

structured_extraction.program_description: The Casino Local Impact Funds (CLIF) Program distributes a portion of casino gaming revenues to benefit communities surrounding the Horseshoe Casino in South Baltimore. The Baltimore City Department of Planning manages these state-mandated funds and allocates them through annual spending plans to support infrastructure, public safety, sanitation, economic development, housing, and other community needs in the South Baltimore Gateway area. Spending plans are developed with input from City agencies, community partners, neighborhood associations, and the Local Development Council (LDC), an advisory group appointed by the Mayor. The program is guided by nine South Baltimore Gateway Master Plan goals. FY27 budget: $11,391,840 (plus $1,270,000 FY25 supplemental); FY26 budget: $8,372,000. Funded initiatives span transportation, environmental sustainability, safety, community development, economic growth, education, health and wellness, homelessness strategies, job training, youth programs, housing rehabilitation, and park improvements.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Funds are allocated through annual spending plans developed with the nine South Baltimore Gateway Master Plan goals as a foundation, in consultation with City agencies, Local Development Council (LDC) members, community partners, and neighborhood associations. Eligible uses include infrastructure investments, facilities, public safety, sanitation, economic and community development (including housing), environmental sustainability, park improvements, job training and employment services, youth programs, homelessness services, and other public services and investments. Grants to organizations up to $50K are available. Specific amounts and allocation details are available in the annual spending plan documents. FY27 budget: $11,391,840; FY26 budget: $8,372,000.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Organizations, city agencies, community partners, neighborhood associations, community development corporations, non-profits, low-income residents, homeless and housing-insecure individuals, job-seeking and underemployed individuals, youth, seniors, and homeowners serving or residing in the South Baltimore Gateway area surrounding the Horseshoe Casino
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Infrastructure investments, facilities, public safety, sanitation, economic and community development including housing, environmental sustainability and park improvements, transportation/complete streets projects, homelessness outreach and diversion services, job training and employment support, educational partnerships, health and wellness programs, housing code enforcement and homeowner support, community enhancement projects, youth programs, and other public services and investments aligned with the nine South Baltimore Gateway Master Plan goals

structured_extraction.program_description: The Baltimore City Health Department's Childhood Lead Poisoning Prevention Program works to reduce lead poisoning in Baltimore City through primary prevention, lead testing, home visits, case management, advocacy, and enforcement of the city's lead laws. The program offers preventive home visits, community education, point-of-care blood lead testing, and case management services for families with lead-poisoned children.

It also offers free point-of-care blood lead testing at community events, case management services for families of children with elevated blood lead levels (5 ug/dL or above), lead education, and legal enforcement actions against property owners with lead violations.

structured_extraction.program_description: Baltimore City Farms lets city residents rent garden plots in parks across Baltimore to grow vegetables, herbs, and flowers. The program is open to all skill levels, and beginners receive support from experienced gardeners along with tools, lessons, and guides. Gardens include amenities like water access, hoses, wheelbarrows, wood chips, and manure during the growing season.

structured_extraction.program_name: City of Baltimore Lead Hazard Reduction and Healthy Homes Program
structured_extraction.program_description: This program provides lead hazard control and healthy homes interventions for low- to moderate-income households in Baltimore City. It serves homes built before 1978 where children under age six (or children who spend significant time at the property) or pregnant women are present. The program assesses lead hazards and pays for interventions including window replacement, door replacement, wall stabilization, lead abatement, paint stabilization, dust wipe clearance, and minor structural repairs. Healthy homes assessments and interventions, outreach and education sessions, and home visits for education and referrals are also provided. Temporary relocation assistance and referrals to other programs are available. HUD funds $4,100,000 total ($3,600,000 Lead-Based Paint Hazard Control Grant and $500,000 Healthy Homes Supplemental) plus $1,516,000 in local match. Assistance is provided as a grant or loan depending on the applicant's income and financial status; landlords must contribute a portion of the cost. The grant period runs April 1, 2026 to April 1, 2030.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Funding is provided as either a grant or a loan depending on the applicant's income and financial status. HUD funds $4,100,000 total ($3,600,000 Lead-Based Paint Hazard Control Grant and $500,000 Healthy Homes Supplemental) plus $1,516,000 in local match. The program covers lead risk assessments in 200 units, lead hazard reduction in 100 units (window replacement, door replacement, abatement, paint stabilization, wall stabilization, dust wipe clearance), 100 healthy homes assessments, 80 healthy homes interventions, 40 outreach and education sessions, and home visits for education and referrals. Temporary relocation assistance and referrals to other programs are also provided. Both homeowners and landlords may apply; landlords are expected to contribute a portion of the cost. Income limits apply and vary by household size and whether the unit is owner-occupied or renter-occupied.

structured_extraction.program_name: City-Wide Affordable Housing Tax Increment Financing (TIF) District
structured_extraction.program_description: Baltimore City's Affordable Housing Tax Increment Financing (TIF) program, signed into law in December 2024, establishes a citywide, non-contiguous TIF district that issues bonds to fund affordable housing development across Baltimore City neighborhoods. Unlike traditional TIFs focused on specific neighborhoods, this program targets vacant properties in all parts of the city, including East and West Baltimore neighborhoods such as Broadway East, Harlem Park, Druid Heights, Park Heights, Upton, East Baltimore Midway, and Coldstream Homestead Montebello. Up to $150 million in TIF bonds are planned over time, with a first tranche of $65 million approved to rehabilitate approximately 3,900–4,000 vacant housing units. The program provides reimbursement grants for hard construction costs (roofing, framing, flooring, electrical, HVAC, plumbing, and similar items) to eligible developers, nonprofits, LLCs, and individual residents. Bond proceeds also fund homeowner grants to help residents qualify for newly rehabbed homes, public infrastructure improvements (sidewalks, parks, alleys, streets, curbs, gutters, lighting, landscaping, water and utilities), and financing to close home appraisal gaps so that rehabbed homes can be sold at affordable prices. The average TIF grant for housing construction is approximately $50,000, varying based on property size and condition, rental vs. homeownership use, affordability level, and appraisal gap. The total program budget for the first round is approximately $15–18 million, with approximately $3 million allocated to legacy residents, current TIF District residents, and small/emerging developers for privately-owned properties. Funds are provided on a reimbursement basis — applicants must pay costs upfront. The program prioritizes legacy residents, small and emerging developers, and women- and minority-owned businesses, and supports homeownership as a means of building generational wealth and strengthening the City's tax base. Homes can serve households earning up to 115% of area median income (approximately $149,845 for a household of four as of 2025), with priority given to projects serving households at 60% and 80% of AMI. Affordability must be maintained for 5 years from initial occupancy. Only properties included in City Council Bill 24-0595 (City-Wide Affordable Housing Development District) — a total of 3,991 vacant properties identified for redevelopment — are eligible. Bond repayment comes from increased property tax revenues generated by rising property assessments within the TIF district. This program is part of a broader $3 billion vacancy reduction and community redevelopment initiative supported by $300 million from Baltimore City and $900 million from Maryland State. Part of dual legislative initiatives: 24-0594 (Bond Issuance) and 24-0595 (Development District). Established by Ordinance 24-443.
eligible_industries: Real Estate and Rental and Leasing
structured_extraction.assistance_description: TIF bonds totaling up to $150 million are planned, authorized in phases, with the first tranche of $65 million authorized and a total first-round program budget of approximately $15–18 million, with approximately $3 million allocated to legacy residents, current TIF District residents, and small/emerging developers for privately-owned properties. The average TIF grant for housing construction is approximately $50,000, varying based on property size and condition, rental vs. homeownership use, affordability level, and appraisal gap. No set dollar amount per property; based on project financing gap. Developer fee estimated at approximately 12%. Funds are awarded as reimbursement grants for: hard construction costs to redevelop vacant buildings (including excavation, demolition, grading, foundations, framing, roofing, flooring, interior/exterior finishes, mechanical and electrical systems, elevators, fire protection, telecommunications cabling, roofs, doors, windows, porch repair, drywall, and other fixed building equipment such as HVAC and plumbing); public infrastructure required for new city-sponsored homeownership development projects (sidewalks, parks, alleys, streets, curbs, gutters, lighting, landscaping, water and utilities); homeowner grants to help buyers qualify for newly rehabbed homes; and financing to close home appraisal gaps. Funds are provided on a reimbursement basis — applicants must pay costs upfront. Multiple reimbursement requests allowed with proper documentation. Reimbursement can be requested either upon full project completion or through a draw schedule (up to two draws for 90% of approved costs, then a draw upon Use and Occupancy permit, then a draw upon occupancy). Cannot be used for soft costs, architectural/engineering fees, interest, or costs incurred before a grant agreement is executed. Grantees must complete construction and obtain a Use and Occupancy permit within 12 months of executing a grant agreement. Homes can serve households earning up to 115% of AMI, with priority given to projects serving households at 60% and 80% of AMI. Affordability must be maintained for 5 years from initial occupancy. Bond repayment comes from increased property tax revenues generated by rising property assessments in the TIF district. Funding from the first tranche of TIF bonds is expected to begin deployment in the second half of 2025, after City sells TIF Bonds (expected December) and grantees execute Grant Agreement with City.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Baltimore City homeowners and prospective homeowners seeking to purchase rehabbed affordable homes, as well as developers, nonprofits, LLCs, small and emerging developers (completed no more than 5 capital development projects), women- and minority-owned businesses, legacy residents, established development organizations, community organizations, BVRI awardees, licensed contractors, and other entities seeking to rehabilitate or redevelop vacant properties in Baltimore City into affordable housing in targeted neighborhoods including Broadway East, Harlem Park, Druid Heights, Park Heights, Upton, East Baltimore Midway, and Coldstream Homestead Montebello. Prioritizes legacy residents earning at or below 60% of area median income and first-time and emerging developers.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Hard construction costs for redeveloping vacant buildings (excavation, demolition, grading, foundations, framing, roofing, flooring, interior/exterior finishes, mechanical and electrical systems including HVAC and plumbing, elevators, fire protection, telecommunications cabling, roofs, doors, windows, porch repair, drywall, and other fixed building equipment); public infrastructure required for new city-sponsored homeownership development projects (sidewalks, parks, alleys, streets, curbs, gutters, lighting, landscaping, water and utilities); homeowner grants to help buyers qualify for newly rehabbed homes; financing to close home appraisal gaps to enable affordable housing projects to move forward; and conversion of vacant properties into community green space. Cannot be used for soft costs, architectural/engineering fees, interest, or costs incurred before a grant agreement is executed. Supports both rental and homeownership, with emphasis on homeownership.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available citywide across all of Baltimore City, including East and West Baltimore neighborhoods, with a focus on historically disinvested communities. Eligibility can be verified using the Baltimore Affordable Housing TIF property locator map (green dot on the map). The TIF district encompasses approximately 4,000 properties in designated neighborhoods across Baltimore City, including Broadway East, Harlem Park, Druid Heights, Park Heights, Upton, East Baltimore Midway, and Coldstream Homestead Montebello.
