Neighborhoods covered include Broadway East, Harlem Park, Druid Heights, Park Heights, Upton, East Baltimore Midway, and Coldstream Homestead Montebello
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Properties available for open application are identified with each bond series. Applicants should check the DHCD website for available properties and open application rounds. Complete and submit the full application through the Neighborly Platform. Applicants on the Developer Registry or with a Land Disposition Agreement (LDA) are evaluated only for threshold requirements and are not scored competitively. All others are scored competitively. Applications are reviewed by DHCD and the City's Bond Counsel to confirm eligibility and determine award amounts. Some properties are pre-assigned to established development projects or issued via Request for Proposals/Qualifications. Awarded applicants receive an Award Letter, then must execute a Grant Agreement with DHCD. Reimbursement requests are submitted with documentation of completed work verified by a third-party inspector. Funding from the first tranche of TIF bonds is expected to begin deployment in the second half of 2025, after City sells TIF Bonds (expected December). For language assistance requests, contact Scott Davis at ScottC.Davis@baltimorecity.gov. For more information, visit baltimorecity.gov/finance/affordable-housing-tif-overview or Reframe Baltimore at reframebaltimore.com.

structured_extraction.program_description: A neighborhood beautification competition and grant program taking place summer 2026. Clean Corps provides up to $1,500 financial support for block-level cleaning and beautification projects in Baltimore City, drawing inspiration from historic AFRO Clean Block competitions (started 1934) to help residents create healthy and beautiful neighborhoods. Features three award categories: Youth Power, Small but Mighty, and Best Community Glo-up.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Grants of up to $1,500 per project to support block-level cleaning and beautification efforts. Financial support, supplies, technical expertise, and organizing support are provided. Up to 20% of funds may be used for refreshments.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Community organizations and residents in Baltimore City, including nonprofits, faith-based organizations, neighborhood associations, schools, and under- and unemployed city residents and youth
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Trash collection and/or beautification elements (art, plants, lights, seating), volunteer stipends for youth, planting events, weekly clean-up events, community events and activations, supplies for cleaning and beautification, volunteer incentives and marketing costs, and food and drinks for events (up to 20% of funds)
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Baltimore City residents and organizations; all neighborhoods are eligible, with priority given to Clean Corps service areas across 42 neighborhoods in Baltimore
requirements_list: Must be a Baltimore City resident or community-based organization (nonprofit, faith-based organization, neighborhood association, school, or other organization)
Project must involve cleaning or beautifying streets, alleys, or greenspaces at the block level
Priority given to organizations and residents in Clean Corps service areas (42 neighborhoods across Baltimore)
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Complete the interest form available as a PDF or Word document linked on the program page and submit it to apply.

structured_extraction.program_description: The Mayor's Office of Homeless Services (MOHS) coordinates emergency hypothermia shelter and related services for Baltimore City residents experiencing homelessness when nighttime temperatures with wind chill drop to 32°F or below. The program operates warming centers, overnight emergency shelter, and transportation assistance during the winter season. MOHS coordinates efforts between the City of Baltimore and community-based organizations to provide hypothermia shelters and life-saving services, including food services, street outreach, housing navigation, and behavioral health services. Operates November 15, 2025 to March 15, 2026 (may activate before/after for extreme weather).
structured_extraction.assistance_description: When activated (when wind chill reaches 32°F or below), the program provides: overnight emergency shelter from 4:00 pm to 9:00 am at multiple locations across Baltimore City; daytime warming centers operated by Continuum of Care providers; transportation assistance with pick-up and drop-off at designated locations; food and hot beverages; case management; street outreach with survival items; housing navigation consultations; crisis stabilization services; and behavioral health and health/sobering services. Shelter-in-place is provided when temperatures are 20°F or below at the time of morning release. The program operates November 15, 2025 through March 15, 2026.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Baltimore City residents experiencing homelessness, particularly those living unsheltered during cold weather
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Emergency overnight shelter, daytime warming center access, transportation assistance, food and hot beverages, case management, street outreach, housing navigation, and behavioral health/crisis stabilization services during cold weather events
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Baltimore City only
requirements_list: Must be experiencing homelessness in Baltimore City
Must contact the Baltimore City Shelter Hotline (443-984-9540) to connect to emergency overnight shelter when winter shelter is activated
Winter shelter is activated when temperature with wind chill reaches 32°F or below
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Call the Baltimore City Shelter Hotline at 443-984-9540 (Monday–Friday 8:30 am–9:00 pm; Saturday–Sunday 4:00 pm–9:00 pm) to get connected to emergency shelter. For requests between 9:00 pm and midnight, call the Winter Shelter Hotline at 443-695-7378. For crisis information and referral, call 410-433-5175. Walk-in access is available at warming center locations during their posted hours when winter shelter is activated.

structured_extraction.program_description: A 12-week, paid, in-person leadership course for residents and local leaders in Baltimore's Northern District. Participants build practical skills in community development, violence prevention, environmental design, and neighborhood improvement. They also have the opportunity to design and implement grant-funded neighborhood improvement projects in their own communities.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Participants receive a paid, 12-week in-person leadership course covering community organizing, environmental design, public safety strategy, storytelling, grant writing, project planning, and data-informed problem solving. Participants also have the opportunity to design and implement grant-funded neighborhood improvement projects in their own communities. Sessions run from May 18 through August 7, 2026.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Residents and small business owners in Baltimore's Northern District who are passionate about community change and ready to take an active leadership role in their neighborhoods.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Grant-funded neighborhood improvement projects designed and implemented by participants within their own communities.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Applicants must be located in Baltimore City's Northern Police District.
requirements_list: Must be located in Baltimore City's Northern District
Interested in community development, violence prevention, and neighborhood improvement
Committed to taking an active leadership role in their neighborhood
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Apply online via the Microsoft Forms application link before May 3, 2026. Applicants can also attend virtual or in-person information sessions to learn more before applying.

structured_extraction.program_description: DHCD's Community Catalyst Grants program complements the Neighborhood Impact Investment Fund and supports locally-driven community development work through neighborhood-based partner organizations.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Grants to neighborhood-based partner organizations to support locally-driven community development work in Baltimore City.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Neighborhood-based partner organizations engaged in community development in Baltimore City.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Locally-driven community development work.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Baltimore City only.

structured_extraction.program_description: Baltimore City CERT is a free training program that teaches volunteers how to prepare for and respond to emergencies and disasters. Participants learn basic disaster prevention, fire safety, light search and rescue, team organization, communications, and emergency medical procedures. Trained members can volunteer with the Baltimore City Office of Emergency Management to support outreach, emergency response, and recovery operations.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Free two-day in-person training course (8 hours per day) covering disaster preparedness, fire safety, search and rescue, team organization, communications, and emergency medical procedures. Members also participate in quarterly in-person and hybrid training sessions and informational meetings throughout the year.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Baltimore City residents or workers who are at least 18 years of age and want to help their families, neighbors, and community during emergencies.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Not applicable — this is a training program, not a funding program.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Must live or work in Baltimore City, Maryland.
requirements_list: Must live or work in Baltimore City
Must be at least 18 years of age
Register for a FEMA Student Identification number (SID)
Complete an in-person CERT Training Course
Complete online courses: CERT and the Incident Command System (IS-315.a) and Introduction to Community Emergency Response Team (IS-317.a)
Support at least one OEM-sponsored preparedness and outreach event per year
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Register for a FEMA SID at the DHS website, then enroll in and complete an in-person CERT training course. Training dates are listed on the program page with links to register via Eventbrite or directly through the hosting organization.

structured_extraction.program_name: Community Land Trusts - Homeownership & Rental NOFAs (2022)
structured_extraction.program_description: Baltimore City's Affordable Housing Trust Fund issued two separate grants — one for CLT rental housing (up to $1.5 million) and one for CLT homeownership projects (up to $4.0 million) — to promote equitable community development and address affordable housing demand in historically disinvested communities. Funds support perpetually affordable housing through a shared equity model. Both application periods closed on September 2, 2022.
eligible_industries: Real Estate and Rental and Leasing
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Grants from the Affordable Housing Trust Fund: Rental NOFA offers up to $1.5 million total (up to $750,000 per project); Homeownership NOFA offers up to $4.0 million total (up to $1,000,000 per project, up to $50,000/unit at ≤50% AMI or $100,000/unit at ≤30% AMI, up to 50% or 66% of Total Development Cost respectively). Up to 25% advancement for predevelopment/acquisition costs and up to 20% of award for operating costs. Funds distributed on reimbursement basis following Board of Estimates approval. DHCD takes a security interest in funded projects. Both application periods closed on September 2, 2022.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Community Land Trust organizations (nonprofit, 501(c)(2)/(3)/(4)) sponsoring rental or homeownership housing projects in Baltimore City; CLTs must be registered as Affordable Housing Land Trusts with Maryland Department of Assessments and Taxation and partner with an experienced developer
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Project development and construction; site acquisition and control; personnel and consultant costs; architecture and engineering fees; community engagement; sustainability features; marketing and sales; local hiring and apprenticeship programs; predevelopment costs
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Projects must be located in Baltimore City, with preference for projects in historically underserved communities experiencing blight and alignment with community/neighborhood revitalization plans
requirements_list: Applicant must be a Community Land Trust (CLT) organized or managed by a nonprofit exempt under §501(c)(2), (3), or (4) of the Internal Revenue Code
CLT must be registered as an Affordable Housing Land Trust with Maryland Department of Assessments and Taxation
CLT applicants must partner with an experienced developer who has completed at least five (5) development projects
Site control documentation required at submission; title must be obtained within 12 months of Funding Agreement execution
Conceptual site plan showing location, amenities, sustainability features, current parks/green spaces
Personnel budget and consultant list (if requesting funds for these)
Management Team documentation with current projects list
Zoning/development requirement compliance; documentation of pre-development meeting with Department of Planning
Community engagement and participation documentation
Market study or analysis (completed within 12 months of submission)
Development budget with all funding sources, uses, and fund status
Letters of interest/commitment from all funding sources
Resumes and qualification statements of applicant and development team members
Marketing and sales pro-forma
At least half of rental NOFA funds must be spent on households earning 30% or less of AMI
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: The application period for both NOFAs closed on September 2, 2022 at 4:00 PM EST. Applications were submitted to DHCD and reviewed by an interagency review panel with scoring and ranking system. Awards are pending Board of Estimates approval. Funds are distributed on a reimbursement basis.

structured_extraction.program_name: Community Land Trusts - Operating Costs NOFA
structured_extraction.program_description: Baltimore City's Affordable Housing Trust Fund provided grants to cover operating costs for Community Land Trust (CLT) organizations. Up to $500,000 was available (up to $100,000 per CLT entity) to provide operational and capacity building support for CLTs that offer affordable housing to low- and very low-income households in Baltimore City.
eligible_industries: Real Estate and Rental and Leasing
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Grants from the Affordable Housing Trust Fund to cover CLT operating costs and capacity building. Total funding pool was up to $500,000, with a maximum of $100,000 per Community Land Trust entity. Eligible costs include personnel, predevelopment, organizational operating costs, market and financial feasibility analysis, carrying costs, financing and lender fees, legal fees, and project management staff.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Community Land Trust organizations providing affordable housing to low- and very low-income households (at or below 50% AMI) in Baltimore City
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: CLT operational costs and capacity building support, including market and financial feasibility analysis, carrying costs, financing and lender fees, legal fees associated with closing/financing/drafting CLT-required documents, project management staff, and general organizational operating costs
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Baltimore City
requirements_list: Applicant must be a Community Land Trust (CLT)
CLT must provide affordable housing to low- and very low-income households in Baltimore City
Must be a nonprofit organization exempt from taxation under § 501(c)(2), (3), or (4) of the Internal Revenue Code, or a legally organized business entity managed by such a nonprofit
Must serve residents at 50% or below area median income (AMI)
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Submit application by October 6, 2023 at 4:00 PM EST. Awards are subject to Board of Estimates approval. Contact DHCD.AHTFNOFA@baltimorecity.gov for inquiries.

structured_extraction.program_description: A city-funded initiative that expands Baltimore's capacity to reduce gun violence through non-law enforcement approaches. It funds community-based organizations providing outreach, mediation, violence intervention, hospital-based response, life coaching, and victim services. The program grew from 10 to at least 50 contracts with community organizations.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: City contracts awarded to community-based organizations for violence intervention services. Over $3 million has been allocated to hospital-based violence intervention programs alone. Funding is sourced in part from Baltimore's American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) investment.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Community-based organizations, hospitals, and other non-law enforcement entities providing violence intervention, outreach, mediation, life coaching, and victim services in Baltimore City.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Outreach and mediation services, hospital-based violence intervention, life coaching, victim services, and school-based violence intervention programs.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Baltimore City only.
requirements_list: Must provide violence intervention-related services such as outreach, mediation, hospital-based response, life coaching, or victim services
Must operate within Baltimore City
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: MONSE contracts directly with selected organizations. The page does not describe an open application process; contracting is conducted by the agency.

structured_extraction.program_description: Baltimore City's Department of Transportation (DOT) allows community groups to create projects in public spaces like streets, sidewalks, and alleys. Projects can improve neighborhood appearance, slow traffic, and create gathering spaces. Examples include painted street art, landscape plantings, planters and barriers, signage, parklets, and special installations like lighting or plazas. The community group is responsible for funding, building, and maintaining the project.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: DOT provides approval, oversight, and technical guidance for community groups to install placemaking projects in the public right-of-way. DOT reviews and approves designs, materials, and locations. The program does not provide funding — applicants must pay for their own projects. DOT's Planning Division can help community groups planning parklets.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Community groups including neighborhood associations, local businesses, nonprofits, and school parent groups who want to create projects in Baltimore City public spaces such as streets, sidewalks, alleys, and roadways.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Projects must be used for improvements in the public right-of-way, including painted street art, landscape plantings, planters and barriers for traffic calming, signage, parklets (temporary public spaces in parking spots), and special projects like plazas or public art installations.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available only within Baltimore City public right-of-way maintained by the Baltimore City Department of Transportation.
requirements_list: Applicant must pay for the project themselves
Submit a design rendering
Provide the location(s) of the project
List the materials to be used
Submit letters of support or signed petitions from adjacent occupants (60% of block occupants for mid-block projects; 60% of occupants of three properties in each direction for intersections)
Provide proof of property owner support from properties directly abutting the project
Provide proof that your organization is in good standing with the State of Maryland
Commercial liability insurance ($1 million per occurrence, $2 million aggregate) is required for parklets and special projects
Submit a maintenance plan for the project
Projects must not contain obscene, vulgar, or violent messages
Projects must comply with ADA accessibility requirements
Projects must not block sight distance or create roadway safety hazards
Projects must not include harmful or poisonous plants
Paint must be pre-approved by DOT (pre-approved options listed on the program page)
If traffic calming elements are included, they must be installed before the art is implemented
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Submit project designs and documents through the Community-Led Placemaking Program Application linked on the program page. If your project includes traffic calming elements, either submit a traffic calming request to 311 first and wait for installation, or hire a contractor to install the elements with DOT-approved plans. Once approved, DOT provides a written agreement outlining approval details, timeline, maintenance responsibilities, and special conditions.

structured_extraction.program_description: Baltimore City residents can sign up to receive a free monthly supply of condoms, HIV/STI prevention supplies, and sexual health and testing information mailed to their home in an unmarked envelope. The subscription renews automatically each month.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Free monthly subscription mailing of condoms, other HIV/STI prevention commodities, and sexual health and HIV/STI testing information in an unmarked envelope. The subscription renews automatically every month. Recipients must have a Baltimore City mailing address.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Baltimore City residents seeking free condoms and HIV/STI prevention supplies
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Free monthly supply of condoms and HIV/STI prevention commodities
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Must have a mailing address within Baltimore City
requirements_list: Must have a mailing address within Baltimore City
Must complete the confidential subscription form
Must renew subscription annually by emailing HIVSTI.condoms@baltimorecity.gov
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Fill out the confidential online form on the program page to start your free monthly subscription. To stop your subscription or change your address, email hivsti.condoms@baltimorecity.gov.

structured_extraction.program_description: The Mayor's Office of Homeless Services (MOHS) in Baltimore City administers an annual competitive grant program that allows qualified organizations to submit one consolidated application and be considered for multiple funding sources simultaneously. Awards support services for individuals and families who are at risk of homelessness, currently homeless, low-income and living with HIV or AIDS, or at risk of crises including those with behavioral health needs. Funded programs may provide emergency shelter, drop-in/day centers, transitional housing, HIV/AIDS housing and services, permanent supportive housing, rapid re-housing, street outreach, housing stabilization, homelessness prevention, eviction prevention, and comprehensive street outreach services. Funding is drawn from multiple sources including: HUD Emergency Solutions Grant (ESG), State of Maryland Homeless Solutions Program (HSP), Baltimore City Department of Social Services (DSS) funds, HUD Housing Opportunities for Persons with AIDS/HIV (HOPWA), Maryland Department of Health State Special Funds (SSF), Baltimore City Opioid Restitution Fund, and Baltimore City General Funds. The program recurs annually, with each fiscal year cycle covering a July 1–June 30 performance period. The most recent open cycle is FY 2027, with applications due March 20, 2026.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Competitive grants drawn from multiple funding sources including HUD Emergency Solutions Grant (ESG), State of Maryland Homeless Solutions Program (HSP), Baltimore City Department of Social Services (DSS) funds, HUD Housing Opportunities for Persons with AIDS/HIV (HOPWA), Maryland Department of Health State Special Funds (SSF), Baltimore City Opioid Restitution Fund, and Baltimore City General Funds. Project grants typically fall between $25,000 and $150,000, with total anticipated funding of approximately $20,446,394 (FY2024 cycle) and $22,436,354 (FY2025 cycle) and approximately $22.2 million (FY2026 cycle). Grant performance periods run July 1 through June 30 of the applicable fiscal year (e.g., July 1, 2026–June 30, 2027 for FY 2027).
structured_extraction.program_audience: Qualified organizations (non-profits and government agencies) providing services to individuals and families who are at risk of homelessness, currently homeless, low-income and living with HIV or AIDS, or at risk of crises including those with behavioral health needs in Baltimore City. Also includes unaccompanied youth and young adults experiencing homelessness or at-risk (including those aging out of foster care ages 18-24), domestic violence survivors, and persons with behavioral health needs including mental illness and substance use disorders.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Homeless services including emergency shelter, drop-in/day centers, transitional housing, street outreach, comprehensive street outreach, rapid re-housing, permanent supportive housing, housing stabilization, homelessness prevention, eviction prevention, and housing and services for people with HIV/AIDS. Eligible costs include personnel/labor, case management, supportive services, temporary financial assistance (rental assistance, security deposits, utilities), emergency medical/mental health services, transportation, food, housing costs, office supplies, facility lease/rental costs, travel and mileage, in-kind donations and volunteer coordination, staff training (conflict resolution, de-escalation, cultural competency, trauma-informed care), meal provision, legal services, substance abuse treatment, employment assistance, life skills training, and lodging vouchers.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Services must be provided in Baltimore City.

Must serve individuals and families in Baltimore City
Must submit all application materials via the Neighborly portal or by email in earlier cycles
Must have an authorized individual certify and submit the application

Joint applications accepted with lead agency and subrecipient structure
Fair Housing Agreement signature required

Coordinated Access participation required

Employ Baltimore compliance for contracts $50,001–$300,001

structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Create an account and log into the Neighborly portal (portal.neighborlysoftware.com/MOHS-BALTIMOREMD/Participant). Add two points of contact for your organization. Complete all application questions (which differ for new vs. renewal applicants), including the Application Cover Sheet & Narrative (PDF format). Complete the appropriate budget workbook template for the project type (e.g., emergency shelter, transitional housing, street outreach, rapid re-housing, permanent supportive housing, housing stabilization/homelessness prevention, or HIV/AIDS housing and services). Supplemental Word documents aligned with Appendix A Scope of Work may be submitted if additional characters are needed. Have an authorized individual upload all materials, certify, and submit the application by the stated deadline. Neighborly will send an automated confirmation upon receipt. A Bidder's Conference webinar is held prior to each cycle's deadline, with recordings and FAQs available. Applications are reviewed the following month, with conditional award notifications sent approximately two months after the deadline.

structured_extraction.program_description: The Mayor's Office of Homeless Services (MOHS), in partnership with the Baltimore City Continuum of Care, sought proposals from one qualified collaborative applicant to address and reduce homelessness by adding new units of permanent supportive housing (PSH) through new construction, acquisition, or rehabilitation. The program makes approximately $175 million available nationally under HUD's CoC Builds funding, with approximately $110 million reserved for CoCs in states with populations over 2.5 million (including Baltimore City CoC, MD-501). The selected applicant was expected to provide both supportive services and property management services, either within one organization or via a memorandum of understanding (MOU) between two or more organizations. Funding supports individuals and families experiencing homelessness where at least one household member has a disability.
eligible_industries: Real Estate and Rental and Leasing
structured_extraction.assistance_description: One-time grant award from HUD's CoC Builds program, with approximately $110 million of the total $175 million reserved for CoCs in states with populations over 2.5 million (including Baltimore City CoC, MD-501). Awards range from $1,000,000 to $10,000,000. Funds support capital costs for new construction, acquisition, or rehabilitation of permanent supportive housing (PSH) units. Up to 20% of budget may be used for other eligible CoC Program costs (supportive services, operating costs, project-based rental assistance, case management). Up to 10% of budget for project administration. Non-capital costs may be eligible for renewal through annual CoC Program Competition. A 25% match requirement applies (of awarded grant amount minus leasing funds); match can be cash or in-kind resources.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Organizations or qualified collaborative applicants that can serve as developer, property manager, and service provider (or a partnership via MOU) for permanent supportive housing in Baltimore City, seeking to develop housing for people experiencing homelessness, including people experiencing chronic homelessness, seniors, veterans, families with children, youth (18-24), persons living with disabilities, mental illness, substance use disorder, domestic violence, or HIV/AIDS
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: New construction, acquisition, or rehabilitation of permanent supportive housing (PSH) units; project-based rental assistance; supportive services (case management, life skills, health care, mental health services, substance use treatment, etc.); operating costs (maintenance, property tax, insurance, utilities); project administrative costs (up to 10%); program reporting and evaluation; building improvements and property development
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Baltimore City, Maryland (Baltimore City Continuum of Care, MD-501). Project must be consistent with HUD-approved Consolidated Plan and align with City of Baltimore 2021-2025 Consolidated Plan.

structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Applicants submitted a written proposal electronically (one PDF) by October 18, 2024 at 3:00 pm EST to BaltimorePSH@lesardevelopment.com. The application narrative must be submitted using the provided Application Template with eligible costs entered in specified tables. Match funding documentation and commitment letters must be included. If using in-kind services, provide MOU or partner agency commitment letter. MOHS and the CoC Board reviewed and scored proposals, conducted interviews if needed, and may request additional information for clarification. MOHS issued final award notices. The selected applicant's CoCBuilds application was then submitted to HUD via grants.gov by November 21, 2024.

structured_extraction.program_description: An annual federal grant competition administered by HUD that funds nonprofit organizations and state and local governments to reduce homelessness by providing housing and support services. Baltimore City participates in this competition through its Mayor's Office of Homeless Services to fund local projects focused on rapid re-housing, permanent supportive housing, and Homeless Management Information System (HMIS) improvements. More than 75% of CoC funding in Baltimore City goes to Permanent Supportive Housing, which combines long-term housing subsidies with supportive services for people who are chronically homeless.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Annual competitive federal grants for permanent housing (including Permanent Supportive Housing with long-term housing subsidies and supportive services), rapid re-housing, supportive services only, and HMIS projects serving people experiencing homelessness. Over 75% of funds support programs providing both housing and services to people who have been homeless for an extended period. HUD releases a Notice of Funding Availability (NOFA) annually; communities typically have 60–75 days to apply.
structured_extraction.application_deadline_string: Changes each year; communities typically have 60 to 75 days after the annual NOFA release to submit applications.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Nonprofit organizations and state and local government agencies providing homeless services in Baltimore City, serving homeless individuals and families.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Permanent housing, rapid re-housing, supportive services, and HMIS improvements for people experiencing homelessness.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Baltimore City
requirements_list: Projects must align with HUD's funding priorities
Projects must address community needs
Must use Coordinated Entry system
Must follow a Housing First approach
Must address racial inequalities in program access and promote equal access regardless of race
Must use proven methods and track results using data to evaluate program effectiveness
Must coordinate with mainstream services
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: HUD releases a Notice of Funding Availability (NOFA) each year. Baltimore City's Mayor's Office of Homeless Services coordinates the local competition during the application window (approximately 60–75 days after NOFA release). Applicants submit applications for either renewal or new projects. Baltimore City selects projects to submit to HUD's national competition.

structured_extraction.program_description: Trained Coordinated Access Navigators help individuals and families experiencing homelessness gather the information needed to complete housing applications.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Navigators assist individuals and families experiencing homelessness with collecting required information and completing housing applications.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Individuals and families experiencing homelessness in Baltimore City.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Application navigation support to help secure housing.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Baltimore City
requirements_list: Must be experiencing homelessness
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Find a Navigator through the linked page.

structured_extraction.program_description: MONSE (Mayor's Office of Neighborhood Safety and Engagement) deploys coordinated responses in select Baltimore City neighborhoods following traumatic events such as mass shootings, youth-involved shootings, police-involved shootings, major law enforcement takedowns, and rapid response situations. The program brings together government agencies and community partners to address quality-of-life issues and help residents recover from trauma. Each response is tailored to the specific community's needs and can last up to 45 days or longer.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Coordinated neighborhood stabilization responses lasting up to 45 days (or longer in special cases), tailored to each community. Responses address direct and residual trauma using data from 211, 311, and 911 systems, and involve agency and community partners addressing community-identified quality-of-life issues.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Baltimore City residents and neighborhoods affected by traumatic events such as mass shootings, youth-involved shootings, police-involved shootings, major law enforcement takedowns, and rapid response situations.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Addressing direct and residual trauma, and resolving community-identified quality-of-life issues following qualifying traumatic events.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available in select Baltimore City neighborhoods on a proactive or reactive basis following qualifying traumatic events.
requirements_list: Neighborhood must be affected by a qualifying activation event: mass shooting, youth-involved shooting, police-involved shooting, major law enforcement takedown, or rapid response situation
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: MONSE activates responses proactively or reactively based on qualifying events. Communities do not apply directly; MONSE coordinates using 211, 311, and 911 data.

structured_extraction.program_description: CEAS is a pre-event credentialing program that helps businesses quickly access their facilities after a major emergency or disaster. It issues secure ID cards recognized by the Baltimore Police Department, allowing critical employees to enter restricted areas so they can assess damage, maintain IT systems, meet regulatory obligations, and secure vital records.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Businesses receive a secure identification card that allows credentialed employees to access restricted areas following a declared emergency or disaster in Baltimore City. This enables rapid business recovery by permitting entry to affected work sites during emergency travel restrictions or access limitations.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Baltimore-based businesses of all types and sizes that want to maintain access to their facilities and quickly recover following a major emergency or disaster.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Access to restricted areas after a disaster to assess damage, maintain core IT systems, meet regulatory obligations, and secure or remove vital records and data.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available to businesses located in Baltimore City.
requirements_list: Business must be located in Baltimore City
Must enroll in the program prior to an emergency (pre-event credentialing)
Critical employees must be authenticated and receive a CEAS secure ID card
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Visit www.ceas.com to learn more and enroll in the pre-event credentialing program.

structured_extraction.program_description: Baltimore City provides capital funding to nonprofit cultural organizations for eligible physical improvements to their facilities. Organizations can apply every two years for General Obligation bond funding to support capital projects such as roof replacements, elevator upgrades, building envelope improvements, and exhibit expansions. The program is intended to support organizations that promote arts and culture in Baltimore City and contribute to the City's unique identity.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Up to $1 million per year is available in total for FY2026 and FY2027. Individual awards will not exceed $200,000 over two years, with typical awards ranging from $50,000 to $100,000 over a two-year period. Funds come from General Obligation (GO) bonds and must be used for eligible capital improvements. Funds are provided on a reimbursement basis.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Nonprofit museums, galleries, theaters, and other arts or cultural venues located in Baltimore City, particularly those in designated arts and entertainment districts.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Physical capital improvements to facilities with a minimum 15-year service life, including building system upgrades (roof, HVAC, windows, elevators), interior and exterior renovations, fire protection, ADA and accessibility improvements, building expansions, plaza/entrance upgrades, and museum/exhibit expansions. Projects must cost at least $50,000. Not eligible: projects under $50,000, vehicular equipment, emergency repairs, routine maintenance under $100,000, general salaries, operating support, relocation costs, loan repayment, or religious purposes.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Organizations must have a physical location in Baltimore City and must own the facility or hold a minimum 15-year lease with primary responsibility for capital improvements. The facility must be open to the general public.
requirements_list: Must be a registered nonprofit in good standing with the Maryland State Department of Assessment and Taxation
Must have a physical location in Baltimore City
Must own the facility or have a minimum 15-year lease and primary responsibility for capital improvements
Facility must be open to the general public
Eligible organization types: nonprofit museums, galleries, theaters; other arts or cultural venues must be in a designated arts and entertainment district
Projects must cost at least $50,000 and have a minimum 15-year service life
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Download the application form from the city website. Attend an optional information session (held in March 2025). Submit the completed application by the deadline. Awards are subject to approval of the FY26 and FY27 capital budget.

structured_extraction.program_description: Allows businesses to apply for use of curbside space in Baltimore City for commercial activities such as outdoor dining, retail, or other permitted uses.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Permits businesses to use curbside space for commercial purposes in Baltimore City.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Businesses seeking to use curbside space in Baltimore City for commercial activities.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Use of curbside space for outdoor dining, retail, or other permitted commercial activities.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Baltimore City only.

structured_extraction.program_description: A business-driven training program that helps Baltimore City employers cover the cost of training new employees in hard-to-fill positions. Employers or groups of employers can provide occupational skills training tailored to their needs. MOED reimburses up to 50% of training costs and handles marketing, recruitment, and pre-screening of applicants.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: MOED reimburses businesses up to 50% of training costs, which may include wages, tools, uniforms, and training courses. Training positions must be full-time permanent jobs paying at least $10 per hour.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Baltimore City employers looking to hire and train new employees in hard-to-fill positions across any industry.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Wages, tools, uniforms, and training courses for new hires in hard-to-fill positions.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available to employers operating in Baltimore City.
requirements_list: Employer must commit to hiring trainees who successfully complete the training program
Training positions must be full-time permanent positions
Wages must be at least $10 per hour
Training must be for new employees in hard-to-fill positions
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Complete the Customized Training/OJT Business Application on the Baltimore City website at https://www.baltimorecity.gov/moed/contact/customized-training-ojt-business-application.

structured_extraction.program_name: DOT Public Bike & Scooter Parking Program
structured_extraction.program_description: Baltimore City's Department of Transportation (DOT) accepts requests for free bicycle rack and scooter parking corral installations in the public right-of-way and at City-owned facilities. The program promotes use and safety of active transportation (walking, bicycling, e-scooters), supports Complete Streets guidelines, and helps encourage ridership, increase business patronage, and ensure proper parking. Property owners, business administrators, or the general public can submit a request. DOT evaluates each location and, if approved, adds it to an installation queue.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Free installation of bicycle parking racks and scooter parking corrals in the public right-of-way or at City-owned facilities, subject to available staff time and budget. DOT installs standard green U-racks (maximum 3 per location) and basic corrals (minimum 6 feet by 12 feet) with at least 2 bike racks and a painted scooter parking area. Optional upgrades are available (e.g., aesthetic barriers like planters instead of flex posts). Racks can be integrated into mobile applications for rented vehicles (Lime, Spin). Installation queue is approximately 6 months for bike racks and 3 months for scooter corrals. Making a request does not guarantee installation.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Property owners, business administrators, developers, event organizers, and members of the public in Baltimore City who want bicycle or scooter parking installed in the public right-of-way near their location.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Installation of bicycle racks or scooter parking corrals in the public right-of-way or at City-owned facilities, including racks, corrals, signage, barriers (flex posts or planters), and long-term parking solutions (lockers, bike rooms).
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available within Baltimore City public right-of-way and at City-owned facilities. DOT will not install racks on private property or property owned by other public agencies.
requirements_list: Adjacent property owner approval is required for bike rack installations and for scooter corrals that include bike parking. For scooter-only corrals, a two-week notice period is required and installation may proceed if no objections are filed.
Installation must leave at least 4 feet of navigable sidewalk or path space.
No more than 25% of scooter corrals may be located in any single planning district.
Commercial areas and locations near bike facilities and transit are prioritized.
Installation cannot be performed when temperatures are below 40 degrees Fahrenheit.
Minimum bicycle parking spaces based on land use and gross floor area (for new developments and significant redevelopments subject to zoning code).
Short-term parking must be simple racks within 50 feet of destination; long-term parking must be in controlled access areas, bicycle lockers, or covered facilities with weather protection.
At least 10% of racks must accommodate alternative bikes (adaptive, cargo bikes).
Minimum aisle widths of 5–6 feet for bicycle maneuvering.
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Complete the Bicycle Parking Rack Request Form as the owner, administrator, or a member of the public. Submit the request to DOT. A DOT representative will contact the requestor within 30 days to confirm an exact location. If the location is deemed suitable, the request is added to the installation queue (approximately 3–6 months). DOT will call 5–25 days prior to installation.

structured_extraction.program_name: Department of Housing and Community Development Weatherization Assistance Program
structured_extraction.program_description: Helps low-income Baltimore City homeowners and renters reduce energy costs by installing energy-saving materials and products in their homes. Services include energy audits, heating and cooling system repairs, insulation, air sealing, LED lighting, appliance replacement, and safety alarm installation. Assistance is available to applicants with incomes at or below 200% of the Federal Poverty Level (or up to 80% HUD FY25 or 250% Federal Poverty Level depending on household size). Available for both owner-occupied and rental properties.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Free weatherization services including energy audits, safety testing and repair of heating and cooling systems, attic insulation, air sealing, LED bulb replacement, water heater insulation, low-flow fixtures, carbon monoxide and smoke alarm installation, and Energy Star appliance replacement when existing appliances are inoperable or inefficient. Assistance may also include grants, forgivable loans (forgiven after 5 years if primary residence is maintained), and deferred loans (due when property is sold) for home repairs including disability accessibility modifications, electrical work, energy efficiency improvements, HVAC systems, lead paint hazard reduction, plumbing, roof repairs, sewer line, and water line repairs. A Quality Control Inspection is conducted after all work is complete.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Low-income homeowners and renters in Baltimore City who meet income eligibility guidelines (up to 200% Federal Poverty Level or 80% HUD FY25 / 250% Federal Poverty Level depending on household size), including households with members having disabilities and households with pregnant women or children under 6.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Installation of energy conservation materials and products, appliance replacement, heating/cooling system repairs, disability accessibility modifications, electrical repairs, energy efficiency improvements, HVAC systems, lead paint hazard reduction, plumbing, roof repairs, sewer line, and water line repairs to reduce energy costs and improve home safety and comfort.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available to owner-occupied and tenant-occupied properties in Baltimore City only.
requirements_list: Income at or below 200% of the Federal Poverty Level (or up to 80% HUD FY25 or 250% Federal Poverty Level; maximum annual income varies by household size, e.g. $72,950 for 1 person up to $137,550 for 8 people)
Must prove ownership of the housing unit (property tax bill, deed, SDAT sheet, or similar documentation)
Rental property owners must provide ownership documentation, sign a Permission to Enter form, and sign an Owner Agreement form
Some programs have waiting lists
Some programs require liens on properties for loans
Forgivable loans require 5-year primary residence occupancy
Properties built before 1978 subject to lead-based paint requirements
Must be current on mortgage, ground rent, and property taxes (for homeowners)
No outstanding judgments or recent bankruptcy
Landlord consent may be required for renters
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Apply online at the Neighborly Software portal or complete a paper pre-application and mail it to LIGHT Intake & Assessment Unit, 417 East Fayette Street, Suite 1125, Baltimore, MD 21202. DHCD determines preliminary eligibility after submission. Call (410) 396-3023 with questions. More information available at baltimorecity.gov/dhcd/resources-for-homeowners/weatherization-repairs.

structured_extraction.program_description: A program that gives money to groups, non-profits, and homeowners who are making major repairs to vacant homes in targeted Baltimore City neighborhoods, including properties with a Vacant Building Notice (VBN). Funds can help cover the full cost of rehabilitating a vacant home.
eligible_industries: Real Estate and Rental and Leasing
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Financial assistance to help cover the full cost of rehabilitating vacant homes, including those with a Vacant Building Notice, in targeted neighborhood improvement areas of Baltimore City.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Developers, non-profits, organizations, and homeowners rehabilitating vacant homes in targeted Baltimore City neighborhoods
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Rehabilitation and repair of vacant homes
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Targeted neighborhood improvement areas in Baltimore City; properties must be in designated focus areas
requirements_list: Property must be a vacant home
Property may have a Vacant Building Notice (VBN)
Project must be located in a designated program focus area
Must involve major repairs or full rehabilitation

structured_extraction.program_description: Provides grants to Baltimore-based nonprofit organizations to support digital inclusion projects and close the digital divide. Two grant structures have been offered: (1) Education and Outreach grants ($5,000–$10,000) to raise awareness and build capacity, Planning grants (up to $50,000) to develop neighborhood digital inclusion plans, and Implementation grants (up to $75,000) to put digital inclusion plans into action (funded by ARPA); and (2) Tier 1 (digital literacy education for older adults and the wider community at recreation centers, up to $200,000), Tier 2 (IT fundamentals skills training and certification, up to $200,000), and Tier 3 (digital creatives and virtual makerspaces programming at recreation centers, up to $200,000). Organizations may submit proposals for each grant type. The program serves Baltimore residents most affected by the digital divide, including people with disabilities, older adults, racial and ethnic minorities, immigrants, non-English speakers, returning citizens, LGBTQIA+ youth, and people experiencing homelessness.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Multiple tiers of grants available. Earlier round (ARPA-funded): Education and Outreach grants ($5,000–$10,000), Planning grants (up to $50,000), and Implementation grants (up to $75,000). Later round: Tier 1 digital literacy education (up to $200,000), Tier 2 IT fundamentals training and certification (up to $200,000), and Tier 3 digital creatives and virtual makerspaces programming (up to $200,000). Organizations may submit a proposal for each grant type.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Baltimore-based 501(c)(3) nonprofit organizations serving Baltimore residents, with a focus on populations most affected by the digital divide including people with disabilities, older adults, racial and ethnic minorities, immigrants, non-English speakers, returning citizens, LGBTQIA+ youth, and people experiencing homelessness.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Digital literacy education, IT fundamentals training and certifications, digital creatives classes and workshops, virtual makerspace programming, special events at recreation centers, education and outreach activities addressing the digital divide, community-building efforts to develop neighborhood digital inclusion plans, and implementation of digital inclusion plans.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Applicants must be based in Baltimore City and serve Baltimore City residents.
requirements_list: Must be a Baltimore-based 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization
Must serve Baltimore City residents
Must work in close partnership with communities

Must plan to address the needs of groups most likely to be left behind in the digital age (e.g. people with disabilities, older adults, racial/ethnic minorities, immigrants, non-English speakers, returning citizens, LGBTQIA+ youth, people experiencing homelessness)
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Apply through the Baltimore Civic Fund website at baltimorecivicfund.org/digital-equity-fund. Information sessions were held in May and June 2024; slide decks and video recordings are available online. Submit questions to submissions@baltimorecivicfund.org.

structured_extraction.program_description: An official emergency fund established to provide direct monetary support to the families of victims who lost loved ones in the Key Bridge collapse.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: The fund has raised more than $450,000. Funds are disbursed to victims' families in conjunction with a case management effort, with the goal of alleviating financial burden and providing needed resources.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Families of victims who lost loved ones in the Key Bridge collapse.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Financial support for victims' families to cover expenses and needs arising from the tragedy.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Serves families of Key Bridge collapse victims.
requirements_list: Must be a family member of a victim of the Key Bridge collapse
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Contact the Baltimore Civic Fund or the MIMA case management team for assistance.

structured_extraction.program_name: Diversion & Kinship Projects through the Youth Homelessness Demonstration Program (YHDP)
structured_extraction.program_description: The Youth Homelessness Demonstration Program (YHDP) funds a coordinated community approach to prevent and end youth homelessness. This specific grant opportunity, administered by the Mayor's Office of Homeless Services (MOHS), supports a Diversion and Kinship program for unaccompanied youth and young adults (ages 14-24, up to 25) experiencing or at risk of homelessness in Baltimore City. The program connects youth through outreach and coordinated access to quickly assess if they can be diverted from shelter, offers short-term flexible financial assistance (up to 6 months) and supportive services to keep youth housed or quickly re-house them, and connects youth to host homes through referrals including kinship care with relatives or close friends (fictive kin). The selected project must coordinate with existing YHDP projects and the Baltimore Continuum of Care.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Total funding available: $397,804 (Supportive Services Only project). Budget breakdown: Supportive Services ($351,080), HMIS ($10,560), Administrative Costs ($36,164). Administrative funds limited to 10% of total project budget. Requires 25% cash or in-kind match. Provides short-term flexible financial assistance (up to 6 months), supportive services including case management, outreach, housing search/counseling, and wraparound services. Grant is 1-year, renewable annually as part of CoC competition. HUD awarded Baltimore City $3,699,336 through the YHDP third round total.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Unaccompanied youth and young adults (ages 14-24, up to 25) at-risk of or experiencing homelessness in Baltimore City, with special focus on youth of color, minors under 18, LGBTQ+ youth, pregnant or parenting youth, survivors of sexual trafficking/exploitation, and youth involved with juvenile justice, jail, or foster care
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Supportive services, case management, housing problem-solving activities (housing search, family mediation, landlord-tenant mediation, utility/security deposits, moving assistance, rental application fees, rental/utility arrears), staff salaries, HMIS costs, host home and kinship care placements, outreach and assessment, employment services, mental health services, substance abuse treatment, childcare, education services, legal services, transportation, and flexible financial support for kinship/fictive kinship homes
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Baltimore City, Maryland
requirements_list: Must serve unaccompanied youth and young adults where no household member is older than 24
Must coordinate with existing YHDP projects (Permanent Supportive Housing, Rapid Re-housing, Family-Based Setting Diversion, and Transitional Housing)
Must coordinate with the full Baltimore Continuum of Care
Non-profit 501(c)(3) tax-exempt status or city government agency
Articles of Incorporation and Bylaws
Certificate of Good Standing from State of Maryland
Written conflict of interest policy and disclosure compliance
Fair Housing Act compliance
Housing First approach implementation
25% cash or in-kind match requirement
Non-discrimination based on protected class status
Section 504 accessibility compliance
Equal Access Rule compliance
Memoranda of Understanding for in-kind service providers
Joint applications allowed (lead agency + subrecipient with MOU)
Religious organizations permitted if meeting specific conditions (non-discriminatory, secular service delivery)
Completed application (max 25 pages, single-spaced, 11pt Calibri, 1" margins)
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Applications were submitted in response to a Request for Proposals posted January 3, 2022. A Bidder's Conference was held January 21, 2022. Submit completed application (max 25 pages), conflict of interest questionnaire, Fair Housing agreement, Housing First agreement, and match documentation (cash or in-kind letters with supporting MOUs) to HSPApplications@baltimorecity.gov by February 14, 2022 at 4pm. The funding opportunity is now closed.

structured_extraction.program_description: Baltimore City's Department of Housing and Community Development (DHCD) accepts donations of vacant properties and lots from private owners as part of the Reframe Baltimore initiative. Donating a property releases owners from financial burdens like unpaid taxes, liens, legal liability, and maintenance costs. The City covers all settlement costs so there is no cost to the donor.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: The City of Baltimore covers all settlement costs associated with the property donation. Owners of eligible vacant buildings or lots can donate their property to the City at no cost, relieving them of taxes, liens, legal risks, and maintenance obligations. The donation process takes approximately 8–12 months to complete.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Owners of vacant properties or vacant lots in Baltimore City who want to donate their property to the City
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Settlement costs of the property donation are covered by the City; no funds are disbursed to the donor
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available only within Baltimore City for properties with a Vacant Building Notice (VBN) issued by DHCD or vacant lots
requirements_list: Property must be vacant and have a Vacant Building Notice (VBN) issued by DHCD, or be a vacant lot
Property must have a clear title — all non-municipal liens (open mortgages, judgments, federal and state tax liens) must be paid off before donating
Donor's name must be on the deed, giving them legal right to transfer the property
If multiple names are on the deed, all owners must give permission
Companies and corporations are eligible to donate
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: 1. Verify your property is eligible (clear title, vacant with a VBN or vacant lot). 2. Submit the online application form. 3. DHCD reviews your application and contacts you with a status update. 4. If approved, DHCD sends a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) for you to complete and return. 5. The donation goes to Baltimore City's Board of Estimates for approval. 6. The donation is prepared for settlement and the property is fully transferred. The process takes 8–12 months.

structured_extraction.program_name: EPSDT Program (Early Protection Does Spectacular Things)
structured_extraction.program_description: Off-site preventive dental care and community education program for children ages 5 and younger and their parents.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Off-site preventive dental care and community oral health education delivered to children ages 5 and younger and their parents at community locations.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Children ages 5 and younger and their parents in Baltimore City.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Preventive dental care and oral health education.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Baltimore City.
requirements_list: Children must be ages 5 or younger
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Call 410-396-4501 for more information.

structured_extraction.program_description: Eating Together is a federally funded congregate nutrition program for seniors 60 and older in Baltimore City. The program provides free nutritious lunches and dinners — including Kosher and Korean meal options — in a social setting at more than 50 sites across the city, including senior centers and older adult housing sites. It aims to reduce isolation, promote health, and offer educational events, group activities, and other social opportunities. Participants include adults 60 and older, their spouses of any age, and disabled persons under 60 residing in a building where the program operates.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Participants receive free nutritious meals (lunch or dinner) at congregate dining sites including senior centers and older adult housing sites. There is no fee to join or for the meal itself. Participants are encouraged — but not required — to make a voluntary donation of $1.25 for a regular meal or $2.00 for a kosher meal. Kosher and Korean meal options are available at select sites. Registration is required.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Baltimore City seniors aged 60 and older, their spouses of any age, and disabled persons under 60 who reside in a residential building where an Eating Together meal program operates.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Nutritious meals in a congregate dining setting at senior centers or older adult housing sites, along with access to educational seminars, health programs, volunteer opportunities, group activities, and social events.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available at more than 50 sites within Baltimore City, including senior center locations and designated older adult housing sites.
requirements_list: Must be 60 years of age or older, OR be a spouse of an eligible participant regardless of age, OR be a disabled person under 60 residing in a building where the program operates
Must register by completing a registration form
Must obtain a membership card to swipe at each meal attendance
Must reserve a meal in advance using the monthly posted menus
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Register for the program by completing a registration form or call 443-573-0161 to sign up and get more information. After registering, participants receive a membership card. Check monthly posted menus to reserve a meal at a preferred site. Call 410-396-1337 or visit the Eating Together website to find the nearest site.

structured_extraction.program_name: Electric Vehicle Charging Station Request Program
structured_extraction.program_description: Baltimore City residents and businesses can request a new publicly accessible electric vehicle (EV) charging station in their neighborhood. The Parking Authority evaluates proposed locations based on electric infrastructure, parking availability, and community feedback.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: The Parking Authority installs publicly accessible EV charging stations on city-owned land or right-of-way. Approved stations are available for public use and subject to relevant laws and regulations. Due to limited equipment, installation may not be immediate — requests are kept on file for future consideration.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Baltimore City residents, businesses, schools, or community members who want a publicly accessible EV charging station installed in their area.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Installation of a publicly accessible EV charging station on city-owned land or right-of-way.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Must be on city-owned land or right-of-way within Baltimore City, adjacent to parking accessible 24/7, near a power source, and in a safe, well-lit area.
requirements_list: Location must be adjacent to parking that is publicly accessible 24 hours per day, 7 days per week
Location must be on city-owned land or right-of-way (sidewalk, public park, or city building)
Location must be accessible to a power source such as a nearby transformer
Location must be in a safe, well-lit area
Location should be near amenities, schools, workplaces, or businesses
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Complete the online request form on the Baltimore City website. The Parking Authority will evaluate the proposed location for electric infrastructure, parking availability, and community feedback.

structured_extraction.program_description: The Mayor's Office of Homeless Services (MOHS) awards competitive grants to organizations that operate emergency homeless shelter sites in Baltimore City. Funded shelters must provide dignified residential settings and 24-hour, 7-day services including case management, emergency preparedness planning, and support for self-sufficiency that help people experiencing homelessness transition back to stable housing, in line with the Baltimore Continuum of Care Action Plan with the goal of making homelessness rare, brief, and nonrecurring.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Competitively awarded grants to fund operation of emergency homeless shelter sites in Baltimore City. Grants cover shelter services including beds for single adults and families, meals (twice daily, 365 days/year), case management, security, facility maintenance, and supportive services. Funding sources include City General Fund, Maryland State Homelessness Solutions Program (HSP), Baltimore City Department of Social Services Shelter Program (DSS), and HUD Emergency Solutions Grant (ESG) Program. The performance period for this round runs from July 1, 2020 to June 30, 2021.
structured_extraction.contact_name: Wade Carver (Program Compliance Officer II); Angela D. McCauley (Emergency Services Coordinator); Jay Wilson (Contract Administrator)
structured_extraction.contact_phone: Wade Carver: (410) 396-4426; Angela D. McCauley: (410) 361-9681; Jay Wilson: (410) 396-3602
structured_extraction.program_audience: Non-profit 501(c)(3) tax-exempt organizations and other city agencies that can operate emergency homeless shelter facilities in Baltimore City, serving homeless individuals and families
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Operating emergency homeless shelter sites providing beds and support services for people experiencing homelessness, including shelter operations and accommodations (beds, bedding, storage, common areas), staff salaries and training, case management services, emergency preparedness planning, food services, facility maintenance and equipment, fire safety compliance, pest management, utilities, HMIS data entry, customer satisfaction surveys, and subcontractor payments for direct services
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Services must be provided within the City of Baltimore
requirements_list: Must be a registered non-profit 501(c)(3) tax-exempt organization or another city agency
Must be certified in good standing with the State of Maryland
Must have current Certificate of Good Standing from State of Maryland
Must have Federal Tax Exemption Determination Letter

Staffing: Program Director (Bachelor's degree + 4 years experience), Residential Aides, Case Managers
All staff must have tuberculosis testing
Case Managers must complete 8 specific trainings within 3 months of hire
McKinney-Vento liaison if serving minors
Equity liaison trained in cultural responsiveness
Bilingual case management services for foreign language needs
24-hour operations, 7 days per week including holidays
HMIS data collection and 95% data quality standard
Coordinated Access permanent housing assessments within 2 weeks of entry
Case manager engagement minimum twice per month
Conduct quarterly fire drills; maintain fire safety equipment and records
Provide Certificate of Occupancy; ensure ADA compliance
Serve meals twice daily following Food Guide Pyramid Serving Sizes

structured_extraction.program_name: Emergency Solutions Grants COVID-19 (ESG-CV) Program – Baltimore City
structured_extraction.program_description: Baltimore City's Mayor's Office of Homeless Services (MOHS) received $15,715,495 in Emergency Solutions Grants COVID-19 (ESG-CV) funding (ESG-CV 1 and ESG-CV 2) from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) through the CARES Act to prevent, prepare for, and respond to COVID-19 among individuals and families who are homeless or at risk of homelessness. More than $10.7 million is dedicated to rapid rehousing and homelessness prevention. Estimated allocations: 45–50% for rapid re-housing, 20–25% for homelessness prevention, 15–20% for emergency shelter, 5–10% for street outreach, less than 3% for HMIS (Homeless Management Information System), and less than 7% for administration. Of the initial ESG-CV 1 allocation of $6,571,738, $657,173.80 goes to administration and the remainder flows to Continuum of Care providers. Funds support expanding project capacity, reimbursing providers for emergency supplies (e.g., PPE, cleaning supplies), medical expenses, and increased food costs.

Estimated overall allocations: 45–50% for rapid re-housing, 20–25% for homelessness prevention, 15–20% for emergency shelter, 5–10% for street outreach, less than 3% for HMIS, and less than 7% for administration. Funds may cover expanding project capacity, reimbursing providers for emergency supplies (e.g., PPE, cleaning supplies), medical expenses, and increased food costs. Additional support provided for data management and program administration.

structured_extraction.program_name: Enterprise Zone and Focus Area Tax Credit Program
structured_extraction.program_description: The Enterprise Zone (EZ) program provides real property and state income tax credits to businesses located in a Maryland Enterprise Zone in Baltimore City in exchange for job creation and investments. Businesses in Focus Areas (specific boundaries within an EZ) can also receive personal property tax credits on new investment and enhanced income tax credits for creating new jobs.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Enterprise Zone benefits: (1) Real Property Tax Credit — 10-year credit on the incremental increase in property taxes from real property improvements: 80% credit in years 1–5, decreasing 10% annually in years 6–10; goes to the property owner. (2) Income Tax Credit — $1,000 per new employee; $6,000 over 3 years for each economically disadvantaged employee hired; credit may be carried forward 5 years. Focus Area benefits (in addition to EZ benefits): (1) Real property tax credit of 80% on increased assessed value for 10 years; personal property tax credit of 80% for 10 years on new investment in personal property; goes to the property owner. (2) Income Tax Credit — $1,500 per new employee; $9,000 over 3 years for each economically disadvantaged employee hired; credit may be carried forward 5 years. Businesses must be certified by the local enterprise zone administrator as eligible.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Businesses located in a Maryland Enterprise Zone or Focus Area in Baltimore City that create new jobs or make investments in real or personal property
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Tax credits offset property taxes on real and personal property improvements, and income taxes based on new job creation including hiring of economically disadvantaged workers
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available to businesses located within designated Enterprise Zones or Focus Areas in Baltimore City, Maryland. Businesses must verify their location using the Maryland Enterprise Zone Map.

Business must be certified by the local enterprise zone administrator as eligible for the credit
Business must create new employment meeting certain requirements to claim income tax credits
Economically disadvantaged employee status required to claim the higher $6,000/$9,000 income tax credit tier
