requirements_list: Must be a Maryland public school or food producer/business supplying Maryland schools
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Contact Karen Fedor at karen.fedor@maryland.gov or (410) 841-5773 for assistance with sourcing local products or participating in the program. Alternatively, call 410-767-0199 to speak with OSCNP staff to determine eligibility.

structured_extraction.program_name: Good Agricultural Practices / Good Handling Practices (GAP/GHP) Training and Assistance
structured_extraction.program_description: The Maryland Department of Agriculture (MDA), in cooperation with the University of Maryland, provides GAP/GHP training and one-on-one technical assistance to fruit and vegetable producers in developing, writing, and implementing food safety programs. This helps farmers reduce the risk of microbial contamination of fresh produce and meet buyer and federal FDA requirements. The program is voluntary and geared towards smaller and/or direct marketers, but may also assist larger farms and wholesale operations. It includes support for FSMA Produce Safety Rule compliance, on-farm readiness reviews, worker hygiene training materials, cost-share for audit costs, and certification services.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: MDA provides GAP/GHP food safety training sessions (offered regionally January through March annually) and individual one-on-one on-site assistance to help Maryland fruit and vegetable producers develop, write, and implement food safety programs. Services include: mandatory GAP training through University of Maryland and MDA; self-assessment guidance using National GAPS Program or University of Maryland Checklist; written food safety plan development; MDA GAP auditors inspecting to verify plan implementation; certification upon passing inspection; cost-share for USDA GAP and Harmonized audit costs; on-farm readiness reviews for FSMA Produce Safety Rule compliance; worker hygiene training materials (DVDs and signs); and recordkeeping forms and educational materials. Program is funded by USDA Specialty Crop Grant to minimize costs to producers.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Maryland fruit and vegetable producers, including small farms, direct marketers, and larger wholesale operations
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Developing, writing, and implementing Good Agricultural Practices (GAP) and Good Handling Practices (GHP) food safety programs on farms; GAP/GHP audits; FSMA Produce Safety Rule compliance reviews; worker hygiene training materials; food safety planning
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available to any Maryland producer of fruits and vegetables
requirements_list: Must be a Maryland producer of fruits and vegetables
Attend approved GAP training program and obtain certificate of completion
Complete self-assessment of food safety risks using National GAPS Program or University of Maryland Checklist
Develop written food safety plan addressing identified risks (including worker hygiene, water, compost/manure, sanitation, and wildlife control)
Implement food safety plan
Schedule and pass MDA GAP/GHP inspection
Regular water testing (surface water: 3 times per season; well water: once per season)
Manure application 120 days prior to harvest for ground-contact crops; 90 days for non-contact crops
Maintain records of water tests, manure applications, and harvests
Provide worker training on handwashing and personal hygiene
Provide accessible toilet and handwashing facilities for workers
Wildlife monitoring and field inspection before harvest
Regular cleaning of harvest materials and packing areas
Requirements updated annually to meet current buyer and regulatory requirements
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: 1. Attend approved GAP training program. 2. Complete self-assessment using National GAPS Program or University of Maryland Checklist. 3. Develop written food safety plan addressing identified risks. 4. Implement food safety plan. 5. Submit MDA GAP/GHP inspection request form; MDA auditor will contact to schedule inspection. 6. Pass inspection and receive Certificate of Compliance. Contact MDA's Food Quality Assurance Program to request assistance.

structured_extraction.program_description: Maryland Department of Agriculture (MDA) provides official grain inspection and weighing services for domestic markets and grain exported in containers, on behalf of USDA's Federal Grain Inspection Service (FGIS). Grain can be examined for damage, foreign material, color, moisture content, and mycotoxins such as vomitoxin and aflatoxin. Services include test weight, moisture content, grade classification, and mycotoxin analysis (qualitative or quantitative). Both on-site sampling and analysis of submitted samples are available through MDA's Annapolis office.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Official USDA FGIS grain inspection and weighing services are provided on a fee basis. Users can choose a full-time contract basis, an as-needed fee basis, or a per-sample fee ($20.00 per sample; $30.00 per sample for mycotoxin testing). Services include sampling, weighing, grading, and mycotoxin testing. Mileage reimbursement charged at $0.56 per mile. An official USDA FGIS certificate documenting the results is mailed, faxed, or emailed to the requester.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Grain farmers, agricultural producers, crop insurance adjusters, and persons with crop insurance claims seeking official quality grading and inspection to determine price or appropriate use of their grain.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Obtaining official grain inspection and weighing certificates for domestic or export markets. Testing services: $20.00 per sample; $30.00 per sample for mycotoxin testing.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Services available through MDA's Annapolis office in Maryland.
requirements_list: Submitters must verify required sample size prior to submission.
Minimum sample size: 3 pounds for wheat, rye, barley; 5 pounds for soybeans.
Larger samples may be required for mycotoxin testing.
Crop insurance claim samples must be submitted by an insurance company-approved person.
Fees charged to users on a full-time contract, as-needed, or per-sample basis.
Minimum 40 hours per week for contract employees.
Minimum hours vary by service type (2-4 hour minimums for non-contract).
Export grain inspection other than containers must be conducted by USDA FGIS Field Office in Toledo, Ohio.
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Submit completed Grain Sample Test Request Form with sample and payment to MDA's Annapolis office. Verify required sample size before submission (minimum 3 lbs for wheat/rye/barley, 5 lbs for soybeans). A Sample Test Request Form is available on the program page. Fees apply based on contract or per-sample arrangement.

structured_extraction.program_description: LEEF is a Maryland Department of Agriculture program established by the Chesapeake Bay Legacy Act (effective July 1, 2025). It recognizes and rewards farmers who voluntarily adopt conservation practices, preserve green space, participate in on-farm research, and contribute to equitable and resilient food systems. The program aims to reduce nutrients in support of Chesapeake Bay Watershed Restoration, mitigate farm emissions, increase carbon sequestration per Maryland's Climate Pollution Reduction Plan, and enhance farm profitability. Farmers earn points for conservation and community practices, qualify for certification tiers (Certified, Silver, Gold, Platinum), and unlock greater incentives at higher tiers.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Participants earn points based on the intensity and statewide value of conservation and community practices they implement on their farms. Higher point totals unlock higher certification tiers (Certified 40–49, Silver 50–59, Gold 60–79, Platinum 80+). Incentives include cost-share for conservation practices, priority access to equipment funding and vendor contracts, priority access to programs and grants, potential tax incentives, infrastructure grants (e.g., processing plant development), equipment and working capital financing, farm acquisition programs, and leverage for business partnerships and applications. Lower loan rates through partner organizations such as MARBIDCO and Horizon Farm Credit are also anticipated. Final incentive structures are still being developed.
structured_extraction.application_deadline_string: Launching Spring 2026; not yet accepting applications
structured_extraction.program_audience: Maryland farmers of all sizes and types, including beginning farmers, young farmers, livestock operations, value-added producers, and urban agriculture operators, who are interested in adopting conservation and community practices on their farms
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Conservation practices (e.g., conservation tillage, cover crops, nutrient reductions, buffers, pollinator habitats, on-farm renewable energy, soil health, wildlife habitat improvement) and community practices (e.g., research partnerships, mentorship of beginning farmers, food bank partnerships, participation in nutrition programs, farmers market participation, local farm certification, service leadership, food resiliency work). Also includes equipment purchases, working capital, processing infrastructure, land acquisition, and energy efficiency improvements.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Statewide Maryland with emphasis on Chesapeake Bay Watershed; practice weights may be prioritized based on location within critical areas or priority BMP locations
requirements_list: Must implement practices from both conservation practices and community best practices categories
Must accumulate a minimum of 40 points to achieve the lowest (Certified) tier (Certified 40–49, Silver 50–59, Gold 60–79, Platinum 80+)
Practices must reflect the farm's unique operational needs and resource concerns
Annual review and documentation/site verification required
Voluntary participation
Documentation of practices required for state funding
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: The program is not yet accepting applications as of early 2026. Practices are assigned weighted points; farms accumulate points to reach tier levels and are reviewed annually. Documentation and verification requirements are to be determined. Interested farmers can join the LEEF mailing list to receive updates. Partners interested in collaboration can contact LEEF.MDA@maryland.gov. MDA will announce application details once the program framework is finalized.

structured_extraction.program_description: MDA's State GAP/GHP certification program is a voluntary food safety program for Maryland fruit and vegetable direct marketers and producers. It covers basic food safety requirements to minimize the risk of microbial contamination through good production practices, based on FDA guidance. Requirements are updated annually to meet current buyer and regulatory requirements. The program is geared towards smaller and/or direct marketers but may also assist larger farms and wholesale sellers as a starting point for implementing comprehensive GAP food safety programs.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: MDA provides a six-step voluntary certification process: (1) mandatory food safety training provided through University of Maryland and MDA (other training accepted with certificate of completion); (2) self-assessment of food safety risks using National GAPS Program or University of Maryland checklist; (3) written food safety plan development (one-on-one assistance available from University of Maryland); (4) implementation of the food safety plan; (5) MDA GAP auditor inspection to verify plan adequacy and implementation, with corrective action recommendations and reinspection as necessary; (6) issuance of Certificate of Compliance upon passing inspection. The program is funded in part by a USDA Specialty Crop Grant to minimize costs to producers.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Maryland fruit and vegetable producers including smaller farms, direct marketers, and larger farms selling wholesale
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Certification of compliance with basic food safety requirements for produce production; program funded by USDA Specialty Crop Grant to minimize costs to producers
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available to Maryland fruit and vegetable producers statewide; regional training sessions offered January through March
requirements_list: Must be a Maryland fruit or vegetable producer
Attend an approved GAP food safety training program
Complete self-assessment using National GAPS Program Self Assessment Checklist or University of Maryland Checklist
Develop a written food safety plan addressing identified risks
Implement the food safety plan
Schedule and undergo an MDA inspection to verify plan adequacy and implementation
Pass inspection to receive Certificate of Compliance
Must meet MDA's basic food safety requirements to receive certification
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Six-step process: (1) attend approved GAP training; (2) complete self-assessment; (3) develop written food safety plan; (4) implement the plan; (5) submit MDA GAP/GHP Inspection Request Form and schedule inspection with MDA auditor; (6) receive Certificate of Compliance upon passing inspection. Reinspection available if needed.

structured_extraction.program_description: This program helps farmers and registered manure brokers cover the cost of transporting manure to farms with low-phosphorus fields or to alternative use facilities. It offers cost-share grants for moving poultry, dairy, and livestock manure to reduce nutrient runoff and support water quality conservation.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: For poultry manure: up to $28 per ton to transport poultry litter, reimbursed at $0.14/ton/mile (most counties) or $0.16/ton/mile (Dorchester, Somerset, Wicomico, Worcester counties), capped at $28/ton. Cost-share also available for manure analysis testing (up to $40). Farmers or registered manure brokers may apply via a standard application or the 'Haul Now, Apply Later FastTrack' option. For dairy and livestock manure: cost-share grants pay up to 87.5 percent of all eligible costs, with payment rates based on transport distance and manure type (liquid or solid); FastTrack option limited to $15,000 per season and $30,000 per year for receiving farms. Also provides up to $45 per acre for manure injection.
structured_extraction.application_deadline_string: Claim for payment must be submitted within 40 days from last date of transport
structured_extraction.program_audience: Eligible farmers, registered manure brokers, and receiving farm operations in Maryland who need to transport poultry, dairy, or livestock manure to fields with low phosphorus levels or to alternative use facilities.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Covering the cost of transporting manure from sending farms to receiving farms with low-phosphorus fields or to approved alternative use facilities. Also covers manure analysis/testing costs and manure injection equipment rental, lease, or custom operator fees.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: The sending farm must be located in Maryland. For poultry manure, the farm must raise broiler chickens for a participating Delmarva poultry company (Amick, Mountaire, Perdue, Tyson). Poultry litter must be transported more than 7 miles from the sending farm; dairy and livestock manure must be transported more than 1 mile. Receiving farm fields must also be in Maryland.
requirements_list: For poultry manure: sending farm must be in Maryland and raise broiler chickens for a participating Delmarva poultry company (Amick, Mountaire, Perdue, Tyson)
Poultry litter must be transported more than 7 miles from the sending farm
Applicant must submit a current nutrient management plan compliant with COMAR 15.20.07
For FastTrack poultry: receiving fields must have a phosphorus Fertility Index Value (P-FIV) less than 101; for Standard option: P-FIV between 100-150; fields exceeding 150 are ineligible
For dairy and livestock FastTrack: receiving farm fields must have a Maryland soil phosphorus Fertility Index Value of 100 or less; Standard option allows up to 150
Dairy and livestock manure must be transported more than 1 mile from the sending source
Only operations receiving the dairy/livestock manure may apply for transport grants
Manure must be applied to crops or hay fields containing less than 25 percent legumes
Either the farmer or the manure broker (not both) may apply for cost-share reimbursement per load of poultry manure
Soil tests no older than 3 years required
Poultry manure analysis no older than 2 years required
Weight tickets required (at least 1 per 5 loads; minimum 2 per project)
Gross vehicle weight not to exceed 80,000 lbs (unless Exceptional Hauling Permit held)
Signature from both sending and receiving operations required
NMP Certification Form must be completed and submitted to local Soil Conservation District (may be submitted at claim stage for manure transport projects)
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: For poultry manure standard option: farmers apply through the local soil conservation district; registered manure brokers apply directly to the Maryland Department of Agriculture. For the FastTrack option: download and complete the FastTrack application and claim form, haul the manure, then submit the claim form for reimbursement within 40 days of last transport date. For dairy and livestock manure: use the Non-Poultry FastTrack Application and Claim Form. Submit NMP Certification Form to local Soil Conservation District office when applying; incomplete applications will not be accepted. Mail completed forms to Maryland Department of Agriculture, Conservation Grants, 50 Harry S. Truman Parkway, Room 207, Annapolis, MD 21401.

structured_extraction.program_description: ACReS is Maryland's official USDA-certified agricultural mediation program. It provides free, confidential, voluntary mediation to help farmers, agricultural lenders, government agencies, and others resolve disputes related to agricultural operations without going to court. Disputes can involve USDA decisions, credit and loan issues, lease conflicts, neighbor disputes, and family farm planning.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Free mediation services for agricultural disputes. The initial consultation and first mediation session are provided at no cost. If additional sessions are needed, nominal costs are shared among participants. Full or partial fee waivers are available based on income. A neutral mediator helps all parties reach a mutually agreeable solution.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Farmers, agricultural lenders, USDA agencies, families, and members of the general public involved in disputes related to agricultural operations in Maryland.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Mediation services to resolve agricultural disputes including USDA agency decisions, credit and lease issues, neighbor conflicts, family farm transitions, and any dispute affecting the profitability of an agricultural operation.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available statewide in Maryland. Agricultural operations include aquaculture, tree farms, beekeeping, horticulture, and urban farming.
requirements_list: Must have a dispute related to agricultural production or an agricultural operation
All parties must agree to voluntarily participate in mediation
Participants must agree to keep mediation communications confidential
Must complete the ACReS Mediation Intake Form to request mediation
Good faith participation and complete and honest disclosure of relevant information required
Parties must sign Agreement to Begin Voluntary Mediation and waive right to civil action against the State of Maryland and mediators
Participants may bring legal, financial, or technical advisors at their own expense
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Contact Maryland ACReS and complete the Mediation Intake Form, providing party information, conflict description, referral source, and prior attempts to resolve the conflict. Staff will confirm the other party's willingness to participate. A mediator is assigned and all parties sign an Agreement to Begin Voluntary Mediation and are notified of the session date, time, and location. Most sessions last two to three hours. Participants can self-refer or be referred by USDA or other agencies.

structured_extraction.program_description: Grant program to support agricultural fair boards by providing financial aid for premiums, awards, ribbons, trophies, and other fair-related expenses at county and state fairs held across Maryland.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Financial aid in the form of grants to qualifying agricultural fair boards. Funds are used to provide premiums, awards, ribbons, trophies, and other fair-related expenses. Grant applications are submitted online through Maryland OneStop. After-activity reports are due within 45 days of the event. Annual renewal is required rather than a full re-application from scratch.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Maryland Agricultural Fair Boards seeking funding to support premiums, awards, ribbons, trophies, and other fair-related expenses.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Premiums, awards, ribbons, trophies, and other fair-related expenses at agricultural fairs and shows.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Statewide — available to qualifying agricultural fair boards throughout Maryland.
requirements_list: Application must be submitted online via Maryland OneStop by January 19, 2026
Create an organization login (not individual) on Maryland OneStop
Fill all sections marked with an asterisk (*)
Input information for each board member
Submit application through the OneStop portal
After-activity report must be submitted within 45 days of the event via the OneStop Dashboard
Annual renewal required (not a full re-application from scratch)
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Log into Maryland OneStop (onestop.md.gov); search and select the grant application; fill all required fields; submit by the stated deadline; receive email confirmation; application is reviewed and potential revisions may be requested via email; board approves or denies and allocates funds; contract sent via email; complete the After Activity Report within 45 days of the event; receive payment upon approval.

structured_extraction.program_name: Maryland Agricultural Water Quality Cost-Share (MACS) Program – Hedgerow Planting
structured_extraction.program_description: Provides cost-share funding to farmers to plant small trees, shrubs, and grasses along the edges of farm fields or roads. Hedgerows filter runoff, act as a living fence and wildlife corridor, protect air and water quality, reduce noise, provide wildlife shelter, and can improve a farm's aesthetic value.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Up to 100% cost-share to plant a hedgerow, plus $2 per planted tree.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Farmers who want to plant hedgerows along farm field or road edges.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Planting small trees, shrubs, and grasses along farm field or road edges to create hedgerows.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Statewide in Maryland; apply through local soil conservation district.
requirements_list: Must be a farmer
Practice must be installed along edges of farm fields or roads
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Contact your local soil conservation district to apply.

structured_extraction.program_name: Maryland Agricultural Water Quality Cost-Share (MACS) Program – Riparian Forest Buffer / Stream Buffers
structured_extraction.program_description: Provides cost-share funding to farmers to plant trees, shrubs, or grasses along waterways and streams. Riparian forest buffers filter agricultural runoff, enhance water quality, control erosion, provide shade for streams, create wildlife habitat, and can help exclude livestock from waterways. Over 40 best management practices are eligible for funding, and free technical assistance is provided for project design and installation.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Up to 100% cost-share funding for certain high-priority practices (including planting riparian forest buffers with trees, shrubs, or grasses along waterways and streams), plus $2 for each tree planted. Up to 87.5% cost-share for other eligible practices. Up to $28/ton for manure transport grants. Free technical assistance provided for project design and installation. Can be combined with federal conservation grants.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Farmers with land adjacent to streams or waterways who want to improve water quality, reduce erosion, and create wildlife habitat. Also applicable to livestock, poultry, and crop producers statewide.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Planting riparian forest buffers (trees, shrubs, or grasses) along waterways and streams; site preparation; tree shelters; weed treatment; erosion control and soil health practices (grassed waterways, terraces, cover crops, etc.); stream protection practices (livestock stream exclusion fencing, etc.); manure and barnyard management; well protection; windbreaks for poultry houses.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Statewide in Maryland; apply through your local soil conservation district. Conservation drainage practices mainly used on the Eastern Shore.
requirements_list: Must be a farmer
Must have land adjacent to a stream or waterway
Practice must be installed along a waterway
Work with local soil conservation district
Select plants suitable for site conditions
Prepare site for plant survival and growth
Treat weed problems prior to planting
Use tree shelters to increase survival rates
Mow grass areas after August 15 to protect nesting birds
Replace dead trees and shrubs as needed
Remove tree shelters 2 years after trees emerge
Control weeds and undesirable vegetation
Repair fences and check livestock crossing damage
Soil Conservation and Water Quality Plan (SCWQP) required for many federal and state programs
Current nutrient management plan required for applicable practices
Soil and manure testing requirements where applicable
Follow federal, state, and local regulations and obtain necessary permits
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Contact your local soil conservation district to apply for this cost-share grant. District staff can provide a free personalized farm plan, help estimate installation costs, and navigate cost-share programs. USDA NRCS, FSA, and University of Maryland Extension may also provide support.

structured_extraction.program_name: Maryland Agricultural Water Quality Cost-Share (MACS) Program – Silvopasture
structured_extraction.program_description: Provides cost-share funding to farmers to introduce trees into active livestock pastures. Silvopasture improves soil and water quality, filters runoff, provides shade and shelter for livestock, and captures carbon from the atmosphere.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Up to 87.5% cost-share to install silvopasture (trees in active livestock pastures), plus $2 per planted tree.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Farmers with active livestock pastures who want to introduce trees to improve pasture conditions.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Introducing trees into active livestock pastures to improve soil, water quality, and livestock conditions.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Statewide in Maryland; apply through local soil conservation district.
requirements_list: Must be a farmer
Must have active livestock pastures
Practice must integrate trees into livestock pastures
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Contact your local soil conservation district to apply.

structured_extraction.program_name: Maryland Agricultural Water Quality Cost-Share (MACS) Program – Small Equine and Livestock Operations
structured_extraction.program_description: Cost-share grants for small equine and livestock operations to install conservation practices that reduce runoff and erosion, protect waterways, and improve farm management. Eligible farms must have at least 1,000 pounds of live animal weight. The program covers practices such as watering facilities, pasture management, animal waste storage structures, heavy use area protection, roof runoff structures, stream exclusion fencing, and interior pasture fencing.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Cost-share reimbursement for conservation practices: Pasture Management (up to 87.5%), Interior Pasture Fencing (up to 50%), Exclusion Fencing (up to 100%) and Crossings (up to 87.5%), Watering Facility (up to 87.5%), Heavy Use Area Protection (up to 87.5%), Riparian Forest Buffer (up to 100%), Roof Runoff Structure (up to 87.5%), and Waste Storage Structure (up to 87.5%). Grants are administered through local soil conservation districts.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Small-scale horse and livestock owners in Maryland with at least 1,000 pounds of live animal weight who want to install conservation practices on their farms.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Installation of conservation best management practices to improve water quality and farm sustainability, including watering facilities, pasture management, animal waste storage structures, heavy use area protection, roof runoff structures, stream exclusion fencing, interior pasture fencing, and riparian forest buffers.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available statewide in Maryland through local soil conservation districts.
requirements_list: Must have at least 1,000 pounds of live animal weight
Must be an equine or livestock operation in Maryland
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Apply through local soil conservation district offices. Free professional help and technical assistance is provided throughout the process.

structured_extraction.program_name: Maryland Agricultural Water Quality Cost-Share (MACS) Program – Tree & Shrub Establishment
structured_extraction.program_description: Provides cost-share funding to farmers to establish trees and shrubs on agricultural land outside the stream corridor. This practice improves water quality and captures carbon from the atmosphere, and can be applied on any site capable of growing woody plants, including land in USDA conservation programs.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Up to 100% cost-share to establish trees and shrubs on agricultural land outside the stream corridor, plus $2 per planted tree.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Farmers who want to establish trees and shrubs on agricultural land outside stream corridors.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Establishing trees and shrubs on agricultural land outside the stream corridor to improve water quality and capture carbon.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Statewide in Maryland; apply through local soil conservation district. Eligible on any site capable of growing woody plants, including land in USDA and other conservation programs.
requirements_list: Must be a farmer
Land must be outside the stream corridor but capable of growing woody plants
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Contact your local soil conservation district to apply.

structured_extraction.program_name: Maryland Agricultural Water Quality Cost-Share (MACS) Program – Windbreak Establishment
structured_extraction.program_description: Provides cost-share funding to farmers to plant trees and shrubs in rows near chicken houses, barnyard areas, and property borders. Windbreaks improve air quality, create visual screens, protect against winter winds, and provide shade and habitat for wildlife.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Up to 100% cost-share for windbreak establishment (trees and shrubs planted near chicken houses, barnyards, and property borders), plus $2 per planted tree.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Farmers, particularly those with poultry operations, who want to plant windbreaks near farm buildings or property borders.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Planting trees and shrubs in rows near chicken houses, barnyard areas, and property borders to create windbreaks.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Statewide in Maryland; apply through local soil conservation district.
requirements_list: Must be a farmer
Practice must involve planting trees and shrubs near farm buildings or property borders
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Contact your local soil conservation district to apply.

structured_extraction.program_name: Maryland Agricultural Water Quality Cost-Share Program (MACS)
structured_extraction.program_description: A state program administered by the Maryland Department of Agriculture that pays up to 87.5 percent of the cost for farmers to install eligible agricultural best management practices (BMPs) to control soil erosion, manage nutrients, and safeguard water quality in the Chesapeake Bay and state waterways. Eligible BMPs include animal waste storage facilities, grassed waterways, spring developments, cover crops, stream protection practices, conservation cover, nutrient management services, and poultry litter transport assistance. The program assists farmers and landowners in implementing agricultural best management practices to control soil erosion, manage nutrients, and reduce agricultural sources of water pollution.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Pays up to 87.5 percent of the cost for farmers to install eligible best management practices (BMPs) on their farms. Eligible BMPs include animal waste management systems, grassed waterways, filter strips, cover crops, riparian buffers, stream fencing, spring developments, nutrient management services, and poultry litter transport assistance.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Individual farmers, partnerships, corporations, trusts, or other businesses operating a Maryland farm who have an existing or potentially critical condition causing soil, nutrients, or pollutants to enter state waters and seek to install conservation practices to reduce soil erosion, manage nutrients, and protect water quality.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Installation of eligible agricultural best management practices (BMPs) such as animal waste management systems, grassed waterways, filter strips, cover crops, riparian buffers, stream fencing, spring developments, nutrient management services, and poultry litter transport assistance that reduce soil, nutrients, and animal wastes entering state waterways.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available statewide across Maryland to farmers operating a Maryland farm.
requirements_list: Must be an individual, partnership, corporation, trust, or other business operating a Maryland farm
Must have an existing or potentially critical condition on agricultural land causing soil, nutrients, or pollutants to move off the land into state waters
Must install eligible agricultural best management practices (BMPs)
Proposed project must improve water quality
Proposed project must meet MACS eligibility criteria and cost-effectiveness requirements
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Contact the Maryland Department of Agriculture Office of Resource Conservation or the USDA Service Center located in each county, or the local soil conservation district, for information on applying. The program website provides a MACS Manual with details on best management practices, forms, and instructions needed for a project to qualify for payment.

structured_extraction.program_name: Maryland Agricultural Water Quality Cost-Share Program (MACS) – Horse and Livestock Watering Facilities
structured_extraction.program_description: Provides cost-share grants to farmers to install frost-free waterers and spring developments that give livestock a clean, dependable water supply away from streams, helping protect waterways and improve pasture management. The program covers over 40 best management practices including erosion control, soil health, stream protection, manure/barnyard management, and conservation drainage, and has been active since 1984.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Up to 87.5% cost-share is available for installing horse and livestock watering facilities, including frost-free waterers and spring developments. Up to 100% cost-share is available for certain high-priority practices. Up to $28/ton for manure transport grants. Funding can be combined with federal conservation grants. State cost-share funds also available on a per-acre basis for manure injection and other practices.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Maryland livestock and horse farmers whose pastures border streams; agricultural operators including dairy, beef, livestock, and poultry operations with conservation goals
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Installation of frost-free waterers and spring developments to provide clean water sources for livestock away from streams; erosion control and soil health practices; stream protection practices; manure and barnyard management; conservation drainage; nutrient management; wildlife habitat creation; installation of conservation best management practices (BMPs) for water quality improvements
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Statewide Maryland across all 24 counties; apply through local soil conservation district. Also applicable to farms in Chesapeake Bay watershed, coastal zone, and western regions.
requirements_list: Must be a farmer with livestock
Pasture must border a stream or have a suitable water source for development
Work with local soil conservation district
Obtain necessary federal, state, and local permits before construction (where applicable)
Follow technical specifications for each practice
Maintain permanent vegetative cover (varies by practice)
Keep accurate records (for pesticide management)
Follow state and local regulations
Many federal and state programs require Soil Conservation and Water Quality Plans (SCWQP)
CAFO-permitted livestock and poultry farms must obtain farm plans
Follow nutrient management plan recommendations
Submit annual fertilizer reports by March 1
Maintain current, non-expired nutrient management plans
Follow nutrient application setbacks
Follow winter nutrient application restrictions
Mix farm chemicals at least 100 feet from wells
Proper runoff outlet placement (minimum 5 feet from buildings)
Regular system maintenance and inspections
Abandoned wells must be properly closed and sealed
Minimum 15 animal units required for roofs and covers cost-share eligibility
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Contact your local soil conservation district for free technical assistance to identify suitable water sources, develop a personalized farm plan, and apply for grants. Reference document available at: http://mda.maryland.gov/resource_conservation/Documents/MDA_ConsChoices_2025_web.pdf

structured_extraction.program_name: Maryland Agricultural Water Quality Cost-Share Program (MACS) – Livestock Exclusion Fencing
structured_extraction.program_description: Provides cost-share grants to farmers to install agricultural conservation practices including erosion control, soil health, stream protection (livestock fencing, riparian buffers, stream crossings), manure/barnyard management, and conservation drainage. Over 40 best management practices are eligible for funding. Provides free technical assistance for project design and installation.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Up to 100% cost-share available for high-priority conservation practices; up to 87.5% cost-share for certain practices (e.g., livestock exclusion fencing); up to $28/ton for manure transport grants. Can be combined with federal conservation grants. Free technical assistance is also provided for project design and installation.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Maryland farmers, including livestock, dairy, beef, poultry, and crop farmers
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Erosion control and soil health practices (grade stabilization, grassed waterways, cover crops, etc.); stream protection practices (livestock fencing, riparian buffers, stream crossings, etc.); manure and barnyard management (waste storage, manure injection, roofs and covers); rotational grazing, silvopasture, pollinator habitat, wetland restoration, and other conservation best management practices
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Statewide Maryland, including Chesapeake Bay watershed, coastal zone, and western Maryland regions; apply through local soil conservation district
requirements_list: Must be a farmer with livestock or agricultural operation
Pasture must border a stream (for fencing practice)
Must obtain a Soil Conservation and Water Quality Plan (SCWQP) or farm plan
CAFO farms must obtain farm plans as part of Maryland Department of Environment permitting
Work with local soil conservation district
Obtain necessary federal, state, and local permits before construction
Comply with federal, state, and local requirements
Develop required nutrient management plans
Maintain annual fertilizer application records and reports (due March 1 annually)
Follow nutrient application setback requirements and winter nutrient application restrictions
Regular inspection and maintenance of installed structures
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Contact your local soil conservation district for free personalized farm plan and technical assistance. District staff help estimate installation costs, design conservation practices, and navigate cost-share programs. Obtain necessary permits before implementation.

structured_extraction.program_name: Maryland Agricultural Water Quality Cost-Share Program (MACS) – Stream Crossings
structured_extraction.program_description: Provides cost-share grants to farmers to implement best management practices for erosion control, soil health, stream protection, manure/barnyard management, and conservation drainage. Includes more than 40 eligible practices such as grassed waterways, riparian buffers, livestock stream exclusion fencing, stream crossings, cover crops, and wetland restoration. Program has been operating since 1984.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Up to 100% cost-share available for certain high-priority conservation practices; up to 87.5% cost-share for other practices; up to $28/ton for manure transport grants. Free technical assistance for design and installation, including free Soil Conservation and Water Quality Plans (SCWQP) from local soil conservation districts.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Maryland farmers and agricultural landowners, including livestock, poultry, dairy, beef, and crop farming operations
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Erosion control and soil health practices (grassed waterways, terraces, cover crops, critical area plantings); stream protection practices (filter strips, livestock stream exclusion fencing, riparian forest buffers, stream crossings, wetland restoration); manure and barnyard management; conservation drainage; pasture management improvements; habitat restoration
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Statewide Maryland, including Chesapeake Bay watershed, coastal zone, and western regions; apply through local soil conservation district
requirements_list: Must be a Maryland farmer or agricultural landowner
Work with local soil conservation district for technical guidance and plan development
Many federal and state programs require a Soil Conservation and Water Quality Plan (SCWQP)
Current nutrient management plan required for applicable practices
Follow state and federal regulations and comply with setback requirements and winter application restrictions
Maintain records and reports (e.g., annual fertilizer reports by March 1)
Soil testing every three years
Manure testing every other year
Necessary permits or authorizations required before construction
Practices must comply with federal, state, and local requirements
Riparian forest buffers should be at least 1/3 of floodplain width or 35 feet wide
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Contact your local soil conservation district for free technical assistance to develop a conservation plan and install eligible practices. All 24 Maryland county soil conservation districts participate in the program.

structured_extraction.program_name: Maryland Agricultural Water Quality Cost-Share Program (MACS) – Stream Protection Practices
structured_extraction.program_description: The Maryland Agricultural Water Quality Cost-Share (MACS) Program provides cost-share grants to farmers for installing stream protection and water quality best management practices. These include livestock exclusion fencing, stream crossings, livestock watering facilities, riparian forest buffers, grassed waterways, erosion control structures, manure management, and more than 40 eligible practices across categories including erosion control & soil health, stream protection, manure & barnyard management, and conservation drainage. The program protects local waterways, reduces erosion and pollution, helps farmers comply with livestock setback and nutrient management regulations, and improves herd health. Free technical assistance and cost-share grants are provided through local soil conservation districts.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Up to 87.5% cost-share is available for livestock watering facilities, stream fencing, and stream crossings. Up to 100% cost-share is available for certain high-priority practices including planting riparian forest buffers, plus $2 for each tree planted. Up to $28/ton available for manure transport grants. The Conservation Reserve Enhancement Program (CREP) provides steady annual rental income for qualifying buffer planting. Free technical planning, design, and installation assistance is provided through local soil conservation districts. Soil Conservation and Water Quality Plans (SCWQP) are provided free of charge.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Maryland farmers and agricultural landowners, including livestock, horse, dairy, poultry, and crop farmers whose land borders streams or waterways in Maryland
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Installation of livestock exclusion fencing, stream crossings, livestock watering facilities (frost-free waterers, spring developments, watering troughs), planting of riparian forest buffers, grassed waterways, grade stabilization structures, manure storage and transport, nutrient management planning, cover crops, rotational grazing, silvopasture, heavy use area protection, well protection, windbreaks, roof runoff systems, and other conservation best management practices
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Statewide in Maryland, covering all 24 counties and the Chesapeake Bay watershed, coastal zone, and western regions
requirements_list: Applicant must be a livestock, horse, or other agricultural farmer/producer
Pasture or agricultural land must border a stream or waterway (for stream protection practices)
Must work with local soil conservation district
Soil Conservation and Water Quality Plan (SCWQP) often required
CAFO farms require farm plans as part of permitting process
Obtain necessary federal, state, and local permits before construction where applicable
Follow NRCS recommendations and guidelines
Maintain permanent vegetative cover where required
Comply with state and local regulations
Follow nutrient management plan requirements (4Rs approach)
Submit annual fertilizer reports to MDA by March 1
Maintain operation and maintenance plans
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Contact your local soil conservation district for free technical assistance, to develop a Soil Conservation and Water Quality Plan (SCWQP), and to apply for cost-share grants. Local district staff provide planning, design, and installation support and help navigate federal and state programs.

structured_extraction.program_description: A recognition program that honors farm families whose land has remained in the same family for at least 100 consecutive years and continues to be productive. The program celebrates the contributions of these families to Maryland's agricultural heritage and economy.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Selected farm families receive official recognition as a Maryland Century Farm, including participation in an award ceremony, a Governor and Secretary of Agriculture-signed certificate, listing on the Century Farms plaque at MDA headquarters, a farm sign for posting, and potential eligibility for State and National Registers of Historic Places benefits. No financial assistance is provided.
structured_extraction.application_deadline_string: A family may apply at any time throughout the year
structured_extraction.program_audience: Maryland farm families with 100 or more years of consecutive family ownership whose farm remains productive.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Recognition only — no financial assistance provided.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Farm property must be located in the State of Maryland.
requirements_list: Farm must have been owned by the same family for at least 100 consecutive years
Farm must be lived on or farmed by a descendant of the original owner
Minimum of 10 acres of the original holding must remain
Farm must gross over $2,500 annually from farm product sales
Documentation of continuous ownership via deeds, abstracts, or tax statements required
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Contact MDA or visit www.mda.maryland.gov for the application form; complete and submit to MDA at 50 Harry S. Truman Parkway, Annapolis, MD 21401; the Century Farm Committee reviews and approves applications; the Secretary of Agriculture certifies approved applications; recognized farms are honored at an annual recognition ceremony.

structured_extraction.program_name: Maryland Department of Agriculture International Marketing Program
structured_extraction.program_description: The Maryland Department of Agriculture's International Marketing Program helps Maryland agricultural producers and suppliers — including farmers, processors, breeders, and watermen — export their products to overseas markets. It introduces them to international buyers and facilitates mutually beneficial trade relationships. The program provides technical assistance with exporting, connects businesses with foreign buyers, organizes trade missions and trade shows abroad, and helps companies navigate shipping, labeling, import restrictions, and other international trade challenges. Through the Southern U.S. Trade Association (SUSTA) Market Access Program (MAP), funding is also allocated directly to Maryland companies for their own export promotions.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: The program provides technical export assistance including: identifying and evaluating export opportunities, developing trade leads and strategies, making introductions to overseas buyers and importers, organizing trade missions and trade shows abroad, providing access to export research and programs, conducting training seminars and informational workshops, and navigating shipping, labeling, and import requirements. Marketing staff connects Maryland agricultural producers with international buyers and provides guidance on navigating export opportunities. Through the Southern U.S. Trade Association (SUSTA) Market Access Program (MAP), funding is also allocated directly to Maryland companies for their own export promotions.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Maryland agricultural producers and suppliers — including farmers, processors, breeders, and watermen — looking to export products to international markets
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Export promotion activities, trade missions, trade shows, and international market development for Maryland agricultural products
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available to Maryland-based agricultural producers and suppliers statewide
requirements_list: Must be a Maryland producer or supplier seeking to export agricultural products
Completion of application form
Current markets and desired markets identification
Company and contact information
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Complete and submit the International Marketing Assistance Form to MDA's International Marketing Director Stone Slade at stone.slade@maryland.gov

structured_extraction.program_description: A voluntary program to minimize the risk of Salmonella enteritidis (SE) contamination of chicken (shell) eggs. Participating egg producers and processors commit to management and monitoring practices that prevent SE contamination. The program does not guarantee eggs are free of SE but assures commitment to these practices. The Maryland Department of Agriculture (MDA) provides oversight, technical advice, and compliance inspections. The Maryland Department of Health and Mental Hygiene (MDHMH) provides technical advice on public health implications. Eggs produced and processed under program guidelines may be identified with the Maryland's Best logo.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: MDA provides oversight, technical advice, and compliance inspections. Participants pay for sampling supplies, culturing costs, training, program monitoring, semiannual flock visits (for producers), and quarterly processing plant visits (for processors). Participants who meet program standards may label their eggs with the Maryland's Best logo. The program includes sample collection and testing for Salmonella, training on SE prevention procedures, semiannual flock monitoring visits for producers, and quarterly monitoring visits for processors.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Egg producers and processors (including egg packing plants) in Maryland who want to demonstrate commitment to Salmonella enteritidis prevention and qualify to use the Maryland's Best logo on their eggs. Flocks outside Maryland may participate at the Department's discretion.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Participants pay for: sampling supplies, culturing costs, training, program monitoring, semiannual flock visits (producers), and quarterly processing plant visits (processors). The program provides technical assistance and oversight rather than financial funding.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available statewide in Maryland to egg producers and processors. Participation of flocks or processing of eggs from outside Maryland may be permitted at the Department's discretion based on equivalent program status.
requirements_list: Obtain chicks from U.S. Sanitation Monitored SE-negative breeder flocks
Swab chick delivery containers and submit for SE culture
Culture manure in pullet facilities at 10-15 weeks of age
Implement rodent control
Clean and disinfect facilities between flocks
Conduct environmental monitoring of pullet and layer houses
Continuously test eggs from environmentally positive houses
Properly handle eggs on farm
Divert SE-positive eggs for pasteurization or hard cooking
Maintain diversion records for at least six months
Entire complex must enter the program (not individual poultry houses)
Cooperate with program personnel and farm visits
Participate in training sessions
Determine sample collection dates and collect samples per protocols
Transport samples to designated laboratories
Maintain standard MDA-approved logs for each flock
Follow washing, refrigeration, labeling, and quality control guidelines for egg processing
Maintain records that all eggs are from Maryland flocks in good standing in MEQAP
Monitor and record wash water temperature (minimum 90°F and 20°F warmer than eggs) and pH (minimum 10) every two hours
Maintain records of corrective actions when wash water falls below minimums
Pack only into new cartons or new fiber filler flats
Maintain plant sanitation records during processing (or rely on USDA grader records if on-site)
Cooperate with MDA monitoring and prevention procedures
Participate in quality control and recordkeeping training
Implement MDA-approved rodent control program
Remove MDA logo from non-compliant egg cartons/cases
Adopt Standard Operating Procedures for sanitation and egg quality per MDA standards
Pay for training and monitoring costs
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Producers submit a MEQAP Producer Application and processors submit a MEQAP Processor Application (Processor Participation Agreement) to MDA's Animal Health and Grading Services/Egg Inspection division. Participants must meet the management and monitoring requirements outlined in the program requirements document.

structured_extraction.program_description: Provides Maryland income tax credits to farmers who donate eligible food products to certified food banks and food pantries. The credit is based on the value of the donated food, calculated using USDA wholesale price listings. Originally a pilot program for tax years 2017, 2018, and 2019, operating in cooperation with the Comptroller.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Farmers may receive a Maryland income tax credit based on the value of food donated to certified food banks or pantries: 50% tax credit for donation of eligible fresh farm products, and 75% tax credit for donation of certified organic produce. Maximum aggregate credit per farm per taxable year is $5,000 (unless increased by the Maryland Secretary of Agriculture up to $10,000). Credit value is determined using USDA wholesale price listings. Credits may only be claimed for tax years 2017, 2018, and 2019 (after December 31, 2016, but before January 1, 2020).
structured_extraction.application_deadline_string: TCCAs may not issue tax credit certificates after December 31, 2019
structured_extraction.program_audience: Qualified farms in eligible counties and 501(c)(3) non-profit organizations seeking TCCA certification to accept eligible food donations.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Tax credit offset for Maryland income taxes, based on the value of food donated to certified food banks and pantries (fresh farm products and certified organic produce for human consumption).
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Farms must be located in Anne Arundel, Calvert, Charles, Montgomery, Prince George's, or St. Mary's County.
requirements_list: Donor must be a qualified farm located in an eligible county
Recipient organization must be a certified Tax Credit Certificate Administrator (TCCA) approved by the Maryland Department of Agriculture
Donated products must be eligible food products (fresh farm products for human consumption)
Food must be donated to a food bank or food pantry certified by MDA
Credit value is calculated using USDA wholesale price listings
50% tax credit for conventional fresh farm products; 75% for certified organic produce
Maximum aggregate credit per farm per taxable year is $5,000 (unless increased by Secretary)
Producer/Farm must complete Food Donation Pilot Program Tax Credit Certificate form
Must provide donation date, farm name, contact information, federal tax ID/SSN
Must specify commodity type, organic/conventional certification status, weight, and measurement/unit
Form must be signed and sent to MDA Marketing Office
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Non-profit 501(c)(3) organizations wishing to accept eligible food donations must become a Tax Credit Certificate Administrator (TCCA) by completing the Application for Tax Credit Certificate Administrator and submitting it to MDA. Once approved, the TCCA can submit eligible food donations from qualified farms by completing the Producer Donation Form (including donation date, farm name, contact information, federal tax ID/SSN, commodity type, organic/conventional status, weight, and unit) and sending it to the MDA Marketing Office by mail or email.

structured_extraction.program_name: Maryland Food and Agricultural Resiliency Mechanism Grant Program (MFARM)
structured_extraction.program_description: MFARM helps people who are food insecure access nutritious food while providing a market for Maryland farmers and seafood providers. The program builds food system resiliency by using Maryland agricultural and seafood products to support food banks and charitable emergency food providers across the state. It is a competitive grant program that provides funding to purchase from Certified Local Farm and Fish Program providers.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Competitive grants ranging from a minimum of $5,000 to a maximum of $40,000. Total funding available is $200,000. At least 80% of grant funds must go toward food costs (purchasing agricultural and seafood products); up to 20% may cover transportation, distribution, staff, and supplies. Funding is disbursed 80% upfront upon agreement signing and 20% upon submission of the final program and financial report.
structured_extraction.contact_name: Karen Fedor, Administrator, Farm and Food Programs
structured_extraction.program_audience: Maryland food banks, charitable emergency food providers, mission-driven nonprofits, faith-based organizations, and food pantries focused on food insecurity or food access that are registered and in good standing with the Maryland Department of Assessments and Taxation, and registered as a charity with the Maryland Secretary of State. Ultimately serves food-insecure residents in Maryland.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Purchase agricultural and seafood products listed in the Certified Local Farm and Fish (CLFF) Directory, and transport those products to Maryland families in need. At least 80% of funds must go toward food costs; up to 20% may cover transportation, distribution, staff, and operational expenses. Products purchased must be distributed to Maryland residents only (not the greater DC area).
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available statewide in Maryland. Recipients must serve Maryland families in need. Purchased products must go to Maryland residents only.
requirements_list: Must be a Maryland food bank, charitable emergency food provider, food pantry, or nonprofit focused on food insecurity or food access
Faith-based or religious organizations must be registered with the Maryland Secretary of State or provide an exemption letter
Must be registered and in good standing with the Maryland Department of Assessments and Taxation
Must be registered as a charity with the Maryland Secretary of State
Must submit a signed W-9 form (signed within past 2 years with matching address)
If you have an established relationship with producers or seafood providers from the Certified Local Farm and Fish Directory, must provide a signed Letter of Support from those producers
Farm partners must be registered in the CLFF directory
Farms must have a nutrient management plan to be listed in the CLFF directory (including nonprofit farmers)
Must have infrastructure to support fresh, local food distribution
Reporting requirements apply, including food donation reporting (sample reports available on OneStop public profile)
Must provide quantifiable, measurable impacts in the application
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Apply online through the OnestopMD application portal linked on the program page. The process is competitive and applicants must provide quantifiable, measurable impacts. Letters of support from producers with established relationships from the CLFF Directory are required where applicable.

structured_extraction.program_description: A registration and licensing program for growers who want to grow hemp commercially in Maryland. The program licenses and regulates the production of hemp in the State, approved by the USDA. Participants may grow, cultivate, harvest, process, manufacture, transport, market, or sell industrial hemp for commercial purposes. Does not apply to institutions of higher education or persons producing hemp under the Hemp Research Pilot Program.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Written authorization (license) permitting a person to cultivate, store, handle, or market hemp in Maryland. Licenses are valid from the date issued through December 31 of the same year. Annual license renewal must be submitted no later than December 1 of the year the license expires. Program includes annual inspections, THC testing requirements (≤0.3% delta-9 THC dry weight basis), record-keeping mandates, and regulatory oversight.
structured_extraction.application_deadline_string: Annual license renewal must be submitted no later than December 1 of the year the license expires; annual USDA reporting deadline is December 15
structured_extraction.program_audience: Maryland growers and farmers interested in growing hemp for commercial purposes, including grain, fiber, and floral material for CBD extraction.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Cultivation, storage, handling, and marketing of hemp. May market: seed, grain, fiber, hurd, or CBD.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available to growers statewide in Maryland. Outdoor production must be 1,000 feet from schools or public recreation areas. Land must be located within Maryland State.
requirements_list: Must be at least 18 years old
No felony convictions related to controlled substances in the preceding 10 years
Must submit FBI criminal background report dated no more than 60 days before application
Must demonstrate legal right to cultivate hemp on proposed land (landowner permission required if applicant does not own the site)
Must provide complete application with GPS coordinates, maps, and legal descriptions of production land
Must maintain records for a minimum of 3 years (planting, harvesting, sampling, testing, disposal records)
Must permit Department and law enforcement access for inspection and sampling
THC concentration must not exceed 0.3% on a dry weight basis; crops exceeding 0.3% THC must be destroyed
Must submit annual production reports by December 1
Must report to USDA Farm Service Agency
Must maintain traceability documentation from seed acquisition to harvest/crop termination
Must submit hemp disposal reports with licensee information, location data, disposal agent details, and records
Must comply with Maryland Nutrient Management and Pesticide Regulations
Must apply online through the Maryland OneStop portal
Must register growing sites with the Maryland Department of Agriculture
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: 8-step process: (1) Determine hemp type (grain, fiber, or CBD floral material); (2) Partner with institution if applying for research program; (3) Develop crop use/destruction plan; (4) Select appropriate growing location; (5) Complete FBI criminal background check; (6) Apply for MDA site registration via the Maryland OneStop portal online; (7) Submit background check with application; (8) Develop compliance plan. Hemp Research Pilot Program applicants should complete a PDF application and mail to MDA headquarters.

structured_extraction.program_description: A program for growers who want to partner with an institute of higher education or the Maryland Department of Agriculture to grow industrial hemp under a supervised research program.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Registration and oversight for industrial hemp grown under a research partnership with an institute of higher education or the Maryland Department of Agriculture.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Growers interested in partnering with an institute of higher education or the Maryland Department of Agriculture to grow industrial hemp for research purposes.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Growing industrial hemp for research purposes, including any aspect of growing, cultivating, harvesting, processing, manufacturing, transporting, marketing, or selling industrial hemp.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available to growers statewide in Maryland.
requirements_list: Must partner with an institute of higher education or the Maryland Department of Agriculture
Must complete a PDF application and mail it with supporting documents to the Maryland Department of Agriculture
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Complete the PDF application and mail it along with supporting documents to: Maryland Department of Agriculture, 50 Harry S. Truman Parkway, Annapolis, MD 21401.

structured_extraction.program_description: This program supports Maryland's horse industry. The board promotes horse-related activities and recreation. It also supports educational projects, job training, and planning for facilities to help the local horse economy grow. The board advises the Secretary of Agriculture and licenses stables in Maryland.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: The board supports the horse industry through promotional activities, educational and research projects, and development efforts like job training and facilities planning. The website's navigation indicates that grants are available, but this page does not provide specific details.
structured_extraction.program_audience: People and businesses in Maryland's horse industry, including horse owners and stable operators.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: The program is available statewide.

structured_extraction.program_name: Maryland Horse Industry Board Grant Program
structured_extraction.program_description: The Maryland Horse Industry Board (MHIB) Grant Program supports the Maryland horse industry by funding research, education, and promotional activities. Developed to promote, bring awareness to and help grow the state's horse industry, the program's main goals are: 1) increase public awareness and participation, 2) advance education and training in youth and adults, 3) support and promote equestrian events, programs, and activities, and 4) preserve access and use of public lands for riding. Each year, the MHIB accepts applications for projects that support horses or the equestrian community, or develop new opportunities for the Maryland horse industry. A Grants Committee meets once a year to review applications and recommend recipients to the board. Funding comes from the Maryland Feed Fund, which collects $6 on every ton of horse feed sold in Maryland, as well as licensing fees paid by commercial equine facilities and voluntary Feed Fund Assessment fees from horse feed manufacturers.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Grants are awarded annually for research, educational, and promotional projects related to horses and the equestrian community. Grant requests should not exceed $2,000; the average grant amount is approximately $1,000. Total grant monies awarded each year up to $30,000. Awards range from $250 to $2,000 for projects advancing the horse industry through education, therapy, career development, outreach, and welfare initiatives. Funding comes from the Maryland Feed Fund, which collects $6 on every ton of horse feed sold in Maryland, as well as licensing fees paid by commercial equine facilities and voluntary Feed Fund Assessment fees from horse feed manufacturers.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Non-profit organizations, clubs and associations, businesses, farms and stables, horse rescues, government entities, schools, educational institutions, individuals, therapeutic riding programs, and other stakeholders involved in or supporting the Maryland horse industry, including adults seeking equine careers, youth, underserved/low-income families, veterans, first responders, at-risk youth, people with disabilities, and equine professionals.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Public awareness and participation initiatives; education and training programs for youth and adults; equestrian events, programs, and activities; public lands access and riding preservation projects; therapeutic services; training and clinics; marketing and outreach; teaching materials; community events; equipment and supplies. Conference/training/certification attendance limited to $500 or less. Less likely to fund: capital expenditures on farms, already-purchased supplies, university overhead/indirect costs, purchase/lease/care of horses.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available statewide in Maryland.
requirements_list: Applicant must be a non-profit or not-for-profit organization, club, association, business, farm, stable, horse rescue, government entity, school, educational institution, or individual
Organization or program must be based in Maryland
Project must support horses, the equestrian community, or develop new opportunities for the Maryland horse industry
Grant requests should not exceed $2,000
Conference/training/certification attendance limited to $500 or less
Projects should be completed by June 30
Applications are evaluated on value to the industry, degree of industry promotion, size and scope, financial need, potential for matching funds, benefits, and quality of written presentation
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Submit a grant application online by October 4th, 2025. The Grants Committee meets once a year to review applications and recommend recipients to the MHIB board. Recipients are typically announced in early January. To be notified of future grant cycles, sign up for the email distribution list via GovDelivery and select 'Grants' under the Horse Industry Board quick subscribe options. Questions can be directed to anne.litz@maryland.gov.

structured_extraction.program_description: The Maryland Organic Certification Program (MOCP) certifies farm operations in Maryland that grow and/or process foods sold or labeled as organic under the USDA National Organic Program (NOP). The Maryland Department of Agriculture (MDA) is accredited by USDA as a certifying agent for producers located in Maryland. Certification covers crops, livestock, wild crops, and small-scale on-farm handling and processing. Certified producers can legally use the term 'organic' for their products. MDA reviews Organic System Plans (OSPs), conducts on-site inspections, and issues organic certification to qualifying operations. Note: MDA does not certify individual processing or handling operations such as food processors, brokers, or importers, and does not certify farms outside of Maryland. An optional exempt registration program is also available for producers with $5,000 or less in annual organic sales, who may register with MDA instead of seeking full certification.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: MDA reviews Organic System Plans (OSPs) and certifies crop and livestock farm operations to USDA National Organic Program (NOP) standards, allowing farms to legally sell, label, and represent their products as certified organic. New applicants pay a $500 application fee and must develop an OSP. Certified producers renew annually by April 1 for a $500 renewal fee. USDA cost-share funding provides 75% reimbursement of certification fees, up to a maximum of $750 per scope, annually. Producers with $5,000 or less in annual organic sales may register as exempt for a $30 fee. Operations earning more than $5,000 annually must be fully certified. MDA does not certify individual processing or handling operations such as food processors, brokers, or importers.
structured_extraction.application_deadline_string: Annual update due April 1 each year; new applicants may apply at any time; exempt registration must be filed annually
structured_extraction.program_audience: Maryland crop and livestock farm operations that grow and/or process foods sold, labeled, or represented as organic, including new applicants and currently certified producers seeking renewal. Also includes small-scale exempt producers with annual organic sales of $5,000 or less.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Certification allows producers to legally sell, label, and represent their products as organic under USDA National Organic Program standards. USDA cost-share reimbursement is available for certification fees (75% reimbursement up to $750 per scope annually).
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available to farm and processing operations located in Maryland only. MDA does not certify farms outside of Maryland.
