structured_extraction.program_name: Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA) Therapy – Maryland Medicaid
structured_extraction.program_description: Maryland Medicaid covers medically necessary Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA) therapy services for members under age 21 with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) through the Early Periodic Screening, Diagnosis, and Treatment (EPSDT) program. ABA is an evidence-based treatment that uses various techniques to increase useful behaviors such as communication and social skills, and to reduce behaviors that interfere with learning or may be harmful. Services are delivered in home, community, clinic, or school settings as medically necessary and include behavior identification assessment, adaptive behavior treatment, family guidance, parent/caregiver training, and group treatment options. Carelon Behavioral Health Maryland (BHASO) administers the program and provides clinical, operational, and provider support including preauthorization and billing. A fee schedule detailing reimbursement rates is available for enrolled providers.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Medicaid covers the cost of medically necessary ABA therapy services for eligible members under age 21 via fee-for-service reimbursement. Covered services include ABA assessments and reassessments, behavior identification supporting assessments, ABA therapy (individual, group, social skills), parent/caregiver training, supervision and direction of behavior technicians, and telehealth delivery for specific service types. Reimbursement is provided through Carelon Behavioral Health Maryland using specified CPT codes and reimbursement rates. Services are discontinued if no longer medically necessary, goals are achieved, or no measurable progress is demonstrated.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Maryland Medicaid members under age 21 diagnosed with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) residing in home or community settings, and ABA therapy providers (licensed psychologists, BCBA-D, BCBA, BCaBA, RBT, BT) seeking to enroll with Maryland Medicaid.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: ABA therapy services to increase communication and social skills and reduce harmful or learning-interfering behaviors in individuals with ASD, including treatment planning, behavioral assessments, parent/caregiver training, and skill generalization.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available statewide in Maryland to Medicaid-eligible individuals under age 21.
requirements_list: Must be a Maryland Medicaid member
Must be under age 21
Must have a confirmed diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD)
Services must be medically necessary
Must reside in a home or community setting
Must be referred by a qualified health care professional
Individualized treatment plan based on medical necessity required
Parent/caregiver training required
Progress toward treatment goals must be demonstrated
Services discontinued if no longer medically necessary or goals achieved
Sentinel events must be reported within 24 hours
No duplication of services
Providers must be enrolled with Maryland Medicaid and registered with Carelon Behavioral Health Maryland
Providers must complete a Provider Application Addendum
Licensed psychologists must complete and submit the ABA Psychologist Attestation Form to mdh.aba@maryland.gov and register with Carelon Behavioral Health
For school-based services, detailed fade-out and generalization plans required
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Providers must enroll with Maryland Medicaid through the provider enrollment process and complete a Provider Application Addendum. Licensed psychologists must also complete the ABA Psychologist Attestation Form, attest to qualification to provide ABA services and acting within scope of practice, and email the completed form to mdh.aba@maryland.gov. All providers must register with Carelon Behavioral Health Maryland at https://maryland.carelonbh.com/behavioral-health-providers/join-the-network/. For enrollment questions, email mdh.aba@maryland.gov or call the Carelon Call Center at 1-800-888-1965 (weekdays 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.; TTY: 711).

structured_extraction.program_name: Assessment, Evaluation and Review Services (AERS) Program
structured_extraction.program_description: AERS is a Maryland program based in local health departments that provides comprehensive evaluations and assistance to frail, aged, medically fragile, disabled, and vulnerable individuals — both children and adults — who are at risk of being placed in a nursing home or other institutional setting. A licensed Registered Nurse, nurse social worker, or multidisciplinary team conducts a comprehensive in-home or facility-based assessment to identify medical and social needs, develop a personalized care plan, and connect clients to community resources and Medicaid-funded long-term services and supports. The program's goal is to promote independence and help individuals remain at home or in the least restrictive environment, preventing unnecessary entry into a nursing home or other residential care facility. Services are available statewide through local health departments, including Baltimore City, Howard County, Queen Anne's County, and Montgomery County. Interpretation and translation services are available. There are no fees for this service.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Comprehensive in-home or facility-based evaluations conducted by a licensed Registered Nurse, nurse social worker, or multidisciplinary team to assess medical and social needs and develop a personalized individualized care plan with recommendations and referrals to community resources and services. The program connects individuals to community services including Community First Choice (CFC) and Community Personal Assistance Services (CPAS), which provide hands-on help with activities of daily living such as bathing, dressing, meal preparation, light chores, and accessing the community. Services also include access to Medicaid-funded long-term services and supports. Available through local health departments across Maryland including Howard County Health Department. Interpretation and translation services are available. There are no fees for this service.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Frail, aged, medically fragile, disabled, and vulnerable Maryland adults and children — including older adults and adults with disabilities — who are at risk of placement in a care facility or institutionalization, have chronic medical conditions, or need help with activities of daily living and want to remain living safely in the community. Available to residents across Maryland counties including Howard County.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: In-home or facility-based evaluation, personalized care planning, and connection to community support services and Medicaid-funded long-term services and supports, including assistance with activities of daily living such as bathing, dressing, meal preparation, light chores, mobility, and community access, as well as referrals to appropriate community resources and services.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available to residents of Maryland counties and municipalities served by local health departments, including Howard County, Queen Anne's County, Montgomery County, and Baltimore City. Howard County residents may visit the Howard County Health Department AERS page. Queen Anne's County residents may use the online referral form or contact the local office directly. Baltimore City residents may call 410-396-6006. Montgomery County residents may call 1-877-463-3464. Residents of other counties should contact their local health department or Maryland Access Point (MAP).
requirements_list: Must be a Maryland resident
Must be an older adult, or a frail, aged, medically fragile, disabled, or vulnerable individual (child or adult) at risk of placement in a care facility or institutionalization
May have chronic medical conditions or need help with activities of daily living
May need to meet specific medical and financial criteria (such as Medicaid eligibility) to qualify for specific programs like CFC or CPAS
Must meet medical, financial, and technical criteria to qualify for Medicaid-funded services
Must apply for Medical Assistance through the local Department of Social Services
Must be certified as medically eligible for nursing facility services (for Level II evaluation)
A physician must complete a Medical Eligibility Review Form (DHMH 3871)
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Submit an AERS Referral Form online (for Queen Anne's County residents), call Maryland Access Point (MAP) at 1-844-MAP-LINK (1-844-627-5465) or dial 211, or contact your local MAP Coordinator at 410-758-0848 (Queen Anne's County). Baltimore City residents may call 410-396-6006 for more information. Montgomery County residents may call 1-877-463-3464. Howard County residents may contact the Howard County Health Department directly. Apply for Medical Assistance through the local Department of Social Services. A physician must complete a Medical Eligibility Review Form (DHMH 3871). Once approved, contact AERS for a Level II evaluation. Residents of other counties should contact their local health department.

structured_extraction.program_name: Assistance in Community Integration Services (ACIS) Program
structured_extraction.program_description: The ACIS program is a Maryland Medicaid initiative that provides housing and tenancy-based case management services and supports to people who are experiencing homelessness or at risk of becoming homeless. A dedicated case manager works with each participant to create a supportive housing plan and connect them with services they need to live safely and independently in their home and community. The program targets high-risk, high-utilizing Medicaid enrollees who frequently cycle through multiple systems and have chronic health conditions, mental illness, substance use disorders, and/or a history of incarceration or homelessness. It provides low- or no-barrier stable housing and well-integrated medical care with wrap-around support services, funded through Maryland's Medicaid 1115 Health Choice Waiver. The program is currently operational in Baltimore City, Cecil County, Montgomery County, and Prince George's County, with expansion opportunities available through provider solicitations open to local health departments and county governments statewide. MDH is awarding 1,520 participant spaces to new and existing providers.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Participants (individuals) receive housing-related case management services including: community integration assessments, person-centered community integration plans, help connecting with social services, assistance communicating with landlords or property managers about accommodations, and training and resource support for managing a home. The program provides low- or no-barrier stable housing and well-integrated medical care with wrap-around support services. The program does not cover room and board or rental costs. For providers (Lead Entities), MDH awards 1,520 participant spaces to local health departments and county governments to deliver housing and tenancy-based services to eligible Medicaid members. Lead Entities receive a bundled rate of $725 per member per month (minimum three eligible services required per month per participant), plus $100 per member per year for annual compliance activities including Housing Supports Care Plan (HSCP) completion. Funding is split 50% State General Funds and 50% Federal Funds. Lead Entities may contract with Participating Entities (public non-profits or private for-profits) to deliver services.
structured_extraction.application_deadline_string: Letters of Intent (LOI): March 13, 2026 at 5PM; Full Application: March 27, 2026 at 5PM
structured_extraction.program_audience: Two audiences: (1) Maryland Medicaid recipients who are experiencing homelessness or at risk of homelessness, have two or more chronic conditions or frequent emergency room or hospital use, and live in a current ACIS service area; (2) Local health departments, county government entities, consortiums of entities serving a county or region, and public non-profit or private for-profit Participating Entities in Maryland that want to become ACIS providers and deliver housing and tenancy-based services to Medicaid members experiencing or at risk of homelessness.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Housing-related case management and community integration services to help participants live safely and independently in their home and community; stable housing placement and integrated medical and wrap-around support services; delivering housing and tenancy-based support services to eligible individuals who are experiencing homelessness or at risk of becoming homeless. Funds cannot be used for room and board or rental costs, and cannot duplicate or supplant existing federal funding.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Statewide expansion available across all Maryland counties (23 counties and Baltimore City). Currently operational in Baltimore City, Cecil County, Montgomery County, and Prince George's County. Provider solicitations are open statewide; providers deliver services within their local jurisdiction. Applicants must be enrolled Maryland Medicaid providers.
requirements_list: Must have Medicaid in Maryland (for individual participants)
Must meet at least one health criterion: two or more chronic conditions (long-term illness), OR four or more emergency room visits or hospitalizations per year (for individual participants)
Must meet at least one housing criterion: experiencing homelessness or at risk of homelessness, OR facing institutional placement (for individual participants)
Must choose to participate in the ACIS program (for individual participants)
Must reside in a current ACIS service area (for individual participants)
Must be fully enrolled as a Medicaid participant (FFS or HealthChoice MCO) (for individual participants)

structured_extraction.program_description: Behavioral Support Services help people with intellectual and developmental disabilities who are experiencing, or are likely to experience, difficulty at home or in the community due to behavioral, psychological, social, or emotional challenges. Services include a Behavioral Assessment and Plan, Behavioral Consultation, and Brief Support Implementation Services (BSIS) — a time-limited service that provides direct assistance and modeling to family members, staff, and other caregivers to help support the individual's behavioral, psychological, and emotional needs. The program uses a person-centered and trauma-informed approach with positive behavior supports (Tier 1, 2, and 3 interventions) to support meaningful social relationships at home, at work, and in the community. A Behavioral Respite component provides short-term support for individuals experiencing behavioral, social, or emotional challenges, including nursing supports, transportation, community integration, and discharge planning. Services are accessible through the Community Pathways Waiver, including a self-direction Budget Authority option, and are delivered by DDA-approved providers following a defined policy framework.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Provides behavioral assessment and plan development, behavioral consultation, and Brief Support Implementation Services (BSIS). BSIS delivers direct assistance and modeling to family members, staff, and caregivers to help them support the individual's behavioral, psychological, and emotional needs using trauma-informed care and positive behavior supports. A Behavioral Respite component offers short-term residential respite services including nursing supports, doctor's appointment assistance, technology use for communication/independence, community integration, transportation, intake assessment, transition planning, and discharge planning. Mobile Crisis services are also available statewide (call or text 988). Services are accessible through the Community Pathways Waiver with a self-direction Budget Authority option, and are delivered by DDA-approved providers following a defined policy framework.

structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Behavioral assessment and planning, behavioral consultation and monitoring, staff training in trauma-informed care and positive behavior supports, direct assistance and modeling for caregivers and family members through Brief Support Implementation Services (BSIS), and short-term behavioral respite services including nursing care, transportation, and community integration.

structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Contact your Coordination of Community Services (CCS) coordinator to determine eligibility and whether this service is appropriate for you. structured_extraction.program_name: CHRC Annual Request for Applications (RFA) Grant Program
structured_extraction.program_description: The Maryland Community Health Resources Commission (CHRC) awards competitive grants to help communities expand access to affordable, high-quality health care services in underserved areas of Maryland. The CHRC provides seed grant funding to nonprofit and community health organizations to help them launch and expand innovative health care programs, acting as an incubator for sustainable health care models. The program focuses on two strategic priorities: advancing health equity by addressing health disparities and social determinants of health, and supporting safety net providers and community-based organizations to participate in state health initiatives. The annual RFA (Call for Proposals) makes funding available across six areas of focus: hospital-community partnerships, chronic disease prevention and management, maternal and child health, dental health, behavioral health and substance use disorders, and support for medically vulnerable populations. Additional focus areas include primary care, infant mortality reduction, and health information technology adoption among safety net providers. In the FY 2026 funding round, $7 million in grants is available. Since the CHRC's inception in 2005, it has awarded 985 grants totaling $396 million, supporting programs in every jurisdiction of Maryland, and has enabled grantees to leverage $59.7 million in additional federal and private/nonprofit resources. Approximately 75% of grants have been sustained one year or more after initial funding expires. Nearly 1 million Marylanders have received services through CHRC-funded programs.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Competitive grants awarded approximately once a year through an annual RFA/Call for Proposals process. In the FY 2026 funding round, up to $7 million in total grant funding is available. Individual grant awards are anticipated at $300,000–$750,000 total per grant (no minimum grant amount), with funding covering up to 3 years. Six areas of focus each have projected funding ranges of $1,000,000–$1,500,000. Cannot be used for major capital expenses, major equipment purchase/lease, construction, clinical trials, non-FDA approved medical devices/drugs, or lobbying/political activity. Indirect costs are capped at 15% of direct costs (or higher if applicant qualifies under Md. Code Ann., State Finance and Procurement § 2-208(c)). Fringe benefits are limited to 25% of total personnel salaries. Since inception, CHRC has awarded 985 grants totaling $396 million. Grant amounts and terms are determined by each Call for Proposals. Proposals are evaluated by independent subject matter experts on criteria including use of evidence-based practices, ability to collect outcomes data, demonstrated community need, program sustainability, and likelihood of success. Awards are expected to be announced in late June 2026.
structured_extraction.application_deadline_string: Letter of Intent due March 30, 2026 at 3:00 PM EDT; Full proposals due April 23, 2026 by 3:00 PM EDT; awards expected in late June 2026

structured_extraction.program_audience: Community-based organizations, nonprofit health care organizations, safety net providers, health care providers, and government entities working to improve community health access in Maryland, serving underserved communities and seeking to expand access to health care services or launch/expand innovative health care programs. Includes federally qualified health centers (FQHCs) and FQHC look-alikes, school-based health centers, outpatient mental health clinics, local health departments, substance use treatment providers, primary health care services providers, hospitals, and access services organizations. Non-profit organizations and government entities working to reduce health disparities are also eligible. Includes safety-net providers and programs supporting primary care, dental care, behavioral health, infant mortality reduction, and health information technology adoption. Serves vulnerable Marylanders including older adults, individuals with disabilities, and residents in low-income neighborhoods. Designated Services providers (outpatient mental health clinics, substance use treatment/prevention providers holding BHA license), home health agencies, residential service agencies, licensed independent providers, and organizations with sliding fee scale compliance are also eligible.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Expanding access to health care services in underserved communities, including chronic disease prevention and management, behavioral health and substance use disorders, dental care, maternal and child health, primary care, infant mortality reduction, hospital-community partnerships, health information technology adoption among safety net providers, care for medically vulnerable populations (older adults and individuals with disabilities), health equity and social determinants of health (e.g., food security, transportation, health insurance), opening new clinic sites, hiring community health workers, home visitation programs, reducing avoidable emergency department visits and hospital admissions, and transitioning programs to sustainable billing or funding models. Allowable costs include project staff salaries and fringe benefits (fringe limited to 25% of personnel salaries), project-related contractual services, data collection and analysis, project-related travel, supplies, minor equipment, furniture, IT/telecom, minor infrastructure improvements, staff training/development, program marketing, and indirect costs (limited to 15% of direct costs, unless a higher rate is qualified under state law). Grant funds must supplement, not supplant, other funding sources.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available statewide across all Maryland jurisdictions, with priority given to underserved areas of the state including Western Maryland and Eastern Shore. Applicants serving ENOUGH Act eligible communities (concentrated low-income neighborhoods, 116 high-need census tracts across the state) receive additional consideration. Past grantees include organizations in Baltimore City, Baltimore County, Montgomery County, Prince George's County, Carroll County, Howard County, Charles County, Frederick County, Washington County, and Talbot County.

LHDs develop programs in coordination with Community Health Coalitions (CHCs) and the Maryland Department of Health. Specific dollar amounts are not publicly stated.

structured_extraction.program_name: Cancer Prevention, Education, Screening, and Treatment (CPEST) Program / Cigarette Restitution Fund Cancer Prevention, Education, Screening and Treatment Program (CRF-CPEST)
structured_extraction.program_description: The Cancer Prevention, Education, Screening, and Treatment (CPEST) Program administers grants from the Cigarette Restitution Fund (CRF) to local health departments, academic centers, health systems, and hospitals to reduce cancer mortality and cancer disparities in Maryland. The program coordinates the State's use of the CRF to create lasting public health initiatives that reduce mortality and morbidity rates for cancer and tobacco-related diseases, with a focus on seven targeted cancers: lung and bronchus, colorectal, breast, cervical, prostate, skin (melanoma), and oral cancers. It provides no-cost cancer prevention education, screening, diagnosis, and treatment services for low-income, uninsured, and underinsured Maryland residents. The program also supports cancer surveillance and evaluation of cancer data, publishes a Biennial Cancer Report, provides regional training and technical assistance, and funds translational cancer research at academic institutions such as Johns Hopkins and the University of Maryland. Applicants must form a Community Health Coalition and submit a cancer control plan to the Maryland Department of Health.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Grants and funding are distributed to local health departments, academic centers, health systems, and hospitals to support cancer prevention education, screening, diagnosis, and treatment services for low-income, uninsured, and underinsured Maryland residents. The program targets seven priority cancers: lung and bronchus, colorectal, breast, cervical, prostate, skin (melanoma), and oral cancers. Funding also supports regional training and technical assistance, cancer surveillance and evaluation, publication of a Biennial Cancer Report, and translational cancer research at Johns Hopkins and the University of Maryland. All funding originates from the Maryland Cigarette Restitution Fund.

structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Cancer prevention education, early detection, screening, diagnosis, and treatment services for targeted cancers (lung and bronchus, colorectal, breast, cervical, prostate, skin/melanoma, and oral cancers); cancer surveillance and evaluation; publication of a Biennial Cancer Report; translational cancer research; regional training and technical assistance.

structured_extraction.program_name: Childhood Lead Poisoning Prevention and Environmental Case Management Program (Healthy Homes for Healthy Kids)
structured_extraction.program_description: A free in-home services program for Maryland families with a child who has been exposed to lead or who has moderate to severe asthma. Trained staff visit the home to help identify and reduce exposures to lead and asthma triggers (including allergens, mold, tobacco smoke, and pests), provide family support and education, and eligible families can have lead hazards removed from their home, apartment, or day care at no cost. The program also provides in-home case management and environmental health services for children with asthma, assessing and addressing home conditions that may worsen asthma. Services are delivered through local county health departments in participating counties and the program is focused on children enrolled in or eligible for Medicaid or CHIP/MCHP. The program also connects families to information on lead abatement funding and resources, including funding to support lead abatement activities to remove or reduce lead hazards in homes.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Lead hazards are removed at no cost to eligible families from the home, apartment, or day care where the child is exposed to lead. The program also provides free in-home visits, case management, and support services to reduce lead and asthma trigger exposures (including allergens, mold, tobacco smoke, and pests), assess and address home environmental conditions that may worsen asthma, and offer family education and support. Families are also connected to lead abatement funding information, including grant funding to support the removal or reduction of lead hazards in homes. There is no specified dollar amount — the program covers the full cost of lead hazard remediation. Services are delivered through local county health departments in eligible counties.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Maryland families with a child 18 years old or younger (under 19) who has a blood lead level of 5 micrograms per deciliter or higher, or moderate to severe asthma (frequent attacks or on a daily long-term controller medication), and is enrolled in or eligible for Medicaid or CHIP/MCHP. Available statewide through local county health departments. Also open to Maryland residents, particularly families with children with lead poisoning, seeking lead abatement funding.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: In-home services to reduce lead exposure and asthma triggers, including removal of lead hazards from the home, apartment, or day care where the child is exposed to lead, as well as in-home visits, case management, family support, and education to improve asthma management and home environmental conditions. Also includes lead abatement activities in the home and connection to lead abatement funding resources.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available statewide in Maryland through local county health departments. Eligibility and availability may vary by jurisdiction. Child must live in Maryland. Historically served Anne Arundel, Baltimore City, Baltimore County, Charles, Dorchester, Frederick, Harford, Montgomery, Prince George's, St. Mary's, and Wicomico counties.

structured_extraction.program_name: Chronic Disease Self-Management Program (CDSMP) / Living Well Chronic Disease Self-Management Program (including Chronic Pain Self-Management Program)
structured_extraction.program_description: A free, evidence-based six-week self-management workshop series offered through Maryland Living Well and local health departments statewide—including Baltimore City, Cecil County, Carroll County, and Prince George's County—to help adults 18 and older with any long-term chronic condition (such as arthritis, diabetes, heart disease, hypertension, chronic pain, fibromyalgia, neuropathic pain, chronic musculoskeletal pain, or cancer) adopt and maintain healthy behaviors and live active, fulfilling lives. Sessions are led by two trained peer/volunteer facilitators (many of whom live with chronic conditions themselves) and meet once a week for approximately 2–2.5 hours in community settings (senior centers, churches, libraries, hospitals) or virtually. Topics covered include managing stress, fatigue, and pain; exercising safely; improving strength and endurance; using medications properly; eating healthy; communication skills; decision-making; action planning; goal-setting; problem-solving; handling frustration; future planning; and working with a health care team. Separate program tracks are available for diabetes, chronic pain (6-week Chronic Pain Self-Management Program / Living Well with Chronic Pain), cancer (Thriving and Surviving), and hypertension (a companion 2.5-hour class for people with high blood pressure). The Chronic Pain Self-Management Program is a dedicated six-week workshop held once a week in a small group format; participants receive a Living a Healthy Life with Chronic Conditions course book, a Chronic Pain Workbook, and the Moving Easy Program CD at no cost. Participants who complete the general program receive a 'Living a Healthy Life with Chronic Conditions' textbook and a 'Relaxation for Mind and Body' relaxation CD (donations appreciated but not required in some locations). Caregivers and family members are also welcome. The program is offered statewide, including virtually in Prince George's County (e.g., 6 FREE classes every Monday online, March 4–April 8, 2024, 4:00–6:30 pm), in-person at senior center sites in Baltimore City, at various community locations throughout Cecil County, and in Carroll County.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Free six-week community and virtual workshops (once weekly, approximately 2–2.5 hours per session) covering chronic disease self-management skills including stress management, healthy lifestyle development, improving strength and endurance, exercise, medication use, nutrition, communication skills, decision-making, action planning, goal-setting, problem-solving, handling frustration, increasing daily activity, emotional coping, future planning, and working with a health care team. Separate tracks are available for chronic conditions, diabetes, chronic pain, cancer (Thriving and Surviving), and hypertension. A companion 2.5-hour class is available for people with high blood pressure, offered before the main 6-week program. A separate 6-week Chronic Pain Self-Management Program (CPSMP) is available for people with chronic pain; participants in that track receive a Living a Healthy Life with Chronic Conditions course book, a Chronic Pain Workbook, and the Moving Easy Program CD at no cost. Participants who complete the general program receive a 'Living a Healthy Life with Chronic Conditions' textbook and a 'Relaxation for Mind and Body' relaxation CD (donations appreciated but not required in some locations). A minimum number of participants is required for classes to run. In Baltimore City, sessions run for six consecutive weeks at senior center sites. In Cecil County, workshops are held at various community locations throughout the county. In Carroll County, workshops are offered in-person and virtually with online registration. In Prince George's County, sessions are available virtually (e.g., every Monday online, 4:00–6:30 pm) and can be accessed by calling 301-265-0039 for a schedule.
structured_extraction.application_deadline_string: Rolling/ongoing statewide; links active until each workshop start date; Baltimore City session begins Thursday, April 23 (six consecutive weeks); Prince George's County session deadline March 8, 2024.

Caregivers and family members are also welcome.

Includes course materials such as the Living a Healthy Life with Chronic Conditions textbook, Relaxation for Mind and Body CD, and for chronic pain track participants: Chronic Pain Workbook and Moving Easy Program CD.

Carroll County residents may also call 410-386-3800 or email LivingHealthy@carrollcountymd.gov for assistance. Cecil County residents may contact Karly Lakavitch at 410-996-8170 or Holly Loss at 410-996-5168.

structured_extraction.program_description: The Cigarette Restitution Fund (CRF) Program uses money from the 1998 Master Tobacco Settlement Agreement with the tobacco industry to reduce the burden of tobacco-related disease in Maryland. It funds tobacco use prevention and cessation programs, cancer prevention and education, cancer screening, cancer treatment, and cancer research programs, as well as a statewide network of community health coalitions focused on cancer and tobacco issues. The program operates through two main components: the Tobacco Use Prevention and Cessation Program and the Cancer Prevention, Education, Screening, and Treatment Program. At the local level, such as in Queen Anne's County, the program offers smoking cessation counseling, free Nicotine Replacement Therapy (NRT) patches, and tobacco use prevention and cessation education to individual residents, community groups, school groups, and businesses.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Grants funded by tobacco settlement money are distributed through two main components: the Tobacco Use Prevention and Cessation Program and the Cancer Prevention, Education, Screening, and Treatment Program. These grants support tobacco use prevention and cessation programs and cancer prevention, education, screening, treatment, and research programs statewide. At the local level (e.g., Queen Anne's County), free Nicotine Replacement Therapy (NRT) patches and smoking cessation counseling are provided at no cost to eligible residents, along with tobacco use prevention and cessation education for community groups, school groups, and businesses. Specific grant amounts and terms are not stated on the program page.

structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Tobacco use prevention and cessation activities; cancer prevention, education, screening, treatment, and research programs; community health coalition support; smoking cessation counseling; free nicotine replacement therapy (NRT patches).

structured_extraction.program_description: The Collaborative Care Model (CoCM) is an evidence-based, patient-centered care model that integrates behavioral health services, including mental health and substance use disorder (SUD) treatment, into primary care settings. It uses a team-based approach — including a primary care provider (PCP), a behavioral health care manager, and a psychiatric consultant — to improve treatment for mental health and substance use disorders while reducing stigma. Primary care provider-led teams receive Medicaid reimbursement for delivering care coordination, systematic monitoring, and psychiatric consultation services under both HealthChoice and Fee-For-Service programs. Services are billed under the PCP's name and provider number, and no prior authorization is required. The program also supports Maryland Medicaid enrollees directly by helping them and their primary care providers coordinate mental health and behavioral health care, including treatment for depression and substance use disorders, at no cost to enrollees.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Medicaid reimbursement (fee-for-service and HealthChoice) for CoCM services billed under the primary care provider's name and provider number. No prior authorization is required for CoCM services under either program. Reimbursement covers care coordination and management, systematic monitoring using validated clinical rating scales, and psychiatric/SUD caseload reviews and consultations. Fee-for-Service reimbursement rates: CPT 99492 (initial 70-minute visit, first month): $161.28; CPT 99493 (subsequent 60-minute visit): $128.88; CPT 99494 (each additional 30 minutes, max 2 per month): $66.60; G0512 (FQHCs/RHCs only, 60+ minutes per month): $145.08. MCOs must reimburse at rates no lower than FFS rates. PCPs may bill one 60- or 70-minute code per month, plus up to two additional 30-minute codes per month. Additionally, free coordinated mental health and behavioral health care services are provided to Medicaid enrollees through their primary care provider and coordinated with their Medicaid insurance plan. See Superseding Guidance document (PT 71-24) for details on reimbursement, coding, and coordination with the Behavioral Health Administrative Services Organization.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Primary care provider (PCP)-led teams including behavioral health care managers and psychiatric consultants participating in Maryland Medicaid (HealthChoice and Fee-For-Service), as well as Maryland Medicaid enrollees who need mental health or behavioral health support, including treatment for depression and substance use disorders. Eligible providers include physicians, physician assistants, nurse practitioners, licensed clinical professional counselors, licensed clinical marriage and family therapists, licensed clinical alcohol and drug counselors, and licensed social workers. Eligible organizations include Managed Care Organizations (MCOs), Federally Qualified Health Centers (FQHCs), Rural Health Clinics (RHCs), adult or pediatric nonspecialty medical practices, and health systems.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Care coordination and management, systematic monitoring and treatment using validated clinical rating scales, psychiatric and/or SUD caseload reviews and consultations for patients who do not show clinical improvement, coordination of mental health and behavioral health care services through a primary care provider, infrastructure development (patient registry, monitoring/reporting/billing tools), staff training, staffing for care management and psychiatric consultation, and implementation and evaluation.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available statewide to Maryland Medicaid providers under both HealthChoice and Fee-For-Service programs, and to Medicaid enrollees throughout Maryland. Rural areas of the State are encouraged to participate.

Refer to the Superseding Guidance document (PT 71-24) for additional details. Enrollees can talk to their primary care provider or call their Medicaid insurance plan to get started; contact information is on the insurance card.

structured_extraction.program_description: Community First Choice (CFC) is a Maryland Medicaid state plan benefit program and Home and Community-Based Options Waiver (1915(c) HCBS Waiver, MD.0265.R06.00) that provides home- and community-based personal assistance services to eligible individuals of any age, including older adults and people with disabilities, who need support with activities of daily living (ADLs) and instrumental activities of daily living (IADLs) as an alternative to institutional care. The program consolidated personal care services from two prior programs (Living at Home Waiver and Older Adults Waiver) to expand access to community-based services. Participants may receive personal assistance, personal emergency response systems, assistive technology, accessibility adaptations, consumer training, nurse delegation and monitoring, home-delivered meals, environmental adaptations, substitute human assistance services, support planning, transition services, respite care, nutritionist/dietitian services, family training, behavioral consultation, senior center services, medical day care, assisted living services, case management, and other home- and community-based supports while living in their own homes or community settings. Services include both flexible services (personal assistance services, home-delivered meals, and items substituting for human assistance) and non-flexible services (supports planning, nurse monitoring, PERS, environmental assessments, accessibility adaptations, assistive technology, transition services, consumer training). Services are delivered through Medicaid waiver authority under 1915(c) HCBS and 1915(b)(4) CFC provisions. The program uses risk-based prioritization (80% of applications) combined with first-come, first-served methodology (20% of applications) to allocate waiver capacity. The waiver is effective January 1, 2023 through December 31, 2027. The program is available statewide in Maryland, with local access supported through county offices such as the Calvert County Office on Aging, the Frederick County Division of Aging and Independence, and the Cecil County Aging and Disability Services. Medical eligibility is determined through interRAI HC or interRAI PEDS HC assessments evaluating needs, strengths, and preferences. The 1915(b)(4) waiver waives freedom of choice of providers for three CFC services: supports planning, nurse monitoring, and transition services. Approximately 7,900 individuals enrolled in first two years; approximately 2,500 applicants per year, with an estimated 400 individuals transitioning annually from institutions to CFC.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Provides home- and community-based services including: Flexible services — personal care and personal assistance (help with bathing, grooming, dressing, eating, toileting, mobility, bed mobility, repositioning, meal preparation, housework, laundry, continence care, g-tube feeding, medication administration, wound care, vital signs monitoring, blood sugar checks, oral suctioning, and light chores), home-delivered meals (nutritionally adequate meals, maximum 14 meals per week/2 per day, menus certified by physician/nutritionist/dietitian), and items substituting for human assistance. Non-flexible services — personal emergency response systems, assistive technology, accessibility adaptations (environmental adaptations based on licensed OT assessment; combined cost of accessibility adaptations and assistive technology limited to $15,780 over three years), consumer training, continuous skilled nursing/private duty nursing, nurse delegation and monitoring (RN visits at minimum every 45 days), environmental assessments and adaptations, substitute human assistance services, support planning, transition services (must be expended within 60 days of transition; maximum $3,000 per transition), medical day care (minimum four hours per day; cannot overlap with PAS), respite care (max 14 days/12 months in facilities), nutritionist/dietitian services, family training, behavioral consultation, senior center services, and assisted living services. All services are pre-authorized via a person-centered Plan of Service (POS). Participants must have community Medicaid and meet a program-specific level of care (nursing facility level of care) based on a medical assessment using interRAI HC or interRAI PEDS HC. There is no age requirement. Services are delivered through Medicaid waiver authority under 1915(c) HCBS and 1915(b)(4) CFC provisions. Cost neutrality requirement applies (cannot exceed 125% of institutional care cost). Fee schedule-based rates with annual increases (3% standard, subject to state budget).
structured_extraction.program_audience: Maryland Medicaid-eligible individuals of any age, including older adults and people with disabilities, who receive full community Medicaid benefits, meet a nursing facility level of care, and need personal assistance and home- and community-based services as an alternative to institutional care. Also includes individuals transitioning from institutions or assisted living facilities to community settings, individuals with chronic illness, medical conditions, or disabilities requiring ADL/IADL assistance, children/pediatric participants with functional needs, individuals with brain injury, HIV/AIDS, medically fragile or technology-dependent individuals, individuals with autism, developmental or intellectual disabilities, mental illness, and serious emotional disturbance. Individuals eligible for long-term care services with an average length of stay of 316 days. Individuals enrolled in Therapeutic/Treatment Foster Care (TFC) through DHS are not eligible.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Personal care and personal assistance services (ADLs and IADLs), home-delivered meals, personal emergency response systems, assistive technology, accessibility adaptations and environmental modifications, consumer training, nurse delegation and monitoring, environmental assessments, substitute human assistance services, support planning and case management, transition services, respite care, nutritionist/dietitian services, family training, behavioral consultation, senior center services, medical day care, assisted living services, delegated nursing functions, medication management, and other home- and community-based supports to help individuals live independently in the community. Direct service provision in home and community-based settings.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available statewide in Maryland to eligible Medicaid participants who reside in the community (not in an institution). Services are generally not available to residents of assisted living facilities. Local access is available through county offices, including the Calvert County Office on Aging (410-535-4606 or 301-855-1170), the Frederick County Division of Aging and Independence (301-600-1234), and Cecil County Aging and Disability Services (410-996-5295). The program is implemented through a local network of Aging and Disability Resource Centers (Maryland Access Point/MAP sites). Services are organized by geographic regions with specific provider availability by region.

structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Contact Medicaid's Long Term Care and Waiver Services at 410-767-1739 or 1-877-463-3464 or visit the Maryland Department of Health website at https://health.maryland.gov/mmcp/longtermcare/pages/Community-First-Choice.aspx for more information. Eligibility is determined based on financial and medical requirements including income and asset review, with medical eligibility determined through interRAI HC or interRAI PEDS HC assessment. Assessment is conducted via the LTSSMaryland data management system using an algorithm-based LOC determination with UCA verification. Participants choose an approved Supports Planning Agency to guide service planning and develop a person-centered Plan of Service (POS). Participants sign Freedom of Choice forms indicating waiver vs. institutional service preference. Service providers submit Plans of Service in the LTSS Maryland system for utilization review and authorization. Provider enrollment is through the ePREP portal. Residents of Calvert County may contact the Calvert County Office on Aging at 410-535-4606 or 301-855-1170. Residents of Frederick County may contact the Division of Aging and Independence at 301-600-1234. Residents of Cecil County may contact Cecil County Aging and Disability Services at 410-996-5295, option 1. Providers and participants can also refer to the Plan of Service Reviewer Training Manual and Standard Operating Procedures listed on the MDH page for guidance on service delivery and eligibility.

structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Funds can be used for capital costs, including: acquiring property, design work, construction, renovation, and purchasing equipment for facilities.

structured_extraction.program_name: Community Health Resource Commission (CHRC) Grants – Prince George's County

Funded projects address women's health, infant mortality, dental care, primary care, behavioral health, diabetes, food security, and obesity. Grantees include health departments, federally qualified health centers, nonprofits, and universities.

Grant terms vary from one to three years. Funds are typically used to support staff salaries, equipment, and program operations.

Grant funds are typically used for salary support and direct service delivery

structured_extraction.program_name: Community Health Resource Commission (CHRC) Grants – Reducing Avoidable ED Visits
structured_extraction.program_description: The Maryland Community Health Resource Commission (CHRC) awards grants to health departments, hospitals, clinics, and other organizations to reduce avoidable emergency department (ED) visits and promote care in the community. Projects address chronic disease management, care coordination, mobile health outreach, and connecting underserved residents to primary and preventive care.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Grants ranging from approximately $90,000 to $2,400,000 awarded to eligible organizations for two- to three-year projects that reduce avoidable ED visits and improve community-based health care access. Examples include grants of $700,000 (TidalHealth), $2,400,000 (University of Maryland School of Nursing), $2,000,000 (Johns Hopkins School of Medicine), and smaller awards to county health departments and clinics.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Health departments, hospitals, clinics, universities, and community organizations serving low-income, uninsured, minority, or chronically ill Maryland residents with high rates of avoidable ED use.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Staff salaries, care coordination, mobile health outreach, community health worker services, patient navigation, health education, transportation, telehealth technology, and partnerships to reduce avoidable ED visits.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Grants have been awarded to organizations serving Baltimore City, Harford County, Wicomico County, Queen Anne's County, Calvert County, Prince George's County, Montgomery County, Anne Arundel County, Charles County, Howard County, and Frederick County.
requirements_list: Applicant must be a health department, hospital, clinic, university, or community organization in Maryland
Project must target reduction of avoidable ED visits or promotion of community-based care
Projects should serve low-income, uninsured, minority, or chronically ill populations facing barriers to care
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Contact the Maryland Community Health Resource Commission (CHRC) through the Maryland Department of Health for information on open grant rounds and application requirements.

structured_extraction.program_name: Community Health Worker (CHW) Specialty Training Modules
structured_extraction.program_description: The CHW Specialty Training Modules program offers free, downloadable training materials to Community Health Worker (CHW) training organizations. The modules cover five specialty health areas — Behavioral Health, Chronic Disease-Asthma, Infectious Disease, Maternal and Child Health, and Older Adults and Aging — and are available in English and Spanish. Each module includes a PowerPoint presentation, student guide, facilitator guide, handouts, activities, and a knowledge assessment. Modules are editable and customizable and can be used in whole or in part. CHWs trained using these modules can count the hours toward the 20 professional development hours required to renew their CHW certificate.

structured_extraction.program_name: Community Health Worker Certification Training Program Accreditation
structured_extraction.program_description: Maryland Department of Health accredits organizations that want to offer Community Health Worker (CHW) certification training programs. Under state regulations (COMAR 10.68.02), all CHW certification training programs must receive accreditation from the Department before they can operate. Programs must provide a minimum of 100 hours of instruction plus a 40-hour supervised practicum. Curriculum must incorporate core competencies including advocacy, communication, cultural competency, ethics, resource navigation, care coordination, health behavior teaching, outreach, and public health literacy. Applications are accepted on a rolling basis.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: The Department reviews and approves (accredits) organizations seeking to offer CHW certification training programs. Accreditation is required before any organization may offer such a program. Programs must meet established standards including minimum 100 hours instruction, a 40-hour supervised practicum, and a curriculum covering 9 core competencies. The CHW team is available to assist applicants through the accreditation process. Accreditations must also be renewed periodically.
structured_extraction.application_deadline_string: Rolling basis (programs in operation by October 1, 2018 had a historical deadline of December 31, 2020)
structured_extraction.program_audience: Organizations that want to offer Community Health Worker certification training programs in Maryland
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Accreditation to operate a CHW certification training program
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Statewide — available to organizations operating in Maryland

Accreditation must be issued before an organization may offer a CHW certification training program
Must review all information and documents on the program page before applying

40-hour supervised practicum verification

Curriculum incorporating 9 core competencies (advocacy, communication, cultural competency, ethics, resource navigation, care coordination, health behavior teaching, outreach, and public health literacy)

Pay the accreditation fee. Application is reviewed by the CHW Training Program Application Review Committee. The Department issues a decision within 120 calendar days. The CHW team is available to assist with the application process. Contact [email protected] or call 410-767-5971 for accreditation applications, or [email protected] for renewal inquiries.

structured_extraction.program_description: The Community Pathways Waiver (CPW) is Maryland's Medicaid Home and Community-Based Services (HCBS) waiver program for people with developmental disabilities. It allows Medicaid-funded services to be provided in community settings as an alternative to institutional care, helping individuals live more independently in their homes and communities. Services are organized into three categories: Meaningful Day Services (such as employment supports, career exploration, day habilitation, and medical day care), Support Services (such as personal support, respite care, assistive technology, behavior support, environmental modifications, housing support, and transportation), and Residential Services (such as group homes, shared living, and supported living). Participants can choose a self-directed service model or a traditional agency-based model. Services are tailored to each individual's needs.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Medicaid waiver funding covers a range of community-based services provided to eligible individuals with developmental disabilities. Services include employment services, career exploration, community development, day habilitation, medical day care, assistive technology, behavior support, environmental modifications, housing support, personal support, respite care, transportation, vehicle modifications, supported living, shared living, and group home residential services. Participants may choose self-directed or agency-based service delivery.

structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Community-based supports and services as an alternative to institutional care, including employment, day programs, personal assistance, respite care, housing support, assistive technology, environmental modifications, transportation, vehicle modifications, and residential services.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available statewide in Maryland to eligible individuals.

structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Apply through the DDA Eligibility Application Process and then the DDA Waiver Application Process. Applicants must meet initial and ongoing technical, medical, and financial criteria. Links to both processes are provided on the program page at the DDA website.

structured_extraction.program_description: The Developmental Disabilities Administration (DDA) funds employment, day, residential, and support services for people with developmental disabilities. To access these services, individuals or someone acting on their behalf must complete and submit an eligibility application. The DDA evaluates the application to determine if the person qualifies for services. Both children and adults can apply at any age, including Transitioning Youth (ages 14–21). Low Intensity Support Services (LISS) do not require an application.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: The DDA funds employment, day, residential, and support services for eligible individuals with developmental disabilities. Services are available to both children and adults of any age. Specific services include: Personal Care, Living at Home Waiver, Medical Day Care Waiver, Waiver for Older Adults, Model Waiver for Medically Fragile Children, Traumatic Brain Injury Waiver, Autism Waiver, REM (Rare and Expensive Case Management), speech therapy, occupational therapy, physical therapy, specialized medical care, behavioral support services, counseling, psychiatric treatment, and case management. Applications can be downloaded online, mailed, or picked up at a regional DDA office. DDA staff can help applicants complete the form.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Individuals with developmental disabilities of any age, including children, Transitioning Youth (ages 14–21), and adults in Maryland, as well as their families or representatives. Applicant must be a Maryland resident.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Employment, day, residential, and support services for individuals with developmental disabilities, including therapeutic and care services addressing disabilities and functional limitations.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available statewide in Maryland through DDA regional offices. Applicant must be a resident of Maryland. Applications are submitted to the appropriate regional office based on county of residence: Central Maryland (Anne Arundel, Baltimore County, Howard, Harford, Baltimore City), Eastern Shore (Caroline, Cecil, Dorchester, Kent, Queen Anne's, Somerset, Talbot, Wicomico, Worcester), Southern Maryland (Calvert, Charles, Montgomery, Prince George's, St. Mary's), Western Maryland (Allegany, Carroll, Frederick, Garrett, Washington).

structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Download the application from the DDA website, request it by mail, or pick it up from a DDA regional office. Fill it out (on a computer or by hand), sign it, and submit it with supporting documentation to the appropriate DDA regional office based on county of residence. DDA staff at regional offices can help applicants complete the application. DDA reviews information within 7 days for a preliminary decision, with a final eligibility decision within 60 days of receipt of a complete application. Extensions are available if additional time is needed for evaluations or meetings.

structured_extraction.program_description: The Developmental Disabilities Administration (DDA) Housing Support Services program provides time-limited technical assistance and support to people with developmental disabilities to help them find, obtain, and maintain housing in the community. Services are delivered through the Community Pathways Waiver by Housing Support Specialists and coordinated by Coordinators of Community Services (CCS). Specific supports include housing information and assistance to help obtain independent housing, housing transition planning to assess needs and develop an individualized housing support plan, and housing tenancy sustaining services to help individuals remain in their current rental or leased home. A self-direction Budget Authority option is available.

A self-direction Budget Authority option is available.

structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Identifying and navigating housing opportunities, overcoming barriers to housing, obtaining housing, developing individualized housing support plans, and maintaining current rental or leased housing in the community.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available statewide in Maryland through the Community Pathways Waiver.

structured_extraction.program_description: Maryland's Developmental Disabilities Administration (DDA) Medicaid Waiver Program provides home and community-based services to individuals with intellectual and developmental disabilities. Eligible individuals on the DDA Waiting List or in reserved priority categories can apply for a waiver slot, which allows them to receive community-based supports instead of institutional care. Services are based on each person's assessed needs as outlined in their Person-Centered Plan, and a Coordinator of Community Services (CCS) assists throughout the application and service planning process. Enrolled participants can also access Maryland HealthChoice Program services, and children are entitled to Early Periodic Screening Diagnosis and Treatment (EPSDT) services.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Waiver provides funding for home and community-based services to individuals with intellectual and developmental disabilities who meet technical, medical, and financial eligibility criteria. Services are based on each person's assessed needs as outlined in their Person-Centered Plan. A Coordinator of Community Services (CCS) helps complete the application and explore service delivery models, services, and provider options. Participants can also access Maryland HealthChoice Program services, and children are entitled to Early Periodic Screening Diagnosis and Treatment (EPSDT) services.

structured_extraction.program_description: A statewide collaboration between public health and public safety that allows Emergency Medical Services (EMS) clinicians to leave naloxone (an opioid overdose-reversal medication) kits on-scene with overdose patients and their support network — family, friends, and roommates — after responding to a nonfatal overdose. The goal is to reduce fatal opioid overdoses by putting naloxone directly in the hands of at-risk individuals and the people around them. Naloxone kits are provided at no cost to EMS agencies by the State of Maryland. Since 2018, more than 62,000 doses have been distributed to over 27,000 Marylanders. Since July 2025, all Maryland EMS agencies may participate by default under updated state EMS medical protocols. MIEMSS offers free online training for EMS clinicians, including a 0.25-credit course on the leave-behind program and a 0.5-credit course on naloxone administration.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Naloxone kits are provided at no cost to EMS agencies by the State of Maryland. EMS clinicians leave these kits on-scene with overdose patients and their support networks. Since 2018, more than 62,000 doses have been distributed to over 27,000 Marylanders. EMS clinicians are also connected to treatment and recovery resources for patients. MIEMSS (Maryland Institute for Emergency Medical Services Systems) offers free online training for EMS clinicians: a 0.25-credit course on the leave-behind program and a 0.5-credit course on naloxone administration.

structured_extraction.program_description: This voluntary program authorizes trained staff at youth camps, food service facilities, and institutions of higher education (including recreation and wellness facilities) to obtain and administer auto-injectable epinephrine to individuals experiencing anaphylaxis (a severe allergic reaction) when a doctor or emergency medical services are not immediately available. Participants must complete an approved training course and receive a certificate from the Maryland Department of Health before they can obtain epinephrine from a pharmacy. The program issues certificates to qualifying individuals upon submission of the required application form (MDH 4783) and written policy. The department is also in the process of updating COMAR 10.13.04 to expand the program to additional food service facilities.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: The program issues certificates to trained individuals employed at qualifying facilities (youth camps, food service facilities, and recreation or wellness facilities at institutions of higher education) that authorize them to obtain a prescription for and administer auto-injectable epinephrine (e.g., an EpiPen). Participants must first complete an approved training course (taught by a licensed physician, registered nurse, or certified nurse practitioner), then submit application form MDH 4783 along with a written policy to receive the certificate. The certificate allows the holder to obtain auto-injectable epinephrine from a pharmacy for use in emergencies. Training instructors must submit form MDH 4782 along with credentials and written training materials for MDH approval. Applicants for the certificate must be at least 18 years old. Participation is voluntary.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Staff employed at youth camps, food service facilities, and recreation or wellness facilities at institutions of higher education in Maryland who may need to administer emergency epinephrine to individuals experiencing severe allergic reactions; also training instructors (physicians, registered nurses, certified nurse practitioners) seeking course approval.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Obtaining and administering auto-injectable epinephrine to individuals experiencing anaphylaxis in emergency situations when a physician or emergency medical services are not immediately available.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available statewide in Maryland for qualifying facilities (youth camps, food service facilities, and institutions of higher education including recreation and wellness facilities) and their staff.
requirements_list: Applicant must be at least 18 years old.

Must meet requirements set out in Health-General §13-7A-02 and COMAR 10.13.04.
Must complete an MDH-approved emergency epinephrine educational training course.
Must attach a copy of the training certificate.
Must submit application form MDH 4783 to receive a certificate.

Incidents where epinephrine is administered must be reported to the Department.
Training instructors must hold a valid license as a Physician, Registered Nurse, or Certified Nurse Practitioner.
Training instructors must submit form MDH 4782 with training manual, handouts, presentations, exams, and completion certificates for MDH approval.
Comply with COMAR 10.16.07, COMAR 10.13.04, and Md. Code Ann. Health-General Title 13 (Subtitles 7, 7A) and Title 14, Subtitle 4.

structured_extraction.application_process_overview: 1. Verify eligibility by reviewing the relevant statutes and regulations (Health-General §13-7A-02 and COMAR 10.13.04). 2. Complete an MDH-approved training course (a list of pre-approved courses for youth camps is available on the program page; contact mdh.envhealth@maryland.gov for food service and higher education course approvals). 3. To have a new training course approved, submit form MDH 4782 with instructor credentials and written training materials to the Environmental Health Bureau for review. 4. After completing training, submit form MDH 4783 along with a copy of your training certificate and a written facility policy to the Maryland Department of Health to receive a certificate. Alternatively, email mdh.envhealth@maryland.gov to express interest in participating.

structured_extraction.program_description: The EID Program is a Medicaid buy-in program that allows working people with disabilities to purchase Medicaid health coverage even if their earnings would normally make them ineligible for standard Medicaid. Participants pay a sliding-scale monthly premium based on their income, ranging from $0 for individuals earning less than $15,960/year up to 7.5% of monthly countable income for individuals earning $95,760 or more per year. A Hardship Exemption is available for those temporarily unable to pay their premium, waiving monthly fees for up to 6 months for individuals experiencing severe financial hardship. The program is designed to help working individuals with disabilities maintain health insurance coverage and remain employed without losing access to needed health care.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Participants buy into Medicaid coverage by paying a sliding-scale monthly premium based on income. Premiums range from $0 (for individuals earning less than $15,960/year) up to 7.5% of monthly countable income (for individuals earning $95,760+/year). A Hardship Exemption is available for those temporarily unable to pay their premium, waiving monthly EID program premiums for up to 6 months for those experiencing severe financial hardship where premium payment would compromise ability to obtain basic food, shelter, and clothing. The program provides Medicaid health coverage to eligible workers with disabilities who would otherwise be ineligible due to earnings. The program also coordinates with Medicare Part B and seeks payment from private/public health insurance and liable third parties.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Working individuals with disabilities aged 16–64 who are employed or self-employed, live in Maryland, and meet Social Security's disability criteria and program asset limits, and who would otherwise be ineligible for Medicaid due to their earnings. Also applicable to household members and spouses of eligible individuals.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Medicaid health coverage for eligible workers with disabilities, including health insurance benefits provided through the Maryland Medicaid program. Assistance covers medical payments to doctors and medical suppliers, and coordinates with Medicare Part B benefits.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Must live in Maryland. Available statewide.
requirements_list: Be at least 16 years old but not yet 65 years old
Be working for pay (employed or self-employed, with earnings subject to taxes)
Have a disability that meets Social Security's medical criteria
Be a U.S. Citizen or a qualified non-citizen
Live in Maryland
Meet the $10,000 asset limit (joint and individually owned assets count; spouse-only assets do not)
Must not currently receive Medicaid through other eligibility pathways
Earnings must be subject to taxes (no under-the-table work)
Must provide Social Security numbers for all household members
Must report all income sources and assets/resources
Must report changes affecting eligibility or benefit amount within 10 days
Must cooperate with Department in securing third-party payments
Must authorize inspection and review of medical records
Must provide verification of birth, social security card, marriage/divorce certificates
Must provide four recent consecutive weeks of pay stubs or signed employer statement showing regular pay (for employed); earnings records and recent tax return (for self-employed)
Must provide documentation of resources (bank statements, savings bonds, stock certificates, vehicle registrations, property tax bills)
Must provide health insurance identification cards for applicant and family members
Must provide proof of citizenship/immigration status (Medicare card or immigration documentation)

For Hardship Exemption: financial hardship must be severe enough that premium payment would compromise ability to obtain basic food, shelter, and clothing; must provide documentation of all income sources and expenses; exemption limited to maximum 6 months
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Complete the EID Program application (available as fillable PDF or printable with blue/black ink), providing household, income, and demographic information. Submit required documentation including pay stubs (4 weekly, 2 bi-weekly, or 3 monthly), bank statements including first day of application month, Schedule C or business ledger if self-employed, proof of citizenship/immigration status, and health insurance cards. An interview is required (can be conducted by telephone in most cases). Sign and date application under penalty of perjury. Mail completed application and supporting documents to the Eligibility Determination Division, EID Program, Maryland Department of Health, 6 St. Paul Street, 4th Floor, Baltimore, MD 21202. Applications may be processed within 30 days. Disability agencies and Centers for Independent Living can assist with applications. Applicants may also contact a DORS (Maryland Division of Rehabilitation Services) counselor, who can connect them with a benefits planner to discuss EID eligibility and next steps. For Hardship Exemption: request DHMH EID 2A form from caseworker, complete with hardship explanation, income/expense information, and supporting documentation, and mail to Eligibility Determination Division; decision provided within 30 days.

structured_extraction.program_description: The Community Health Resource Commission (CHRC) of the Maryland Department of Health awards grants to organizations across Maryland to expand access to primary care, dental care, behavioral health, preventive services, and health infrastructure for low-income, uninsured, and vulnerable residents. Grantees include local health departments, hospitals, free clinics, community health centers, nonprofits, and universities that provide care coordination, school-based health centers, mobile health clinics, telehealth services, community health workers, and other community-based health programs targeting low-income, uninsured, minority, and other vulnerable populations.
