Screening is by appointment only and must be completed within 90 days of arrival.

structured_extraction.program_description: The Regrounding Our Response (ROR) Training Series is a workforce development program that reduces stigma, increases understanding of trauma and trauma-informed care, and supports linkages to behavioral health services and quality care for people who use drugs. The program trains Master Presenters to share information with the broader community and federally qualified health centers, and measures stigma levels using the Shatterproof Addiction Stigma Index (SASI). Free, on-demand online courses are available covering topics such as Adverse Childhood Experiences, Medications for Addiction Treatment, Comprehensive Care Framework for People Who Use Drugs, Social Determinants of Health, and Stages of Change. Technical assistance is also available by email.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Free, on-demand online training courses covering harm reduction topics including Adverse Childhood Experiences, Medications for Addiction Treatment, Comprehensive Care Framework for People Who Use Drugs, Social Determinants of Health, and Stages of Change. Also trains Master Presenters for sustainable community dissemination. Technical assistance is available by email at mdh.harmreduction@maryland.gov.

structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Workforce development, stigma reduction, trauma-informed care training, overdose prevention, and linkages to behavioral health services
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available statewide across Maryland
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Visit the Regrounding Our Response website at ror-mdhealth.thinkific.com to access free on-demand courses. For technical assistance, email mdh.harmreduction@maryland.gov.

structured_extraction.program_name: Reminders for Stroke Risk Identification: Transcranial Doppler (TCD) Program
structured_extraction.program_description: A joint program of the Maryland Department of Health and Johns Hopkins University that helps families of children with sickle cell disease stay on schedule with annual Transcranial Doppler (TCD) ultrasound screenings. The TCD scan checks blood flow in the brain to assess stroke risk so doctors can begin treatment early if needed. Program staff send reminders and provide support to families to ensure children receive this important test on time, enabling early identification of children at high risk for stroke and timely initiation of treatment.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Program staff send reminders and provide support to families to help schedule and complete annual TCD brain ultrasound screenings for children with sickle cell disease, allowing early identification of stroke risk and timely treatment.

structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available statewide in Maryland

Child must be between ages 2 and 16
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Contact the program by email or by calling 410-614-0052 to enroll and receive scheduling reminders for annual TCD screenings.

structured_extraction.program_description: A federally funded program administered by the Maryland Department of Health under a cooperative agreement with the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) that empowers Maryland to strengthen rural communities by improving healthcare access, quality, and outcomes. Maryland applied for and received $168,180,837.61 in federal funding (Budget Period 1 award received December 29, 2025; funds unrestricted for use by CMS on February 25, 2026) to modernize health care across 18 state-designated rural areas. The program is organized around three pillars: (1) transforming the rural health workforce ($26 million), (2) promoting sustainable access and innovative care including behavioral health, health information technology, and school-based and mobile health ($126 million), and (3) empowering rural Marylanders to eat for health through post-harvest cold storage infrastructure, food aggregation, and local foods purchasing ($15 million). Funding is renewable over five years (up to $1 billion maximum over five years assumes maximum CMS award) and distributed to partners and subawardees through subcontracts, subawards, and competitive procurement processes including Requests for Applications (RFAs) and Requests for Proposals (RFPs). Each transformation area includes immediate impact funds for shovel-ready activities and transformation funds for competitive, longer-term planning opportunities. Maryland gathered public feedback via an RFI, public webinars, and 17 local listening sessions before submitting its program narrative to CMS. Subawards are made to partners for initiatives including health service expansion, health information technology advances, behavioral health expansion, innovative care models, cold storage infrastructure for food producers, and food system aggregation and local foods purchasing strategies. The program is funded under H.R. 1 (Public Law 119-21), enacted July 4, 2025, which created a $50 billion federal fund administered by CMS.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Maryland received a CMS notice of award for $168,180,837.61 in Budget Period 1 (funds unrestricted for use February 25, 2026), with funding renewable over five budget periods through approximately October 2030 (maximum $1 billion over five years assumes maximum CMS award). Maryland will award a series of subawards and subcontracts totaling $163.7 million, with $134.8 million available through competitive procurement. Funding is distributed across three pillars: Pillar 1 (workforce, $26M total) includes $3.5M for apprenticeship and allied health expansion and $15M for pipeline training and provider recruitment/retention; Pillar 2 (access and care, $126M total) includes $6.3M for primary care expansion, $73M for service expansion and behavioral health including health information technology (HIT) advances, $6.7M for school-based health centers, and $23M for mobile health and innovative care models; Pillar 3 (food and health, $15M total) includes $3.7M for post-harvest cold storage infrastructure for producers, $1.6M for NourishMD expansion, and $4.7M for food aggregation, hubs, and local purchasing; $1M for governance. Each pillar includes immediate impact funds (shovel-ready activities) and transformation funds (competitive opportunities). Non-Competing Continuation (NCC) applications are due 60 days before end of each budget period (Budget Period 1 NCC due August 30, 2026). Specific amounts and terms are determined per initiative and posted as individual RFAs or RFPs. Lead applicants for competitive RFAs must be non-profit; for-profit entities may participate as partners or subcontractors. Current opportunities may be listed as 'coming soon' or 'TBA'.
structured_extraction.application_deadline_string: Competitive funding announcements primarily between April and August 2026; varies by initiative; some opportunities listed as TBA or coming soon; Budget Period 1 Non-Competing Continuation application due August 30, 2026

structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Workforce development, apprenticeship and training programs, health workforce data systems, primary care and specialty practice expansion, telehealth and health information technology infrastructure, school-based health centers, mobile health programs, behavioral health services, innovative care models, value-based care model development, emergency trauma response, post-harvest cold storage infrastructure for agricultural producers, small grocer equipment and renovations, food aggregation and local purchasing, demand creation for healthy foods, provider recruitment and retention with rural service commitments, nutrition education, one-time infrastructure costs, cybersecurity planning and implementation, and transforming health care delivery in rural Maryland communities. Minor renovations/alterations (linked to program goals, up to 20% of total funding per budget period, requires CMS approval), provider payments for health care services filling coverage gaps (up to 15% of total funding per budget period), Electronic Medical Record (EMR) system replacement (up to 5% if previous HITECH-certified system exists), Rural Tech Catalyst Fund initiatives (up to 10% or $20M whichever is less), infrastructure and equipment upgrades for rural health care facilities, health care clinician salary supports. structured_extraction.program_description: The Self-Directed Services (SDS) Program is a Medicaid waiver-based service model administered by Maryland's Developmental Disabilities Administration (DDA) that gives individuals with intellectual and developmental disabilities greater choice and control over how their services are delivered, who provides them, and how their allocated budget is spent. Participants decide how, when, where, and by whom their services are delivered, act as the employer of record for their support staff, manage a fixed allocated budget, hire and supervise their own staff, and set wages, allowing them to live more independently. The program is available through the DDA Community Pathways Medicaid waiver. Participants may hire family members as staff and select vendors and providers to meet their individualized needs. Support is available through a Coordinator of Community Services, an optional Support Broker, and a required Financial Management and Counseling Services (FMCS) provider who handles payroll and fiscal tasks. As of October 6, 2025, FMCS providers act as Organized Healthcare Delivery System providers to directly purchase approved services, goods, and items on behalf of participants. Participants can choose to self-manage (Option 1), appoint a designated representative (Option 2), or appoint team members for specific tasks (Option 3).
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Participants receive a self-directed fixed allocated budget to purchase approved waiver services and supports available under the DDA Community Pathways Waiver. They act as the common law employer of record, choosing their own service providers and managing their own staff, including hiring, training, supervising, and setting wages. Participants may also hire family members as staff (a Family as Staff Form is required in that case), subject to a maximum of 40 hours per week and DDA reasonable and customary wage standards. Participants are required to work with a Financial Management and Counseling Services (FMCS) provider to manage budget and payment responsibilities, including payroll. As of October 6, 2025, FMCS providers directly purchase approved services, goods, and items as Organized Healthcare Delivery System providers. Participants may optionally work with a certified Support Broker (up to 15 hours initial orientation, 4 hours/month ongoing) to assist with employer duties. Day-to-Day Administrative Supports are available up to 10 hours/month. Recruitment and Advertising support is available up to $500/plan year. Individual and Family Directed Goods and Services are available up to $5,000/plan year. Respite camp funding is available up to $7,248 per plan year. Hourly rates vary by service type (e.g., Personal Supports: $43.64/hour standard; Respite Care: $34.64/hour, max 720 hours/year; Support Broker: $70.30/hour). Enhanced supports are available with approved behavioral or nursing care plans. Wage exceptions are available under specific circumstances (required certifications, specialized training, 10+ years experience, 8+ years longevity). Training modules and guidance materials are available to help participants manage their self-directed services. Specific counties (Calvert, Charles, Frederick, Montgomery, and Prince George's) receive enhanced vendor maximum rates. Participants can choose to self-manage their employer authority and budget authority (Option 1), appoint a designated representative (Option 2), or appoint team members for specific tasks (Option 3).

structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Participants work with their Coordinator of Community Services (CCS) to express interest in self-direction and begin the self-direction process. They complete a Self-Directed Services Orientation (including a three-module video training series covering self-direction overview, self-directed services team, and person-centered planning, and review of FAQs), sign a Participant Agreement, and choose one of three management options (self-manage, appoint designated representative, or appoint specific team members for specific tasks). They develop a self-directed budget as part of their person-centered plan, and work with a required Financial Management and Counseling Services (FMCS) provider to manage budget and payment responsibilities, including payroll. Participants may also choose to engage an optional certified Support Broker for employer responsibilities. If hiring family members or relatives, participants must complete a Family as Staff Form. Participants complete form selections for service choices and submit demographic and budget information. Coordinator of Community Services attestation is required. All applicable team members review and sign the Participant Agreement. Participants review the FAQ orientation tool and sign the Self-Directed Services Orientation Checklist.

structured_extraction.program_name: Statewide Standing Order for Naloxone Dispensing by Pharmacies
structured_extraction.program_description: A statewide standing order issued by the Maryland Department of Health (Behavioral Health Administration) that allows all Maryland-licensed pharmacists to dispense naloxone (an opioid overdose reversal medication) and any necessary supplies for administration to any individual, without requiring a personal prescription. Issued by Rachel Talley, MD, Chief Medical Officer of the Behavioral Health Administration. Effective August 28, 2025; Expires June 30, 2027.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Maryland-licensed pharmacists can dispense two (2) doses of naloxone hydrochloride and necessary administration supplies to any individual under this standing order. Unlimited prescriptions and refills authorized. Pharmacists provide counseling on overdose recognition, naloxone administration, rescue breathing, and emergency services. Individuals who cannot afford naloxone or related co-pays can be referred to Overdose Response Programs to receive a naloxone kit free of charge.

structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available statewide in Maryland to any individual through any Maryland-licensed pharmacy.

Keep standing order on file and accessible to staff
Bill using Dr. Talley's NPI #1083034615
Label naloxone per prescription requirements
Provide educational materials to recipients
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Visit any Maryland-licensed pharmacy to request naloxone under the standing order. Pharmacists may fax a copy of the standing order if needed. Individuals who cannot afford naloxone can be referred to an Overdose Response Program for a free kit.

structured_extraction.program_name: Veterans Auto and Education Improvement Act (VAEIA) Recognition Program
structured_extraction.program_description: A federal law (PL 117-333) allowing licensed pharmacists and pharmacy technicians from other states who are active-duty servicemembers (or their spouses) stationed in Maryland under military orders to practice in Maryland without obtaining a Maryland pharmacy license, as long as they remain in good standing in their original state of licensure and meet other requirements set by the Maryland State Board of Pharmacy. The recognition lasts for the duration of the servicemember's station in Maryland; for spouses, recognition remains valid until divorce or the servicemember's reassignment out of Maryland.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Eligible servicemembers and their spouses may practice as pharmacists or pharmacy technicians in Maryland without obtaining a Maryland license. For servicemembers, recognition lasts for the duration of their military station in Maryland. For spouses, recognition remains valid until divorce or when the servicemember is no longer stationed in Maryland. Applicants must submit a notarized application with a copy of their military orders, certified letters of good standing from all states where licensed, a passport-size photograph, and agree to comply with Maryland's standards of practice, discipline, and continuing education requirements. There is no fee for the application.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Active-duty military servicemembers (Army, Navy, Air Force, Marine Corps, Space Force, Coast Guard, NOAA, Public Health Service) and their spouses who are licensed pharmacists or pharmacy technicians in another state and are stationed in Maryland under military orders.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Authorization to practice as a pharmacist or pharmacy technician in Maryland without obtaining a Maryland license. No fee is required for the application.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available statewide in Maryland for servicemembers and their spouses who reside in Maryland as a result of military duty station orders.
requirements_list: Must be a servicemember (or spouse of a servicemember) under military orders to serve in Maryland
Must be licensed as a pharmacist or pharmacy technician in another state
Must have actively practiced under the out-of-state license within 2 years preceding relocation to Maryland
Must provide a copy of military orders indicating service in Maryland (spouses must also provide a marriage certificate)
Must remain in good standing in the original state of licensure and any other state licensed in
Must provide certified letters with state seal from each state confirming good standing status
Must demonstrate good character and fitness with no pending investigations or disciplinary charges
Must submit a notarized application with a passport-size photograph (2x2 color, 1"-1.4" head size, taken within 2 years, plain white/off-white background)
Must submit to the authority of the Maryland State Board of Pharmacy for standards of practice, discipline, and continuing education requirements
For spouses: recognition ends upon divorce or when the servicemember is no longer stationed in Maryland
No application fee
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Complete a notarized application form and submit to the Maryland State Board of Pharmacy along with: a copy of military orders documenting Maryland service, certified letters of good standing (with state seal) from all states where licensed, a passport-size photograph with notarized affidavit, marriage certificate if applying as a spouse, and all other required documentation. Mail the completed application and supporting documents to the Maryland State Board of Pharmacy.

structured_extraction.program_description: A USDA-funded nutrition program that provides annual cash-value benefits to qualifying WIC participants and low-resource seniors to purchase fresh fruits and vegetables at authorized farmers markets across Maryland. WIC participants receive approximately $30 per year and Senior Farmers Market Nutrition Program participants receive $35 per year in benefits, loaded onto the family's eWIC card or distributed through the Healthy Together app, redeemable at WIC-authorized farmers and farm stands between June 1 and November 30. Benefits are subject to limited supply and are distributed at WIC clinics during summer months. Farmers authorized by the Maryland State Department of Agriculture can redeem these benefits and must complete a joint application process. Over 100 authorized farmers markets participate statewide.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: WIC participants receive approximately $30 per year and seniors receive $35 per year in benefits to purchase fresh fruits and vegetables at authorized farmers markets between June 1 and November 30. Benefits are loaded onto the family's eWIC card (for WIC participants) and are redeemable at WIC-authorized farmers and farm stands. Farmers can accept these benefits digitally through the Healthy Together app. Supplies for WIC participants are limited. There is no cost or deadline for farmers to participate.
structured_extraction.application_deadline_string: No deadline for farmers to participate; 2026 Senior application opens June 1st; WIC participants should contact their local WIC agency as supplies are limited
structured_extraction.program_audience: Qualifying WIC participants, low-resource seniors, and authorized farmers or farmers market vendors interested in accepting FMNP benefits in Maryland
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Purchase of fresh fruits and vegetables from WIC-authorized farmers and farm stands at authorized farmers markets (for consumers); for farmers, funds are received in exchange for selling eligible fresh produce to program participants
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available statewide in Maryland through local WIC agencies and at 100+ authorized farmers markets and participating farm stands across the state.
requirements_list: Must be a current WIC participant or qualifying low-resource senior to receive consumer benefits
WIC participant benefits subject to limited supply
Benefits redeemable only at WIC-authorized farmers and farm stands between June 1 and November 30
Farmers must attend a Maryland Department of Agriculture training session
Farmers must submit a Farmer Application Package via MDOneStop (onestop.md.gov)
Farmers must be approved by MDH
Farmers must sign the Farmer Agreement electronically once approved
Farmers must download the Healthy Together app to accept digital benefits
Farmers must receive instructions for accepting benefits

To be listed in the directory, a farmers market must have been in operation for at least two seasons, have at least two farmers selling fruit, vegetables, meat, dairy, or eggs, and have at least one farmer who accepts FMNP benefits and/or SNAP
WIC participants enroll during clinic appointments beginning in June
Seniors apply online starting June 1 or through their local Area Agency on Aging

Complaints must include: date of incident, time of incident, description of persons involved, detailed description of what happened, UPC information if applicable, receipts and pictures of items if applicable
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: For WIC participants: Contact your local WIC agency to find out how to obtain FMNP benefits for your family. Supplies are limited. Enroll during WIC clinic appointments beginning in June. For seniors: Apply online at mda.maryland.gov starting June 1, 2026, or contact the county Senior Nutrition Program/local Area Agency on Aging. For farmers: (1) Attend a Maryland Department of Agriculture training session. (2) Create an account and submit the Farmer Application Package at MDOneStop (onestop.md.gov). (3) Once approved by MDH, MDA sends an FMNP Farmer Handbook, posters, and pricing signs. (4) Sign the Farmer Agreement electronically. (5) Download the Healthy Together app and begin processing transactions. To file a complaint: Complete Sections 1-3 of the complaint form and submit via email to mdh.wicvendor@maryland.gov; Section 4 is completed by WIC staff.

structured_extraction.program_name: WIC Fruit and Vegetable Benefits (FVB) for Authorized Farmers (monthly electronic benefits)
structured_extraction.program_description: The Maryland WIC Program provides monthly fruit and vegetable benefits (FVBs) to eligible WIC participants. Authorized Maryland farmers can accept these electronic benefits (eWIC) at farmers' markets and farm stands using the free S3 Merchant Link app, with no setup, transaction, or cancellation fees. This program expands sales opportunities for farmers while ensuring WIC participants have access to fresh produce.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: WIC participants receive monthly fruit and vegetable benefits: $26 for children, $47 for pregnant women, and $52 for breastfeeding mothers. Authorized farmers can redeem these eWIC benefits at no cost using the free S3 Merchant Link app — no setup fees, transaction fees, cancellation fees, or additional equipment required. The app includes a built-in barcode scanner and supports barcode system or printed codes for transactions. Farmers must have a smartphone or tablet with cellular data (Android v5.0+ or Apple iOS v14.0+).
structured_extraction.application_deadline_string: There is no deadline to sign up, you may do so at any time
structured_extraction.program_audience: Maryland farmers who are already FMNP-authorized and wish to also accept WIC fruit and vegetable eWIC benefits, as well as eligible WIC participants seeking fresh produce at authorized farmers' markets and farm stands.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Purchase of fresh fruits and vegetables at authorized farmers' markets and farm stands; farmers receive payment for produce purchased by WIC participants using their monthly benefit allotment.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available statewide in Maryland at participating farmers' markets and farm stands.
requirements_list: Farmers must first be authorized by the Maryland State Department of Agriculture to accept FMNP benefits before applying to accept WIC FVBs
Attend a Maryland Department of Agriculture training session
Complete the farmer application on Maryland's One Stop portal (covers both FMNP and FVB authorization)
Sign the Farmer Agreement electronically once approved
Download and use the S3 Merchant Link app to process eWIC transactions
Must have a smartphone or tablet with a data connection (cellular service required; Wi-Fi not required)
Device must run Android v5.0+ or Apple iOS v14.0+
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: 1. Email Andrea Tompkins (andrea.tompkins@maryland.gov) to sign up. 2. Receive an email invitation from Solutran to complete setup. 3. Attend a Maryland Department of Agriculture training session. 4. Complete the joint farmer application on Maryland's One Stop portal. 5. Once approved, sign the Farmer Agreement electronically. 6. Download the S3 Merchant Link app to your smartphone or tablet to begin accepting eWIC fruit and vegetable benefits. Locations and users can be added at any time.

structured_extraction.program_description: The Maryland Department of Health (MDH) Youth Camps Program licenses, regulates, and certifies all youth camps in Maryland to protect the health and safety of children attending camps. Camp operators must apply for certification and demonstrate compliance with minimum standards covering criminal background checks for staff, health programs, supervision ratios, health and safety procedures, incident reporting, and facility maintenance. MDH issues a Certificate, Letter of Compliance, or Acceptance Letter to qualifying camps that demonstrate substantial compliance with state regulations.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: MDH reviews applications and issues a Certificate, Letter of Compliance, or Acceptance Letter to youth camp operators who demonstrate substantial compliance with Maryland regulations. Licensure establishes requirements for director/counselor qualifications, staff screening/training, counselor-to-camper ratios, health/safety policies, medical services, emergency procedures, food safety practices, and accommodation of campers' special needs. Application fees apply: new Day Camps pay $190 and new Residential Camps pay $500 at the time of application, with any remaining balance due at the end of camp. Fees can be paid by credit card, ACH, check, or money order.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Operators of youth day camps and residential camps in Maryland serving children ages 3.5 to 18; also provides informational guidance for parents selecting youth camps for their children.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Certification to legally operate a licensed youth camp in Maryland; ensures compliance with health and safety regulations.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available statewide in Maryland to all youth camp operators.

Residential camps must have campers stay away from parents for at least 5 days (4 nights)

Qualified, trained, and screened director and counselors
Appropriate counselor-to-camper ratios and camper grouping
Health and safety policies including emergency management procedures
Collection of campers' medical records and special needs information
Accommodation for dietary restrictions and special needs
On-site or on-call medical staff with medication administration capability
Supervised camp trips
Food service health practices

structured_extraction.program_description: This program helps homeowners aged 55 and older make accessibility improvements to their homes so they can age in place and remain living independently. It funds modifications such as ramps, widened doorways, grab bars, accessible showers, first-floor laundry facilities or bathrooms, lever-style door and sink hardware, railings, and adding a bedroom and bath on the main level for the homeowner. The program is administered statewide by the Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development (DHCD) in partnership with the Maryland Department of Aging through all 19 local Area Offices on Aging across the state, including locally in Baltimore County through the Baltimore County Department of Aging and in Frederick County through the Frederick County Area Office on Aging / Senior Services Division. Zero percent interest deferred loans are available for up to 30 years, and grants of up to $25,000 are also available to senior homeowners who do not qualify for loan funding.
structured_extraction.agency: Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development
structured_extraction.assistance_description: The program offers zero percent interest, deferred loans with no payments required for up to 30 years. The maximum loan amount is up to 110% of the property value (or up to 85% in some county implementations), accounting for any existing mortgages. There is no fixed loan minimum; the average loan is typically around $10,000–$15,000 but can be higher. Loans are secured by a lien on the property and must be repaid upon sale, transfer, or refinancing of the property. Repayment is not triggered when the home passes to a family member who continues to live there as their primary residence. Monthly payment arrangements can be made upon request. If the borrower refinances and takes cash out, the loan must be repaid in full. All closing costs are included in the loan. If the homeowner still resides in the home at the end of 30 years and cannot repay, the State may extend the deferral period. Grants of up to $25,000 are also available to senior homeowners who do not qualify for loan funding. Income limits apply and vary by household size and geographic location (DC PMSA vs. Rest of State): income limits are higher for the Washington, DC PMSA region (Calvert, Charles, Frederick, Montgomery, and Prince George's Counties) and lower for the rest of the state. Households at 80% AMI qualify at 4.5%–6.0% interest; those at 60% AMI at 0%–4.5%; deferred payment options available for those at 50% or 30% AMI with no repayment capability. Funds may only be used for the actual costs of making the home accessible or functional.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Maryland senior homeowners age 55 or older (only one household member needs to meet the age requirement for couples) who need accessibility modifications to their primary residence and meet income requirements (household income at or below 80% of the statewide or Washington DC MSA median). Income limits vary by household size and geographic location (DC PMSA vs. Rest of State). Manufactured homes on a permanent foundation with owned land may also qualify. Condominiums are considered on a case-by-case basis. The program is available statewide, including locally in Baltimore County through the Baltimore County Department of Aging and in Frederick County through the Frederick County Area Office on Aging / Senior Services Division.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Accessibility improvements to the home such as widening doorways, installing accessible showers, ramps, grab bars, railings, lever-style door and sink hardware, first-floor bathroom and laundry room additions, adding a bedroom and bath on the main level, indoor plumbing improvements, lead hazard reduction, and other modifications that help the homeowner remain safely and independently in their home.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available to Maryland residents statewide through local County Housing Offices, Maryland Access Point Agencies, or the local Area Office on Aging. All 19 local Area Offices on Aging across the state are accepting applications. Income limits vary by geographic location: the Washington, DC PMSA region (Calvert, Charles, Frederick, Montgomery, and Prince George's Counties) has higher income limits, while all other Maryland counties fall under the Rest of State limits. In Baltimore County, contact the Baltimore County Department of Aging (410-887-2594). In Frederick County, contact the Frederick County Area Office on Aging / Senior Services Division. Other counties may also offer the program.
requirements_list: Must be at least 55 years old (only one occupant needs to meet the age requirement for couples)
Must own and occupy the home as a principal residence (seniors living with relatives considered on a case-by-case basis)
Must be the owner of record on the property; all other names on the deed must provide consent
Home must be structurally sound and free of health and safety hazards

Household income must not exceed 80% of the statewide or Washington DC MSA median; income limits vary by household size (1–8 persons) and geographic location (DC PMSA vs. Rest of State); income limits effective as of 7/1/2025
Must not have any outstanding federal or state tax liens, open bankruptcy, or foreclosure
Mobile homes are eligible only if permanently affixed to a foundation and the applicant owns the land beneath it
Condominiums are considered on a case-by-case basis subject to condo covenants
Rental properties are not eligible (must be owner-occupied); landlords with 1–4 units should apply to the Maryland Housing Rehabilitation Program instead
If refinancing with cash out, the AHFS loan must be repaid in full
If senior resides in a relative's home, eligibility is based on the owner's income and considered case-by-case
Must be a Maryland resident
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Applications are available at local County Housing Offices, Maryland Access Point Agencies, or the local Area Office on Aging. In Baltimore County, contact the Baltimore County Department of Aging by calling Senior Information and Assistance at 410-887-2594. In Frederick County, contact the local Area Office on Aging. Staff can assist in completing the application at the agency or schedule an in-home appointment if needed. A DHCD or local government housing network staff member will inspect the property and prepare a work write-up listing all work to be done. The applicant then obtains contractor bids. Once work is completed and the homeowner confirms satisfaction, an inspector authorizes payment via a two-party check made out to both the homeowner and contractor; the homeowner signs it and delivers it to the contractor. You may also contact DHCD directly by phone at (301) 429-7409 or email at DHCD.SpecialLoans@maryland.gov for more information.

structured_extraction.program_description: The Baltimore Regional Neighborhood Initiative (BRNI) is a state-funded revitalization program administered by the Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development that provides capital and operating funding to Community Development Organizations and local governments to support strategic neighborhood revitalization projects in the Baltimore region. The program targets communities experiencing physical, economic, or social decline, focusing on improving local housing and businesses to grow the local tax base and improve quality of life. Projects must be located in Sustainable Community Areas within the BRNI boundary, covering Baltimore City and surrounding counties. In Anne Arundel County, the program specifically targets the Greater Baybrook area (Brooklyn Park, Brooklyn, and Curtis Bay). For FY2025, approximately $20 million in capital funding and $2 million in operating funding is available. Projects must be in a Sustainable Community and targeted by an eligible BRNI applicant's five-year strategic neighborhood revitalization plan.
structured_extraction.agency: Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development
structured_extraction.assistance_description: $20 million in capital funding and $2 million in operating funding available for FY2025. Funding is provided to Community Development Organizations and local governments for neighborhood revitalization projects. Eligible uses include down payment assistance, acquisition or rehabilitation of vacant or blighted properties, property improvements, energy efficiency upgrades, mixed-use development, community open space improvements, workforce development, strategic demolition, and operating costs for community enhancement projects. Projects must be in a Sustainable Community and in an area targeted by an eligible BRNI applicant in their five-year strategic plan.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Community Development Organizations, nonprofits, and local governments in the Baltimore region seeking to revitalize neighborhoods within Sustainable Community Areas, particularly those with an approved or submitted five-year strategic neighborhood revitalization plan. Also targets communities, housing projects, and businesses in the Greater Baybrook area (Brooklyn Park, Brooklyn, and Curtis Bay) experiencing physical, economic, or social decline.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Down payment assistance, acquisition or rehabilitation of vacant or blighted properties, residential and business property improvements, energy efficiency and weatherization, mixed-use development, community open space or public infrastructure, workforce and employment development, strategic demolition, capital projects, and operating costs for community enhancement projects. Local housing and business investment to support community revitalization, grow the tax base, and improve quality of life.

structured_extraction.program_name: Baltimore Vacants Reinvestment Initiative (BVRI) / Reinvest Baltimore
structured_extraction.program_description: The Baltimore Vacants Reinvestment Initiative (BVRI), operating under the broader Reinvest Baltimore initiative, is a coordinated program between the State of Maryland, Baltimore City, and nonprofit and for-profit partners designed to eliminate concentrations of vacant properties, strengthen neighborhoods, and increase access to homeownership in disinvested Baltimore City neighborhoods. Administered by the Maryland Community Investment Corporation (MCIC) as financial intermediary and supported by the Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development (DHCD), the program deploys flexible 'pay for performance' grants and construction loans to public, nonprofit, and for-profit community development organizations. With $30 million allocated for FY26, the initiative supports up to 20 organizations in acquiring, rehabilitating, stabilizing, demolishing, and returning vacant properties to productive use as affordable housing, green space, and mixed-use or community developments. The broader Reinvest Baltimore initiative aims to move at least 5,000 vacant properties into homeownership or other positive outcomes between Fiscal Year 2025 and Fiscal Year 2029. A Support Fund also covers capital-enabling expenses incurred by participating organizations. Awardees participate in a statewide community development cohort facilitated by MCIC, and funding is drawn down as redevelopment milestones are completed. The initiative leverages community, corporate, philanthropic, and government leaders to achieve neighborhood revitalization and improved quality of life for Baltimore City residents. Projects must be located in Sustainable Community Areas within Baltimore City, with special consideration given to projects within the Baltimore City Vacancy Reduction Priority Geography.

structured_extraction.program_name: BeSMART Energy Efficiency Loan for Homeowners Program
structured_extraction.program_description: The BeSMART Home Loan Program provides financing to Maryland homeowners to improve the energy efficiency and comfort of their homes. Homeowners can replace and upgrade appliances, heating, ventilation and cooling (HVAC) systems, and make whole-house building envelope improvements such as insulation and windows to save on utility bills. The program offers unsecured loans at 6.99% APR with a minimum of $5,000 and a maximum of $30,000, with terms up to 10 years. Financing for solar photovoltaic installation is capped at 50% of the total loan amount, and up to 25% of energy measure costs can cover related health and safety improvements such as mold remediation and radon mitigation. Licensed and insured contractors can also participate as eligible contractors to help homeowner borrowers complete their projects.
structured_extraction.agency: Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Unsecured loan at 6.99% APR with a minimum of $5,000 and a maximum of $30,000 for energy efficiency improvements, with terms up to 10 years. A 30% draw is provided upfront and the remaining 70% is disbursed upon project completion. Financing covers appliance replacements, HVAC system upgrades, and whole-house building envelope improvements such as insulation and windows. Eligible measures include insulation, air sealing, ENERGY STAR heating and cooling systems, hot water heaters, appliances, windows, doors, lighting, smart thermostats, ceiling fans, ventilation fans, geothermal heat pumps, and solar photovoltaic systems. Financing for solar photovoltaic installation is capped at 50% of the total loan amount. Up to 25% of the total loan can cover related health and safety improvements such as mold remediation and radon mitigation. Cannot finance projects already purchased or completed. Work cannot begin until BeSMART funding check is received. Participating contractors must provide a W-9 form, a certificate of insurance, and a Maryland HVACR or MHIC license.

structured_extraction.program_name: Broadband Equity, Access, and Deployment (BEAD) Program – Maryland
structured_extraction.program_description: The BEAD program provides federal funding to expand high-speed internet access across Maryland by funding planning, broadband infrastructure deployment, and adoption programs. Maryland received $267,738,400.71 from the National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA) to close remaining broadband coverage gaps concentrated in rural, low-income, and difficult-to-serve areas — approximately 9,000 locations and 1,300 community anchor institutions representing the last 0.5% of Maryland. The Maryland Office of Statewide Broadband (OSB) administers the state's BEAD Grant Program, selecting and distributing funds to subgrantees who deploy broadband infrastructure (including fiber-to-the-home, hybrid fiber-coax, and low-earth orbit satellite) in unserved and underserved locations statewide. The program also supports digital equity, workforce development, digital inclusion, and affordability initiatives, and fosters a well-trained and diverse Maryland workforce for broadband construction.
structured_extraction.agency: Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Maryland received $267,738,400.71 in federal BEAD funding from NTIA, with approximately $321 million in total construction spending anticipated when including a 25% match requirement, plus an additional $170 million from ARPA Capital Projects Fund. The Office of Statewide Broadband awards fixed-amount subgrants to eligible applicants — including internet service providers, local governments, cooperatives, electric utilities, and nonprofits — to deploy high-speed broadband infrastructure in unserved and underserved locations across Maryland. Eligible costs include capital costs for broadband facility installation and extension, equipment, shelters, wireless radios, and access points meeting BEAD Minimum Network Requirements (100 Mbps download/20 Mbps upload, max 100ms latency). Funds are disbursed on a reimbursement basis (quarterly). Ineligible uses include middle mile infrastructure, spectrum licenses, personal equipment, operating expenses, maintenance costs, and warranties. Subgrantees are selected through a competitive application process with scoring based on BEAD outlay offers and technical proposals, subject to a 15% BEAD outlay gating threshold. Non-deployment activities (digital literacy, workforce development, digital equity implementation, cybersecurity training, broadband sign-up assistance, multi-lingual outreach) may also be funded if funds remain. Administrative expenses are capped at 2% maximum. Deployment is anticipated to serve approximately 40% of eligible locations via cable (HFC), 38% via fiber-to-the-home (FTTH), and 22% via low-earth orbit satellite.

structured_extraction.program_audience: Internet service providers, units of local government, nonprofit organizations, cooperatives, electric utilities, and public-private partnerships seeking to deploy broadband infrastructure in unserved and underserved areas of Maryland. Also serves community anchor institutions (schools, libraries, healthcare facilities) and residents/small businesses in unserved/underserved areas. Includes minority- and women-owned businesses (MBEs/WBEs), workforce development providers, training institutions, and low-income households seeking affordable broadband access.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Broadband network infrastructure deployment including construction, permitting, equipment, fiber deployment (FTTH), hybrid fiber-coax (HFC), fixed wireless, and low-earth orbit satellite networks. Eligible uses include capital costs for installation/extension of broadband facilities, equipment, shelters, wireless radios, access points, and antennas. Funds may also be used for workforce training and development, digital equity and inclusion programs, digital literacy, cybersecurity training, broadband adoption support, low-cost service options for low-income households, infrastructure resilience improvements, and non-deployment activities if funds remain. Administrative and programmatic expenses (IT systems, grant administration, subgrantee monitoring, staff training) are eligible up to a 2% cap. Funds may not be used for middle mile infrastructure, spectrum licenses, personal equipment, operating expenses, maintenance costs, or warranties.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Statewide, with focus on rural, low-income, and difficult-to-serve areas identified as unserved or underserved in approved location data. Covers all 23 Maryland counties and Baltimore City, with priority on western Maryland due to geography and topography challenges. Six counties are already fully served and excluded from some bidding. Grant Areas are determined by OSB based on cost modeling, community needs, and technical viability from the Challenge Process. Climate and natural hazard risk areas (coastal flooding, ice storms, mountainous terrain) are also considered in network design requirements. There are no federally recognized tribal lands in Maryland.

structured_extraction.program_description: The Business Boost Microgrant Program provides direct microgrants of $20,000 to $50,000 to eligible small for-profit businesses located in designated Sustainable Communities areas across Maryland. Administered through the Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development's Neighborhood BusinessWorks (NBW) program, the initiative aims to activate vacant spaces, create jobs, and strengthen local economies by providing capital for business growth and/or expansion. Total program funding is up to $2 million. Eligible businesses must have 3 to 50 full-time equivalent employees and annual revenue between $50,000 and $1 million. Applicants must provide a matching contribution equal to or greater than the grant amount requested. Preference is given to home-based businesses seeking their first commercial location, Minority Business Enterprises, minority- or women-owned businesses, innovative businesses focused on regional strengths, and businesses leveraging partnerships with school districts or other education institutions in Maryland.

structured_extraction.program_name: Community Development Block Grant Disaster Recovery Assistance (Hurricane Sandy)
structured_extraction.program_description: Federal disaster recovery funding awarded to Maryland after Hurricane Sandy in October 2012. The State received $8.6 million (Grant #1) and $20 million (Grant #2) from Congress through the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development's Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) program to support recovery activities primarily in Somerset County, which experienced the most significant storm damage, as well as Allegany, Charles, Dorchester, and Garrett Counties. Funds support disaster relief, long-term recovery, restoration of infrastructure and housing, and economic revitalization in most impacted and distressed areas from Hurricane Sandy, Hurricane Irene, Tropical Storm Lee, the Derecho, and other eligible storm events in calendar years 2011, 2012, and 2013. Priorities include infrastructure projects protecting vulnerable residents and vital infrastructure from future flooding and building stronger, more resilient communities with mitigation of future flood and sea level rise risk.
structured_extraction.agency: Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development
structured_extraction.assistance_description: $8.6 million (Grant #1) and $20 million (Grant #2, awarded November 18, 2013) in federal CDBG Disaster Recovery funds, primarily directed to Somerset County as the most impacted and distressed county (receiving 83.6% of total funding, approximately $16,726,410). Funds cover housing recovery activities (rehabilitation and replacement, avg. $60,000 per unit for rehab, $130,000 for replacement; deferred loans repayable upon sale/transfer; housing elevation; property acquisition and demolition in floodplains); infrastructure improvements (dredging, culverts, drainage, shoreline stabilization, dock replacement, breakwater and jetty construction, tidal dike repair, bulkhead replacement, street resurfacing); public facility improvements (generators for water/sewer systems, emergency shelters, senior housing, municipal buildings); homeless shelter construction; economic recovery for small businesses (grants up to $5,000 for facades; loans of $15,000–$60,000 for working capital/construction); job training; broadband infrastructure; planning/needs assessment; blight removal; and wastewater infrastructure decommissioning and construction. Original grant end date: July 3, 2016; extended for Phase #3 funds to January 31, 2018; Phase #5 projects to be completed by August 2019. Expenditure deadline: October 1, 2022. Contracts over $25,000 are publicly posted per federal regulations.

structured_extraction.program_description: Federal grant funds distributed by Maryland to help strengthen communities by expanding affordable housing opportunities, creating jobs, stabilizing neighborhoods, and improving the overall quality of life. Projects must benefit low- and moderate-income persons, eliminate slum and blight, or meet an urgent community need. The program is administered by the Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development (DHCD), Division of Neighborhood Revitalization, and provides funding through two categories: Community Development grants (awarded competitively once per year) and Special Projects grants (for planning, economic development, and special-criteria projects, submitted any time after written approval).
structured_extraction.agency: Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Federal Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) funds are awarded through two categories: (1) Community Development grants (82% of allocation), awarded competitively once per year; and (2) Special Projects grants (15% of allocation) for planning, economic development, and special-criteria projects, which can be submitted any time after written approval (maximum $800,000 per application, first-come first-serve). Funds support housing (acquisition, rehabilitation up to $40,000 grant per single-family house, new construction), public facilities (water/sewer, streets, broadband, childcare/senior/community centers, shelters), economic development, and planning activities. Over any three-year period, 70% of the state's allocation must benefit low- and moderate-income persons. While eligible applicants are units of local government, public or private entities (including non-profits and for-profits) may participate as sub-recipients under an eligible local government.
structured_extraction.application_deadline_string: Community Development applications due Friday, October 24th by 2:00 p.m. (SFY 2026 round); Special Projects applications accepted at any time after written approval
structured_extraction.program_audience: Non-entitlement local governments in counties with fewer than 200,000 residents and cities/towns with fewer than 50,000 residents. Multiple jurisdictions may jointly apply. Public or private entities (including non-profits, CBDOs, CHDOs, and for-profit businesses in good standing) may be sub-recipients under an eligible local government.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Housing acquisition, renovation, and resale (max $200,000 per house); single-family owner-occupied housing rehabilitation (max $40,000 grant per house); rental housing renovation and construction; water and sewer system construction/extension; infrastructure improvements (roads, bridges, broadband, electrical systems); public facilities renovation and construction (senior centers, community centers, childcare centers, shelters, health centers); economic development projects including job creation and retention; planning activities (comprehensive plans, feasibility studies, preliminary engineering); site preparation and clearance; radon testing and mitigation (for grants after July 1, 2024); generator installation; administrative costs.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available in non-entitlement counties and municipalities in Maryland. Projects must generally be located in a Maryland Priority Funding Area. NOT available in Anne Arundel, Baltimore County, Harford, Howard, Montgomery, and Prince George's counties as entitlement jurisdictions, nor in the cities of Annapolis, Baltimore, Bowie, Cumberland, Frederick, Gaithersburg, Hagerstown, and Salisbury (or municipalities within the excluded entitlement counties), though some non-entitlement areas within entitlement counties may be eligible.
requirements_list: Applicant must be a unit of general local government in a non-entitlement county with fewer than 200,000 residents or a non-entitlement city/town with fewer than 50,000 residents

Project must meet one of three national objectives: benefit low- and moderate-income persons, eliminate slum and blight, or address an urgent need of recent origin threatening public health and safety

Projects in entitlement counties (Anne Arundel, Baltimore County, Harford, Howard, Montgomery, Prince George's) and entitlement cities (Annapolis, Baltimore, Bowie, Cumberland, Frederick, Gaithersburg, Hagerstown, Salisbury) are not eligible
Special Projects applicants must receive written approval before submitting an application
Special Projects: maximum $800,000 per application; first-come, first-serve basis
Minimum 105 points (70% of total) required for funding consideration (Community Development grants)
Citizen Participation Plan required (5-year validity, must be current)
Public hearing required prior to application submission
Non-profit subrecipients must have mission statement and bylaws clearly stating service to LMI persons
For housing rehabilitation: rehabilitation cost cannot exceed 50% of assessed property value
Compliance with local Standard Livability Code (minimum Section 8 Housing Quality Standards)
Debarment checks required on all contractors
Full and open competition required for all CDBG-funded procurements
Written Conflict of Interest Policy required
Single Audit compliance if $750,000+ federal funds expended annually

Economic development projects must exclude adult entertainment, check cashing, gambling, gun shops, liquor stores, massage parlors, medical marijuana, pawn shops, tanning salons, tattoo parlors, and professional sports teams
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: The State notifies eligible localities about available funds and conducts training sessions on application development. Community Development applications are submitted through a competitive process once per year (SFY 2026 deadline: October 24 by 2:00 p.m.). Applications should be submitted to the Maryland Clearinghouse (mdp.clearinghouse@maryland.gov) as required. Special Projects applications can be submitted any time after receiving written approval from the State; applicants must first consult with CDBG staff. All procurements require competitive bidding or cost analysis with proper documentation.

structured_extraction.program_description: Community Health and Safety Works provides grants to Maryland nonprofits (including faith-based organizations) and local governments to improve the livability and economic potential of Maryland communities through targeted investments in the physical environment that impact health and safety. The program supports crime control and prevention strategies through physical design improvements, making facilities, business districts, and public and private spaces safer and more defensible.
structured_extraction.agency: Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Grants are awarded to fund physical design improvements that enhance safety in facilities, business districts, and public and private spaces, supporting crime control and prevention strategies and improving community health and safety.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Maryland nonprofits (including faith-based organizations) and local governments seeking to improve community health and safety through physical environment investments
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Crime control and prevention strategies through physical design improvements to make facilities, business districts, and public and private spaces safer and more defensible
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Statewide Maryland

structured_extraction.program_description: The Community Investment Tax Credits (CITC) program supports 501(c)(3) nonprofit organizations by awarding allocations of State tax credits. Nonprofits use these credits as incentives to attract charitable contributions of $500 or more from individuals, businesses, and financial institutions. Donors receive a tax credit equal to 50% of the value of their contribution (cash, goods, or real property) on their Maryland state tax return — a dollar-for-dollar reduction of Maryland taxes owed — in addition to standard federal and state charitable deductions. For example, a $2,000 donation earns a $1,000 Maryland tax credit. Projects must be located in or serve residents of a Priority Funding Area. The program has leveraged nearly $27 million in charitable contributions to approximately 700 projects statewide. In 2026, $1.75 million in awards were announced, including $10,000 in tax credit allocations to Main Street Historic Chestertown for operating support. Participating nonprofits such as Healthy Neighborhoods Inc. can certify eligible donations to DHCD, which then issues Tax Credit Certificates to donors. Individuals claim the credit on Form 502CR; businesses and banks use Form 500CR. See also www.GiveMaryland.org.
structured_extraction.agency: Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Nonprofits receive allocations of State tax credits (maximum $50,000 per award, minimum typical award $10,000) to offer donors as incentives. Total annual statewide funding is $1.75 million. Awardees must raise double the tax credits requested (e.g., $50,000 in credits requires $100,000 in donations). Donors who contribute $500 or more receive a tax credit equal to 50% of the value of their money, goods, or real property contribution (e.g., a $2,000 donation earns a $1,000 Maryland tax credit). The credit is a dollar-for-dollar reduction of Maryland state income taxes owed, in addition to standard federal and state charitable deductions. Donors complete a Donor Acknowledgement/Donor Form provided by the participating nonprofit; the nonprofit certifies the donation to DHCD; DHCD issues a Tax Credit Certificate. Individuals claim the credit on Form 502CR; businesses and banks use Form 500CR. Credits must be applied against taxes owed in the year the contribution was made and cannot be carried back to prior years. Technical assistance and information are also available to participating nonprofits.
structured_extraction.program_audience: IRS-designated 501(c)(3) nonprofit organizations seeking tax credit allocations to attract contributions for projects in or serving Priority Funding Areas. Also relevant to Maryland individuals, businesses, and financial institutions looking to reduce their state tax liability by making charitable contributions of $500 or more in exchange for Maryland State tax credits.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Capital and/or operating projects including education and youth services, housing and community development, job and self-sufficiency training, neighborhood and business district enhancement, arts and historic preservation, economic development and tourism, technical assistance and capacity building, and services for at-risk populations. Tax credits are issued to donors who make eligible charitable contributions to participating nonprofits.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Projects must be located in or serve residents of a Priority Funding Area in Maryland. Additional priority is given to projects in ENOUGH Act designated areas and Just Communities. Available to Maryland taxpayers (individuals, businesses, and financial institutions) statewide.
requirements_list: Applicant nonprofit must be an IRS-designated 501(c)(3) organization
Nonprofit must be in good standing with Maryland Department of Assessments and Taxation (SDAT)
Nonprofit must be registered as a charity with Maryland Secretary of State
Affiliates of larger umbrella organizations are eligible with parent organization documentation
Religious organizations with exemption from charitable registration are eligible with proper documentation
Projects must be located in or serve residents of a Priority Funding Area
Donors must contribute $500 or more to qualify for tax credits
Donor must owe Maryland state income tax
Donation must qualify as a charitable contribution under federal and Maryland law
Donors must complete a Donor Acknowledgement/Donor Form provided by the participating nonprofit
Tax credits must be applied against taxes owed in the year of contribution — cannot be applied retroactively
Real property donors must contact the nonprofit prior to making the donation
Eligible business donors must conduct a trade or business in Maryland and be subject to applicable State taxes
Eligible individual donors must be natural persons or fiduciaries with personal tax liability in Maryland
Gift can be made by check, online, or approved in-kind contribution
Awardees must raise double the tax credits requested (e.g., $50,000 in credits requires $100,000 in donations)
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Nonprofits apply through the DHCD Application Portal (https://projectportal.dhcd.state.md.us/). Applicants must first register as a new user and allow up to 72 hours for approval. Once registered, they can complete and submit the application. The application period is annual and competitive. Donors connect with participating nonprofits via the GIVE Maryland portal or directly with individual nonprofits. To claim the credit: make a qualifying gift of $500 or more, complete the Donor Form provided by the nonprofit, the nonprofit certifies the donation to DHCD, DHCD sends a Tax Credit Certificate, and at tax filing attach the certificate and claim the credit using Form 502CR (individuals) or Form 500CR (businesses/banks).

structured_extraction.program_description: The Community Legacy Program provides competitive grants to local governments and community development organizations for projects that stabilize communities, reverse economic or physical decline, and encourage sustainable growth. Eligible projects include business retention and attraction, homeownership initiatives, commercial revitalization, streetscape improvements, façade improvement programs, mixed-use development, real estate acquisition (including land banking), site development, construction, building renovations, and strategic demolition. Projects must generally be located in designated Sustainable Communities or qualifying Opportunity Zones in Allegany, Garrett, Somerset, or Wicomico Counties. Approximately $8 million in capital funding is available for FY2025.
structured_extraction.agency: Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Competitive grants awarded to local governments and community development organizations for community stabilization and revitalization projects. Approximately $8 million in capital funding is available for FY2025. Specific award amounts vary by applicant; example awards include $100,000 (Main Street Rock Hall) and $150,000 (Town of Betterton) in Kent County in one funding round. Projects must be located in a designated Sustainable Community or in an Opportunity Zone in Allegany, Garrett, Somerset, or Wicomico Counties.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Local governments, community development organizations (such as county councils, community development corporations, main street organizations, downtown partnerships, and nonprofits), and groups of local governments sharing a common purpose, seeking to stabilize or revitalize communities in Sustainable Communities or qualifying Opportunity Zones.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Local housing, community, and economic development revitalization projects including mixed-use development, business retention and attraction, streetscape improvements, homeownership and home rehabilitation, residential and commercial façade improvement programs, real estate acquisition including land banking, strategic demolition, site development, construction, and building renovations.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available statewide in Maryland. Projects must be located in designated Sustainable Communities or in an Opportunity Zone in Allegany, Garrett, Somerset, or Wicomico Counties.
requirements_list: Applicant must be a local government, community development organization, or group of local governments
Project must be located in a designated Sustainable Community or an Opportunity Zone in Allegany, Garrett, Somerset, or Wicomico Counties
Project should help achieve strategies outlined in the local government's Sustainable Communities Action Plan
Project should stabilize a community, reverse social/economic/physical decline, or encourage sustainable growth
First-time applicants should contact a regional project manager for eligibility determination
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Register for application training webinar and view program information at the DHCD State Revitalization Programs website (https://dhcd.maryland.gov/Communities/Pages/StateRevitalizationPrograms/default.aspx). First-time applicants should contact a regional project manager for eligibility determination. Use the Neighborhood Revitalization Mapper to determine geographic eligibility. Submit application by the published deadline.

structured_extraction.program_description: The Community Services Block Grant (CSBG) program funds a statewide network of seventeen Community Action Agencies (CAAs) in Maryland to provide direct services that help low-income individuals and families achieve self-sufficiency. The program addresses the causes and conditions of poverty through a one-stop service delivery system available in all 23 Maryland counties and Baltimore City, covering areas including employment, education, better use of available income, housing, nutrition, emergency services, and health. Services include employment and training activities, energy assistance, case management, whole family approach services, workforce development, eviction prevention, utility assistance, food distribution, youth development, and emergency food and nutrition services.
structured_extraction.agency: Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development
structured_extraction.assistance_description: The federal government annually appropriates CSBG funds administered by the Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development. Ninety percent of Maryland's allocation goes directly to the seventeen designated Community Action Agencies to operate anti-poverty programs and services. The state may use up to five percent as discretionary funding for Community Action Agencies, non-profits, and local government units to eliminate poverty, promote self-sufficiency, and revitalize communities. Discretionary funds may also support training and technical assistance and coordination among Community Action Agencies. Funds are allocated based on poverty rates, unemployment data, and rural community status. Training includes Organizational Standards, Reporting Requirements, Monitoring, and Governance/Tripartite Board composition.
structured_extraction.application_deadline_string: The FY25 application round is closed. Check this page for information about future funding rounds.
structured_extraction.contact_name: Angela Fraser, Assistant Director, Division of Homeless Solutions
structured_extraction.program_audience: Maryland's seventeen designated Community Action Agencies are eligible for the 90% allocation. Community Action Agencies, non-profit organizations, and units of local government serving individuals and families at or below 200% of the federal poverty guidelines are eligible for CSBG Discretionary funding. Also serves low-income families and individuals, homeless individuals, migrant or seasonal farmworkers, elderly low-income individuals, TANF recipients, and youth in low-income communities.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Direct services to help low-income individuals and families achieve self-sufficiency; programs and activities that address causes of poverty including employment, education, housing, nutrition, emergency services, and health; training and technical assistance; coordination among Community Action Agencies; community revitalization; eviction prevention; utility assistance; food distribution; affordable housing support; entrepreneurship programs; transportation services for elderly; youth development and crime prevention; emergency food and nutrition services; workforce development.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: All 23 Maryland counties and Baltimore City. Services reach individuals and households in urban and rural areas with incomes at or below 200% of the federal poverty guidelines. DHCD serves as Balance of State Continuum of Care for seven counties: Allegany, Calvert, Cecil, Charles, Garrett, St. Mary's, and Washington.
requirements_list: Must be one of Maryland's seventeen designated Community Action Agencies (for 90% allocation) or a Community Action Agency, non-profit, or unit of local government (for Discretionary funding)

Applicants for 90% allocation must have a qualifying tripartite board of directors: at least one-third elected public officials or designees, at least one-third representatives chosen democratically to represent low-income persons, and the remainder from business, labor, religious, welfare, education, or other community interests
Proposed program must display measurable outcomes that help families and individuals move toward self-sufficiency (for Discretionary funding)
Must serve individuals and families at or below 200% of the federal poverty guidelines
Must conduct community needs assessments and develop community action plans
Must participate in Results Oriented Management and Accountability (ROMA) or alternative performance measurement system
Must comply with Organizational Standards
Must certify compliance with federal requirements including lobbying restrictions, drug-free workplace, and debarment certifications
Must maintain drug-free workplace policies and avoid debarred/suspended contractors
Debarment certification required; no criminal convictions for antitrust violations, embezzlement, theft, forgery, bribery, falsification of records, false statements, or stolen property
Environmental Tobacco Smoke compliance: smoking prohibited in facilities serving children under 18 funded by federal programs
Subgrantees must include same certifications in subawards
Must report State Accountability Measures and meet single audit requirements
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Community Action Agencies receive funds through the state's annual allocation process. For Discretionary funding, applicants apply during published funding rounds. The FY25 discretionary application round is closed; check the program page for future rounds. Community needs assessments and community action plans are required as a condition of funding. Contact the Community Action Agency that serves your county for information about programs and services.
