structured_extraction.program_name: Pocomoke River Restoration Project – Landowner Funding Incentives
structured_extraction.program_description: A multi-agency partnership project to restore the hydrology of the channelized Pocomoke River floodplain by breaching spoil levees along 9 miles of the river mainstem between Route 50 and Porters Crossing Road. The goal is to reconnect the river with its forested floodplain wetlands, improving flood storage, water quality, nutrient and sediment removal, and resilience to climate variability and intense storms. The project encompasses approximately 4,000 acres of floodplain in Wicomico and Worcester counties, Maryland, including areas within Pocomoke State Forest and surrounding lands. Financial incentives are offered to private landowners who allow levee breaches to reconnect the river to its forested floodplain. Total project funding was $1,500,097 from the Chesapeake and Atlantic Coastal Bays Trust Fund, leveraged with $2,382,000 in additional funds from The Nature Conservancy.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Two incentive options are available to landowners in the priority area: (1) 100% of restoration costs covered plus a $250 per acre incentive payment from The Nature Conservancy in exchange for a 10-year landowner agreement, or (2) 100% of restoration costs covered plus approximately $1,980 per acre (2016 rate) for a permanent conservation easement held by NRCS. Rates for the NRCS easement option are evaluated yearly and may change based on real estate market conditions. Total project funding was $1,500,097 from the Chesapeake and Atlantic Coastal Bays Trust Fund, leveraged with $2,382,000 in additional funds from The Nature Conservancy. Funding is contingent on available funds.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Private landowners within the approximately 4,000-acre floodplain priority area along the Pocomoke River mainstem between Route 50 and Porters Crossing Road in Wicomico and Worcester counties, Maryland.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Restoration of floodplain hydrology through levee breaches to reconnect the river channel to its forested floodplain wetlands, including coverage of all restoration construction costs and an additional per-acre payment to the landowner, restoring wetland acreage, and improving water quality and flood storage capacity.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Priority area is along 9 miles of the channelized Pocomoke River mainstem between Route 50 and Porters Crossing Road in Wicomico and Worcester counties on Maryland's Eastern Shore, encompassing approximately 4,000 acres of floodplain, including areas within Pocomoke State Forest and surrounding lands.

structured_extraction.program_description: A certification program administered by the Maryland Department of Natural Resources (DNR) Power Plant Research Program (PPRP) that recognizes commercial ground-mounted photovoltaic solar facilities greater than 1 acre as pollinator-friendly. Solar developers who plant and manage pollinator habitat on their solar sites according to DNR guidelines can receive a two-year certification. The program effectuates requirements of Ch. 372, Acts of 2017. The program requires submitting an application with facility details (name, location, whether proposed or existing, tax map information, acreage, contact information, and a short description), a pollinator habitat management plan, using approved seed mixes appropriate for the Maryland region, passing a site inspection by a DNR-approved inspector, and submitting a final Solar Site Pollinator Habitat Planning and Assessment Scorecard. Upon approval, a two-year certification is issued, renewable within 90 days of expiration.

The developer may apply for renewal by contacting PPRP within 90 days of expiration. This is a certification/designation program rather than a direct financial assistance program.

structured_extraction.program_name: Program Open Space (POS) Local Annual Programs
structured_extraction.program_description: Program Open Space is a nationally recognized Maryland program established in 1969 that uses a small percentage of the state real estate transfer tax (0.5%), funds from the Outdoor Recreation Land Loan of 1969, and federal Land and Water Conservation Fund dollars to fund acquisition of open space for state parks, natural resource areas, and local park land. The Local Annual Programs component provides financial and technical assistance to local governments (counties, municipalities, and Baltimore City) for planning, acquiring, and/or developing recreation land or open space areas to meet local land conservation and recreation goals. Funds are allocated annually to Maryland's 23 counties and Baltimore City based on a formula, and may be used to acquire or develop land for public recreation or open space use — including ballfields, playgrounds, tennis courts, boating facilities, swimming pools, fishing sites, hunting areas, forests, golf courses, hiking trails, greenways, wildlife areas, historic sites, and other natural community resources. Acquisition and planning projects do not require a local match; development projects require a 10% or 25% local match depending on the county's Land Preservation, Parks and Recreation Plan (LPPRP) results. Each year, participating counties and Baltimore City submit an annual program of proposed acquisition and development projects to the Maryland Department of Natural Resources (DNR) for approval and the Department of Planning for review. Once approved by DNR and the Board of Public Works, allocated funds are encumbered for those projects. The program has acquired more than 150,000 acres for state parks and natural resource areas and more than 25,000 acres of local park land, with over 6,700 projects funded to date. It also administers Waterway Improvement Fund grants for boating-related infrastructure. Funded projects must align with local Land Preservation, Parks and Recreation Plans. Municipalities may receive funds through their county's allocation. DNR staff also provide technical assistance including grant writing workshops. Allegany County administers its share of POS Local funding locally, accepting public comments on proposed projects for each fiscal year. Planning grants are available up to $25,000 per fiscal year for updating Local Land Preservation and Recreation Plans.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Reimbursable grants allocated annually to counties and Baltimore City based on a formula, with municipalities eligible to receive a share of their county's allocation. Funds may be used for planning, land acquisition, and development of parks and recreation facilities — including ballfields, playgrounds, tennis courts, boating facilities, swimming pools, fishing sites, hunting areas, forests, golf courses, hiking trails, greenways, wildlife areas, and historic sites. Acquisition and planning projects do not require a local match. Development projects require a 10% or 25% local match depending on the county's LPPRP results. Acquisition projects are eligible for 100% funding reimbursement based on average of two property appraisals or purchase price (whichever is lower). Development/enhancement/rehabilitation projects are eligible for up to 75% (or up to 90% in some counties) of project costs. Planning grants are available up to $25,000 per fiscal year for updating Local Land Preservation and Recreation Plans. Partial reimbursements are permitted to help with cash flow; advance payments may be considered on a case-by-case basis. Funds are encumbered after review by the Department of Planning and approval by DNR and the Board of Public Works. Also administers Waterway Improvement Fund grants for boating-related infrastructure. Technical assistance is available for planning, acquisition, and development of recreation land or open space areas, including grant writing workshops. Cannot be used for operating and maintenance costs.

structured_extraction.program_audience: Local governments — Maryland's 23 counties, municipalities, and Baltimore City — seeking to plan, acquire, or develop open space, park land, and natural resource areas through Program Open Space.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Planning, land acquisition, and development of parks and recreation facilities; acquisition of open space for state parks and natural resource areas; Waterway Improvement Fund grants for boating-related infrastructure; acquisition or development of land for public recreation or open space use consistent with local Land Preservation, Parks and Recreation Plans; completion of the county Land Preservation, Parks and Recreation Plan (LPPRP). Eligible project types include ballfields, playgrounds, tennis courts, boating facilities, swimming pools, fishing sites, hunting areas, forests, golf courses, hiking trails, greenways, wildlife areas, historic sites, ADA-compliant upgrades, pavilions, community centers, athletic fields, trails, waterfront access improvements, LED lighting retrofits, court renovations, boardwalk repairs, pavilion and roof replacement, dugout replacement, golf course improvements, museum and interpretive facilities, wetland conservation areas, stormwater management facilities, pedestrian bridges, dog parks, restroom facilities, kayak/canoe launches, pool facility modernization, park rehabilitation, pickleball courts, pump tracks, boat launches, community gardens, park land acquisition, design and construction of pedestrian crossings and trail overlooks, multi-purpose fields, multi-purpose buildings, parking lots, boathouse replacement, landscaping and signage, park master plan implementation, school-to-trail connections, shooting range renovations, site remediation, amphitheater construction, shade structures, roadway and pathway improvements, urban forest demonstration projects, equestrian facilities, bocce courts, field lighting installation, fence replacement, walking trails with porous surfacing, basketball court rehabilitation and resurfacing, joint school/recreation facility development, railroad right-of-way acquisition for trails, supporting infrastructure (roads, water, sewer lines, utility connections), preliminary site planning costs, construction and site preparation, equipment for facility operations (not maintenance), informational and interpretive signage/facilities, force account labor and equipment costs, incidental acquisition costs (surveys, appraisals, title searches, legal fees, settlement fees, recording costs), and acknowledgment signage costs. Cannot be used for operating and maintenance costs.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available to all 23 Maryland counties, municipalities, and Baltimore City participating in Program Open Space. Municipalities may receive funds through their county's allocation. Statewide in Maryland. Allegany County administers its local allocation for projects within Allegany County. In Frederick County, projects must be located within municipalities or Priority Funding Areas (PFA); county unallocated acquisition projects may be outside PFAs. In Howard County, projects must be within Planned Service (Smart Growth) Areas and conform to Howard County General Plan and Smart Growth Initiative. Projects must conform to the county's Local Land Preservation and Recreation Plan and be consistent with the State Land Preservation and Recreation Plan. Applicant must own property in fee simple or hold a minimum 20-year lease for development projects. Replacement property for conversions must generally serve the same community/area as the converted site.

structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Contact the Local Grants Administrator for your area. Local jurisdictions include projects in their POS Local Annual Program and authorize funding. Applications are submitted using the appropriate application form (acquisition, development/capital renewal, or planning). Local jurisdictions submit an annual program of proposed acquisition and development projects to the Department of Planning for review and to the Department of Natural Resources for approval by July 1 each year. DNR staff review for completeness and program consistency, then submit to the State Clearinghouse and other DNR units for review. After reviews, the project is scheduled on the Board of Public Works (BPW) agenda for approval. The full process takes approximately 2–3 months. Projects can request a Letter of Concurrence (written concurrence from POS Local) for urgent situations before full application submission. Upon review and approval, and after Board of Public Works approval, allocated funds are encumbered. Programs may be revised and resubmitted for approval. For acquisition projects: prepare required attachments (road map, acquisition line map, two independent appraisals, planning agency approval, deed documentation, photographs, funding authorization) before completing the application; coordinate site inspection with POS Program Administrator; submit application with all required attachments for Board of Public Works approval. For development/capital renewal projects: prepare and assemble ten required attachments including road map, site plan, planning agency approval, reforestation compliance, capital renewal justification, photographs, floor plans, deed/lease/SDAT documentation, retention of rights explanation, and funding authorization; contact POS Program Administrator for site inspection and application review. For planning grants: complete application form with project information, location, description, funding, federal funds designation, applicant information, and local coordinator details; obtain local government authorization signature; submit for Maryland Board of Public Works approval. For reimbursement of acquisition costs: submit completed reimbursement request form with required attachments (deed with required covenant, evidence of title, settlement sheet, invoices, canceled checks, cost breakdown by parcel) to county Local Grants Administrator via email. For reimbursement of development/capital renewal costs: submit reimbursement request with supporting documentation including invoices/requisitions with itemized costs, proof of payment (canceled checks), cost summaries, in-house labor documentation, equipment usage records, project completion photos, grant acknowledgement sign photos, and required certifications. In Allegany County, residents and stakeholders may submit public comments on proposed POS funding allocations to the local administrator by the county's public comment deadline. Some counties (e.g., Talbot, Wicomico, St. Mary's, Worcester) involve local advisory boards, recreation commissions, planning commissions, and/or county commissioners in project review and approval before submission to DNR. In Wicomico County, municipalities and local recreation councils submit project lists; the 14-member Recreation Commission recommends projects; the County Executive approves; the budget is submitted to the County Council; then submitted to the State. Annual program revision submissions to DNR may include written correspondence with project descriptions and funding requests, and counties may request to revert or reallocate prior year funding. For conversion proposals: contact DNR 6–12 months before submitting a conversion proposal; preliminary review by Assistant Regional Administrator; formal application with required documentation submitted if approved; appeal process available if denied.

structured_extraction.program_description: Program Open Space Stateside (POS Stateside) preserves natural areas for public recreation, watershed protection, and wildlife protection across Maryland. It acquires land through fee simple purchases and conservation easements from willing landowners. Fee simple purchases are managed by the Department of Natural Resources (DNR) as State Parks, Forests, and Wildlife and Fisheries Management Areas. The program also funds permanent Conservation Reserve Enhancement Program (CREP) easements. It is funded primarily by a 0.5 percent State property transfer tax, and acquisitions are evaluated based on ecological (Land) and recreational (People) criteria, equally weighted. Regional program administrators cover Central, Eastern, Southern, and Western regions of the state.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: The program purchases land in fee simple or acquires conservation easements from willing landowners to preserve natural areas for public use and environmental protection across Maryland. It is funded primarily by a 0.5 percent State property transfer tax. Acquisitions are evaluated based on ecological (Land) and recreational (People) criteria, equally weighted. Funding is also used to make permanent Conservation Reserve Enhancement Program (CREP) easements.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Landowners and entities across Maryland willing to sell land or grant conservation easements that offer ecological value, public recreation opportunities, watershed protection, or wildlife habitat, as well as government entities seeking to preserve natural lands.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Acquisition of fee simple land and conservation easements to preserve natural areas for public recreation, watershed protection, and wildlife habitat. Also used to make permanent Conservation Reserve Enhancement Program (CREP) easements.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available statewide across all Maryland counties. Regional program administrators cover Central, Eastern, Southern, and Western regions.
requirements_list: Properties are evaluated on Land criteria: wildlife habitat connectivity, presence of rare or endangered species, support of aquatic life, forests important for water quality, location within Targeted Ecological Areas, restoration opportunity, and climate change adaptation.

Properties are evaluated on People criteria: high-value resource-based recreational opportunities, new public access or water access, trail connections, expansion of existing recreation, in-holdings or adjacent parcels addressing long-term management concerns, buffering existing lands, coastal community resilience, and educational, cultural, or historical value.
Land and People components are equally weighted in the acquisition decision.
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Contact the appropriate regional Program Administrator for your county or the statewide conservation easement contact to discuss your property. The Department of Natural Resources evaluates potential land acquisitions using a process that balances conservation attributes with land management needs. Prospective contacts should reach out via the Program Open Space Stateside Contacts page.

structured_extraction.program_description: Project WILD is a hands-on professional development workshop for K-12 educators that builds awareness, appreciation, and understanding of wildlife and natural resources. Participants model interdisciplinary activities covering art, language arts, math, science, and social studies, and receive award-winning curriculum guides with over 100 lesson plans upon completion. Workshops are free or low cost and funded by wildlife license fees. An annual train-the-trainer facilitator workshop is also offered for educators who wish to lead their own workshops.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Free or low-cost 4-6 hour professional development workshops for educators. Participants receive one or two Project WILD curriculum guides with 100+ lesson plans. Educators who attend 3 out of 5 workshops with certified trainers may earn 1 MSDE continuing education credit (CPD: 18-66-13R). Private on-site training is available at no cost for groups of 15 or more. An annual train-the-trainer facilitator workshop is offered for volunteer educators who want to lead their own workshops.
structured_extraction.program_audience: K-12 educators in formal settings (classrooms) and non-formal settings (nature centers, museums, zoos, parks, and scout programs) across Maryland
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Professional development in wildlife and natural resource education; curriculum guides and lesson plans for K-12 instruction and teaching about local wildlife
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available statewide across Maryland

structured_extraction.program_description: Annual reimbursement grant for marinas to cover the operations and maintenance costs of existing boat sewage pumpout stations. Funded through the federal Clean Vessel Act (grant award F25AP02642) and the Maryland Waterway Improvement Fund. Reimburses eligible pumpout O&M expenses up to $5,000 per marina. Terms and conditions are issued each grant year (2026 terms and conditions available).
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Reimbursement grants up to $5,000 per marina for eligible pumpout operations and maintenance expenses. Reimbursement is calculated as Eligible Pumpout O&M Expenses minus Pumpout Income. Eligible expenses include: staff labor for pumpout operations ($3.75 per pumpout, up to $2,000), staff labor for repairs/maintenance ($25/hour, up to 25 hours/$625), licensed plumber/electrician services, replacement parts and equipment, licensed sewage hauler payments, winterization costs, annual pumpout connection fees, and log-keeping ($100).
structured_extraction.program_audience: Marina operators and owners with approved operational marine sewage pumpout facilities providing public pumpout services to transient vessels in Maryland.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Operations and maintenance of existing boat sewage pumpout stations, including: staff labor for pumpout operations ($3.75 per pumpout, up to $2,000), staff labor for repairs/maintenance ($25/hour, up to 25 hours/$625), licensed plumber/electrician services, replacement parts and equipment (factory authorized dealer only), licensed sewage hauler payments for waste removal, winterization costs, annual pumpout connection fees, and log-keeping ($100).
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available to marinas located in Maryland (statewide).
requirements_list: Applicant must be a marina with an existing operational marine sewage pumpout facility
Marina must be approved to participate in the program
Application must be submitted and approved prior to April 15, 2026
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Complete the 2026 Pumpout Operations and Maintenance Grant Application form online. Review the Terms and Conditions before applying. Application must be approved prior to April 15, 2026. Contact pumpouts.dnr@maryland.gov with questions.

structured_extraction.program_description: The Resident Curatorship Program is a public-private partnership administered by the Maryland Department of Natural Resources that allows individuals or non-profit organizations to live in and restore historic structures located on Maryland state public lands (such as State Parks and natural resource areas) in exchange for investing in the property's rehabilitation and ongoing maintenance. The program has been operating since 1982 and has nearly 50 curatorships across Maryland, from Western Maryland to Assateague Island. Curators commit to restoring and preserving historically significant properties while sharing their experience and the property with the public. In return, curators pay no rent to the state and receive lifetime residency rights (or rights of tenancy). Non-profit organizations may receive preference when their mission aligns with the land unit where the property is located, and may also qualify for additional grants and loans for restoration work. The program is designed to preserve historic buildings with minimal modern intrusion while keeping them compatible with the mission of the Maryland Park Service. Curators must follow the Secretary of the Interior's Standards for Historic Preservation and open the property to the public several times per year. The Department of Natural Resources insures the structure against fire, flood, and similar hazards, and a Program Manager provides technical guidance and coordinates required environmental and historic preservation reviews throughout the restoration process.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Approved curators receive a Right of Entry to a historic state-owned property and, upon final approval by the Board of Public Works, a Curatorship Agreement granting lifetime residency rights (or rights of tenancy) in a historic structure located on state public lands at a nominal annual rent of $1.00/year. The state provides no direct financial assistance but insures the structure against fire, flood, and similar hazards. The Program Manager provides technical guidance, coordinates required environmental and historic preservation reviews, and supports curators throughout the restoration process. Curators are expected to invest a minimum of $150,000, with initial improvements typically in the $200,000–$250,000 range and total investment typically $150,000–$300,000 over a five to seven-year restoration period. Non-profit organizations may also qualify for additional grants and loans for restoration work. All improvements become property of the State of Maryland. Curators are responsible for all maintenance, operating costs, utilities, taxes, renters insurance, and liability insurance throughout the term of the agreement. Expenses are generally not tax-deductible.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Individuals and non-profit organizations committed to historic preservation who want to live in and restore a historic house on Maryland state public lands and natural resource areas, particularly those with experience or qualifications in historic preservation.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Restoration and rehabilitation of historic structures on state public lands, including labor, materials, sweat equity, improvements to electrical, plumbing, heating systems, hazardous material remediation, exterior/interior restoration, and ongoing maintenance and operation of the property in compliance with the Secretary of the Interior's Standards for Historic Preservation.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available statewide across Maryland on historic properties located within state public lands such as State Parks and areas managed by the Department of Natural Resources, from Western Maryland to Assateague Island.

structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Prospective curators are encouraged to call the Manager of Curatorships and Cultural Resources to discuss the proposal process before submitting. Review program policies and frequently asked questions on the DNR website, then submit a proposal package electronically or by mail (faxed proposals not accepted) to the Program Manager. The package must include a cover letter, resume(s), a Schedule of Restoration with cost estimates, and a Personal Financial Statement. The Personal Financial Statement must include detailed information on assets, liabilities, and income sources, and must be signed and dated with an affirmation of accuracy. An interagency panel reviews and scores proposals. Selected applicants receive a Right of Entry while the final Curatorship Agreement is drafted. An initial committee review takes approximately three months. After selection, the process from proposal to final approval by the Maryland Board of Public Works takes about six months total. All planned work must be submitted as detailed plans and specifications prepared by certified professionals, reviewed by the Curator Program Manager, and must obtain Maryland Historical Trust review, building permits, and code compliance evidence. The work review process coordinated by the Program Manager typically takes about 30 days. Lease execution requires notarized signatures from all parties and approval by the Maryland Board of Public Works for the agreement to be effective. Contact curatorships.dnr@maryland.gov or peter.morrill1@maryland.gov for more information. No properties are currently available.

structured_extraction.program_name: Resilience through Restoration Initiative – Grants Gateway Outcome 3
structured_extraction.program_description: Provides financial and technical assistance to local governments and non-profit organizations to fund design, permitting, and construction of coastal and stormwater restoration projects that protect communities from erosion, flooding, and other climate change impacts. Eligible projects include living shorelines, tidal marsh restoration, dune restoration, beneficial use of dredged material, rain gardens, bioswales, and other nature-based practices that provide community and ecosystem benefits. Funded by a combination of State of Maryland and federal (NOAA Maryland Coastal Zone Management Award) sources. For the CY2026/FY2027 cycle, only design and permitting proposals are eligible; construction is not funded at this time due to funding limitations. Funding becomes available July 1, 2026 – October 1, 2026 depending on fund source and approvals. Structural solutions such as bulkheads and revetments are not funded.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Grant funding and technical assistance for design, permitting, construction, and adaptive management of coastal habitat restoration and nature-based stormwater projects. For the CY2026/FY2027 cycle, only design and permitting proposals are eligible (construction is not funded at this time). Design and permit projects typically cost between $30,000 and $100,000. Permit fees are not eligible. Up to 1:1 matching funds are encouraged. Community public property is prioritized; funding for private residential properties can be difficult to obtain. Projects on private lands must demonstrate a community-wide benefit. Funding is provided by the State of Maryland and NOAA and becomes available July 1, 2026 – October 1, 2026 depending on fund source and approvals.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Local governments and non-profit organizations seeking to implement nature-based restoration projects that reduce community flood risk and erosion impacts throughout Maryland.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Design, permitting, construction, and adaptive management of coastal habitat restoration, shoreline restoration, beneficial use of dredged material, tidal marsh restoration, dune restoration, rain gardens, bioswales, and other green stormwater and nature-based practices that provide community and ecosystem benefits. Permit fees are not eligible. Projects on private lands must demonstrate a community-wide benefit.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Projects can be located throughout Maryland. Both public and private lands are eligible, but projects on private lands must demonstrate a community-wide benefit. Community public property is prioritized for funding.

structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Applicants submit proposals through the Chesapeake and Coastal Grants Gateway (Outcome 3). Required attachments include a signed transmittal letter, budget table (using provided template), communication and engagement strategy, site photographs, and any applicable landowner agreements or letters of support. Proposals are reviewed based on habitat enhancement, climate change impact reduction, community-wide benefit, and incorporation of climate data. Applicants are encouraged to contact Nicole Carlozo to discuss project ideas or arrange a site visit before applying. Non-profit applicants should contact the outcome contact to confirm eligibility. See the DNR Grants Gateway page for current solicitations and funding availability.

structured_extraction.program_name: Riparian Forest Buffer Initiative / Stream ReLeaf
structured_extraction.program_description: Stream ReLeaf is Maryland's implementation of the Chesapeake Bay Riparian Forest Buffer Initiative. It coordinates state, local, federal, and nonprofit partners to establish, expand, and maintain riparian forest buffers — strips of trees and vegetation planted along streams and shorelines — to improve water quality, reduce nutrient runoff, support wildlife habitat, fish habitat, and wildlife corridors, and contribute to Chesapeake Bay restoration goals. The Maryland Department of Natural Resources Forest Service supports voluntary restoration and conservation of forested buffers, tracks buffer restoration progress toward statewide mileage goals using an official reporting system, provides outreach and education to landowners and partner organizations, and connects landowners with cost-share programs such as the Conservation Reserve Enhancement Program (CREP) that offer incentive payments for buffer plantings. The program has a long-term goal of 70% forest buffer coverage on riparian miles in the Chesapeake Basin, with a state commitment to plant 600 miles of new buffers by 2010 (43 miles per year). Maryland has approximately 38,870 miles of riparian area statewide.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: The program provides staff support, coordination, and technical assistance for the voluntary establishment, expansion, and maintenance of riparian forest buffers along streams and shorelines. Technical guidance includes tracking and reporting of buffer miles, resources, outreach, networking, and buffer width recommendations (at least 35 feet, with 50–100 feet promoted as optimal). It connects landowners and partners with cost-share programs such as the Conservation Reserve Enhancement Program (CREP), through which participating landowners may receive incentive payments, soil rent, signup and practice incentive payments, and establishment cost reimbursement (87.5% total: 50% federal, 37.5% state). Additional funding programs include EQIP (50% cost-share), Conservation Security Program incentives, Forest Legacy and Rural Legacy easements, Chesapeake Bay Trust and National Fish and Wildlife Foundation grants, and carbon sequestration and ozone mitigation funds. Maintenance payments of $7–$10/acre/year are available for fenced buffers under 10–15 year CREP contracts. Annual Stream ReLeaf Recognition Awards are given in five categories: Landowner, Local Government, Education, Community Organization, and Business. The program tracks buffer restoration progress toward statewide mileage goals through an official buffer reporting system. Additional support includes cost-shared herbicide treatments for weed control, seedling cooler storage support, tree protection mechanisms (shelters, collars, repellents), training materials and workshops on buffer establishment and maintenance, support for nursery overstock utilization, technical assistance through third-party providers, urban tree canopy assessment and goal-setting support, and maintenance team development and coordination.
structured_extraction.application_deadline_string: January 1 (for fall planting) and July 1 (for spring planting) for buffer reporting form submission
structured_extraction.program_audience: Landowners (private, agricultural, and public), developers, local governments, educators, students, state, local, federal, and nonprofit agencies and groups, watershed organizations, land trusts, soil conservation districts, volunteer organizations, and natural resource professionals interested in voluntarily restoring, conserving, or reporting riparian forest buffer plantings along streams and shorelines in Maryland.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Establishing and maintaining riparian forest buffers along streams, rivers, and shorelines, including tree planting, buffer width expansion, conversion of grass filter strips to forest, stream stabilization with native vegetation, site preparation (mowing, chemical treatment), weed control, tree shelters and protection, maintenance of buffers to reduce nutrient runoff, improve water quality, support wildlife and fish habitat, and contribute to Chesapeake Bay restoration goals. Funds may also support urban tree canopy assessment and expansion, conservation easements, mitigation banking, training and technical assistance provision, database tracking and GIS system development, and 5-year monitoring of newly established buffers.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available statewide in Maryland; any perennial or intermittent stream or shoreline is eligible. Priority areas include free-flowing perennial streams and first- and second-order (small) streams in the Chesapeake Bay watershed. Program covers all 24 Maryland counties and 134 8-digit watersheds statewide. Priority is also given to watersheds with low forest cover, low percent of streams buffered, high non-point source nutrient loadings, and erodible soils. Chesapeake Bay Lowlands (Southern Maryland and Eastern Shore) and trout stream watersheds are also prioritized. Urban, suburban, and agricultural lands throughout the state are eligible.

To report buffer plantings and include them in statewide accounting, complete the Riparian Forest Buffer Planting Form (RFB Form 9) and submit to the RFB Coordinator at MD DNR Forest Service, Tawes State Office Building E-1, Annapolis, MD 21401. Reporting deadlines are January 1 for fall plantings and July 1 for spring plantings. The reporting form is available on the MD DNR Forest Service website.

structured_extraction.program_description: A regulatory permit program administered by the Maryland Forest Service that governs any tree work—planting, pruning, or removal—performed within public road rights-of-way. Anyone intending to do roadside tree work must first obtain a permit before beginning any work. The program ensures all work meets professional arboricultural standards and is overseen by qualified tree experts, protecting the ecological and public value of roadside trees. An optional Roadside Tree Care training class is also available to prepare applicants for the Roadside Tree Expert examination. Montgomery County residents must apply through the Montgomery County Permits Office instead of the state program.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: The program issues Roadside Tree Permits (either individual Project Permits for single trees or Blanket Permits for ongoing/routine maintenance across multiple sites) authorizing tree work in public road rights-of-way. A Forest Ranger inspects the site and evaluates the application before issuing or denying the permit. Permits are valid for one year from issuance. A $25 application fee applies to non-public agencies. Montgomery County residents must contact the Montgomery County Permits Office at (240) 777-6335 instead.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Individuals, businesses, municipalities, utilities, and contractors who need to perform tree work (planting, pruning, or removal) within public road rights-of-way in Maryland. Also open to individuals and public agency employees seeking to become authorized Roadside Tree Experts.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Obtaining authorization to plant, prune, or remove trees in public road rights-of-way. Project Permits cover individual trees; Blanket Permits cover ongoing maintenance across multiple sites.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available statewide in Maryland for roadside rights-of-way, except residents of Montgomery County must contact the Montgomery County Permits Office at (240) 777-6335 for the county's roadside tree permit.

All commercial roadside tree work must be conducted under the direction of a Licensed Tree Expert (LTE)

For construction or development projects, a site plan must be uploaded/submitted
If the tree is on a boundary between two properties, written consent from both property owners must be provided

Compliance with ANSI Z133 safety standards required

structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Complete the Roadside Tree Permit application form (the online portal is currently temporarily unavailable). Submit the completed application along with payment ($25 fee for non-public agencies) to your local DNR Forest Service office by mail or in person. A Forest Ranger will conduct an on-site inspection and may request additional information. If approved, a permit is issued by mail or email. If denied, a written denial notice is sent with reasons and appeal instructions. Denied applicants may appeal within 10 working days by submitting a written appeal to the Project Manager listed on the original application. To become a Roadside Tree Care Expert (RSTCE), attend the preparatory course offered annually in each region, study the provided guide, and pass the 140-question exam with a 70% passing score.

structured_extraction.program_description: Roots for Resilience is a Maryland DNR initiative designed to help the Lower Eastern Shore adapt to climate change by enhancing nature's ability to store carbon and buffer climate impacts. It supports tree planting, coastal habitat restoration (including living shorelines and tidal marsh), improved forestry management, and community outreach and engagement on private lands and public corridors. Funding is provided through open solicitations (RFPs), including an RFP that opened in January 2026, with support from a U.S. EPA assistance agreement (3D25824) passed through the North Carolina Department of Natural and Cultural Resources.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: The initiative funds wetland restoration activities, living shoreline projects, enhanced forestry management, afforestation, tree planting, coastal habitat restoration, and community outreach and engagement. DNR issues open solicitations (RFPs) for specific project types, including a Living Shoreline Solicitation and an RFP that opened in January 2026. Funding comes from a U.S. EPA assistance agreement (3D25824) passed through the North Carolina Department of Natural and Cultural Resources.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Private landowners, nonprofit organizations, for-profit entities, local governments, and community partners on the Lower Eastern Shore of Maryland interested in climate resilience, habitat restoration, forestry projects, tree planting, and coastal habitat restoration.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Tree planting and afforestation, tidal marsh and wetland restoration, living shoreline installation, improved forestry management practices, coastal resilience management plans, community outreach and engagement, and other activities that build climate resilience and reduce carbon emissions on the Lower Eastern Shore.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Projects must be located in specific Lower Eastern Shore Maryland counties. Living shoreline/marsh protection projects are eligible in Dorchester, Somerset, and Wicomico; enhanced forestry management and afforestation in Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Somerset, Wicomico, and Worcester; coastal resilience management plans in Dorchester, Somerset, Wicomico, and Worcester. Additional Eastern Shore counties (Cecil, Kent, Queen Anne's) may also be eligible depending on project type.
requirements_list: Projects must be located in eligible Lower Eastern Shore Maryland counties depending on project type
Living shoreline projects must be in Dorchester, Somerset, or Wicomico counties
Enhanced forestry management and afforestation projects must be in Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Somerset, Wicomico, or Worcester counties
Coastal resilience management plan projects must be in Dorchester, Somerset, Wicomico, or Worcester counties
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Apply through the Request for Proposals (RFP) process. An open RFP is available for Living Shoreline Solicitation projects, and an additional RFP opened in January 2026. Interested applicants should visit the Open Solicitations page linked on the program website. For questions, contact dnr.rootsresilience@maryland.gov.

structured_extraction.program_name: Roots for Resilience Living Shoreline Solicitation
structured_extraction.program_description: The Maryland Department of Natural Resources is seeking proposals for construction, design/build, and design of living shoreline projects in Wicomico, Somerset, or Dorchester Counties. Funded through the EPA Climate Pollution Reduction Grant (CPRG) awarded to the Atlantic Conservation Coalition, the program uses nature-based erosion control techniques including coir logs, sills, groins, breakwaters, natural materials, and marsh plantings to restore coastal shorelines and protect tidal marsh habitat. The goal is to fund large-scale living shoreline restoration projects that will collectively protect 400 acres of adjacent high-quality tidal marsh habitat in the Chesapeake Bay portions of these Eastern Shore counties.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: $17 million in federal grant funding (100% EPA Climate Pollution Reduction Grant funds) is available for construction, design/build, or design of living shoreline projects in the Chesapeake Bay portions of Dorchester, Wicomico, and Somerset counties. Minimum request is $1 million, though smaller design-only requests may be allowed with DNR approval. No match required (leveraged funds encouraged). Eligible expenses include design, permitting, construction, outreach, and stakeholder engagement costs. Multiple awards expected with monthly reimbursable invoicing. All construction must be completed by July 1, 2029.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Local jurisdictions, non-profit organizations, and institutions of higher education seeking to implement living shoreline restoration projects on Maryland's Lower Eastern Shore. Public land projects are prioritized.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Design, permitting, and construction of living shoreline projects, including: design and engineering services; permit application fees; community engagement and facilitation; contractor/consultant services; native plants and vegetation; project materials/supplies; staff time; and indirect costs (per NICRA or de minimis rate).
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Projects must be located within the Chesapeake Bay portions of Dorchester, Wicomico, and Somerset Counties on Maryland's Lower Eastern Shore.

Project must protect substantial areas of adjacent wetland

Transmittal letter on official letterhead signed by authorized executive

Permits (if available) or permit timeline/schedule

List of project partners with Letters of Commitment detailing roles and contributions
Photographs of current site conditions
Site-specific outputs from Living Shoreline Targeting Tool
Monitoring plan (if available)
Federal procurement compliance for contractual work, including three cost estimates for contracts over $10,000 and competitive solicitation for contracts over $250,000
Compliance acknowledgment with federal employment and non-discrimination requirements
Applicants must maintain liability insurance coverage during project performance

structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Review the RFP and required narrative questions, then submit a complete application via the provided Google Forms link (not as a PDF attachment). Application must include all required documentation. DNR and state agency partners evaluate proposals based on eligibility, project need, cost-efficiency, readiness, and likelihood of long-term success. Multiple awards are expected. Contact Ari Engelberg to inquire about potential project ideas or to request a site visit. An information session recording and mapping tutorial are available online to help applicants.

structured_extraction.program_description: Maryland's Rural Legacy Program, created in 1998 and administered by the Maryland Department of Natural Resources (in consultation with the Maryland Department of Agriculture and Maryland Department of Planning), protects the state's best agricultural, forestry, natural, historical, and cultural rural landscapes through land conservation by providing competitive funding to preserve large, contiguous tracts of land from sprawl development. It creates public-private partnerships and awards competitive grants to local sponsors—local government agencies and non-profit organizations (including land trusts and conservation organizations)—to acquire conservation easements or fee simple estates (full ownership) from willing landowners within designated Rural Legacy Areas. Landowners sell or donate their development rights permanently but keep ownership and can continue farming or other uses consistent with the easement. The program establishes greenbelts of forests and farms around rural communities to preserve cultural heritage and sense of place, preserves critical habitat for native plant and wildlife species, and protects riparian forests, wetlands, and greenways to buffer the Chesapeake Bay and its tributaries from pollution run-off. A major focus is stream buffer protection, with required 100-foot grass and/or forest buffers along streams. Recent offers to landowners range from $8,000 to $10,000 per acre paid as cash at settlement. Since 1997, the program has awarded over $403.5 million, with a total appropriated since inception of $479.538 million. The FY 2025 total appropriation was $15,329,028, and the program has cumulatively conserved 130,668.92 acres as of end of FY 2025. This preserves rural character and supports a sustainable land base for natural resource-based industries such as farming, forestry, tourism, and recreation, while enhancing environmental protection and supporting Chesapeake Bay and local waterway health. The program also protects Civil War historic sites, views surrounding nationally significant sites (Appalachian Trail, battlefields, state parks), and provides water quality benefits to major waterways including the Potomac River, Chesapeake Bay, and drinking water reservoirs. Funding comes from Maryland Program Open Space dollars and general obligation bonds from the state's capital budget; local jurisdictions also contribute matching funds. Currently 36 Rural Legacy Areas exist throughout all 23 Maryland counties. Funds are allocated using an objective scoring approach, with applications evaluated on resource significance, development threat, quality of partnerships, extent of matching funds, and the sponsor's ability to carry out the proposed Rural Legacy Plan. New areas require a Full Application; established areas use an Abbreviated Application for renewal or boundary changes. Conservation easements must conform to the RLP Model Conservation Easement effective January 1, 2025, and must require stream buffers, impervious surface limits, Forest Stewardship Plans, and Soil and Water Quality Conservation Plans where applicable. Grant Agreements are executed after Board of Public Works approval. Applications are due by the second Tuesday in February by 5:00 p.m. at the state level; Anne Arundel County accepts applications with a December 1 deadline each year. State agencies review applications February through April; the Rural Legacy Advisory Committee and Board review April through May; the Board submits final recommendations to the Board of Public Works in July–August; grants are approved August–September. Washington County has paid over $28.5 million to preserve more than 9,400 acres in Rural Legacy Areas near the Towns of Sharpsburg, Keedysville, and Boonsboro and rural villages including St. James, Lappans, Fairplay, Rohrersville, and Gapland. Easement restrictions remain in perpetuity and the program is very competitive. The program administers perpetual conservation easements restricting use, subdivision, and sale of land, protecting conservation attributes including natural, agricultural, forestry, environmental, scenic, cultural, rural, woodland and wetland characteristics. Reserved rights for agricultural, forestry, residential, and limited commercial uses are allowed while preserving conservation attributes. The Rural Legacy Board is established under Md. Code Ann., Nat. Res. § 5-9A-01 et seq.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Competitive grants are awarded annually to approved local sponsors (local government agencies, non-profit organizations, land trusts, and conservation organizations) to fund land conservation activities within designated Rural Legacy Areas. Grants support the purchase of conservation easements or fee simple estates (full ownership) from willing landowners to preserve large, contiguous tracts supporting natural resources, agriculture, forestry, wetlands, and cultural heritage. Funds also support related planning activities including administrative, stewardship, and incidental costs. The FY 2025 total appropriation was $15,329,028; total appropriated since inception is $479.538 million; cumulative conserved acreage is 130,668.92 acres as of end of FY 2025. Recent offers to individual landowners range from $8,000 to $10,000 per acre, paid as cash at settlement. Landowners sell or donate development rights permanently but retain ownership and may continue farming or other easement-consistent uses. Conservation easements must conform to the RLP Model Conservation Easement effective January 1, 2025, and must require stream buffers (including 100-foot grass and/or forest buffers along streams), impervious surface limits (2%), CAFO restrictions, Forest Stewardship Plans, and Soil and Water Quality Conservation Plans where applicable. Funding comes from Maryland Program Open Space dollars and general obligation bonds from the state's capital budget; local jurisdictions also contribute matching funds. Funds are allocated using an objective scoring process evaluated on resource significance, development threat, quality of partnerships, extent of matching funds, and the sponsor's ability to carry out the proposed Rural Legacy Plan. New areas require a Full Application; established areas use an Abbreviated Application for renewal or boundary changes. Grant Agreements are executed after Board of Public Works approval. Washington County has paid over $28.5 million to preserve more than 9,400 acres; easement restrictions remain in perpetuity. Sponsors are eligible for up to 100% reimbursement of allowable project costs including direct land costs, incidental costs (surveys, appraisals, title searches, legal fees, settlement costs), administrative costs (up to 3% of grant amount), and program compliance/monitoring costs (up to 1.5% of easement purchase cost). Acquisition methods include conservation easement purchase (preferred), fee simple purchase, fee simple purchase and resale with conservation easement, donation of fee simple or easement rights, and installment purchase agreements. Conservation easements are perpetual deed restrictions protecting conservation attributes including natural, agricultural, forestry, environmental, scenic, cultural, rural, woodland and wetland characteristics, and restricting industrial uses while allowing reserved rights for agricultural, forestry, residential, and limited commercial uses.
structured_extraction.application_deadline_string: Second Tuesday in February by 5:00 p.m. (state-level); December 1 (Anne Arundel County); prior to February 1st of each cycle year (Washington County); January 15 (GIS submittal deadline)
structured_extraction.program_audience: Local government agencies, land trusts, conservation organizations, non-profit organizations, county governments, soil conservation districts, and resource conservation & development organizations sponsoring land conservation efforts within designated Rural Legacy Areas statewide; also individual landowners and willing sellers within designated Rural Legacy Areas, including those with stream corridors requiring buffer protection. Land trusts must be Maryland nonprofit corporations, tax-exempt under IRC § 501(c)(3), and qualified organizations under IRC § 170(h)(3).
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Acquisition of conservation easements or fee simple estates (full ownership) from willing landowners to preserve large, contiguous tracts and to protect agricultural, forestry, natural, historic, cultural, and wetland resources from sprawl development; payment to landowners for permanent restriction of development rights in designated Rural Legacy Areas (recent offers range from $8,000 to $10,000 per acre paid as cash at settlement); protection of Civil War historic sites, views surrounding nationally significant resources, and scenic landscapes; protection of ecologically valuable properties that most directly impact Chesapeake Bay, Potomac River, local waterways, and drinking water reservoirs; support of farms and forests through cooperation among state and local governments and land trusts; administrative, stewardship/monitoring, and incidental costs related to conservation activities; implementation of enhanced best management practices including stream buffers, impervious surface limitation, CAFO restrictions, soil conservation and water quality plans, and forest stewardship plans; related planning activities within designated Rural Legacy Areas; fee simple purchase and resale with conservation easement; installment purchase agreements; endowment establishment for long-term easement monitoring; preservation of open space, protection of natural habitats, preservation of historically important land areas, outdoor recreation and education, and adjacency to other protected lands.

Additional Rural Legacy Areas include: Agricultural Security Corridor, Bear Creek, Upper Patapsco Watershed, and Piney Run Watershed. Administered locally in Anne Arundel County through the County Agricultural Program Planner. Washington County's Rural Legacy Areas are located near the Towns of Sharpsburg, Keedysville, and Boonsboro and rural villages of St. James, Lappans, Fairplay, Rohrersville, and Gapland.

structured_extraction.application_process_overview: 1. Review the Scoring Description document before completing your application. 2. Prospective new sponsors should read the Rural Legacy Program Grants Manual and meet with the appropriate RLP Program Administrator. 3. Download forms from the Download page. 4. Submit GIS data by January 15 per GIS Submittal Guidelines (coordinate with Maryland Department of Planning contact Ellen Mussman at ellen.mussman@maryland.gov as needed); GIS data must be in zipped shapefile or geodatabase format using NAD_1983_StatePlane_Maryland_FIPS_1900 meters projection. 5. Complete the Full Application (new areas) or Abbreviated Application (established areas) following GIS Submittal Guidelines. Include a Property List Form for abbreviated applications. Applications must include: cover sheet, executive summary narrative (2 pages maximum), executive summary numbers form, matching funds documentation, criteria and general description (4 pages maximum), funding request form, proposed acquisitions form with property details, color map, and GIS data. 6. Local sponsors identify Rural Legacy Areas and apply annually to the Rural Legacy Board for program participation and funding. Applications must be submitted to the Rural Legacy Office by the second Tuesday in February by 5:00 p.m. 7. State agencies review applications February through April. 8. The Rural Legacy Advisory Committee and Board review applications April through May, potentially requesting presentations or site visits. 9. The Board submits final recommendations to the Board of Public Works in July–August. 10. The Board of Public Works approves grants in August–September, after which Grant Agreements are prepared for each funded Sponsor. 11. Once the Grant Agreement is executed by the Chairman of the Rural Legacy Board and the Sponsor, the sponsor may proceed with individual property acquisitions through project agreements. 12. For individual property acquisitions: Sponsor submits BPW package with all required documents (including written and visual description of request, plats, maps, drawings, photographs, and specifications submitted prior to construction and concurrent with permit applications); Program staff reviews and prepares BPW item; project scheduled for BPW agenda; upon approval, project processes for payment; Sponsor receives funds and proceeds to settlement; file closure documentation required. Washington County: Apply prior to February 1st of each cycle year; applications are ranked based on property characteristics. Contact the County's Land Preservation Office for assistance. Anne Arundel County: Contact the Anne Arundel County Agricultural Program Planner; applications are accepted with a December 1 annual deadline. Contact Katrina L. Tucker at KatrinaL.Tucker@maryland.gov or 410-260-8454 with questions.

structured_extraction.program_name: Rural Legacy Program - Agricultural Security Corridor-Eastern Shore Heartland Rural Legacy Area (Specific Project Area)
structured_extraction.program_description: Protects a large block of prime agricultural land on Maryland's Eastern Shore, defined by the Choptank River and several creeks, with a focus on preserving farmland, agricultural businesses, and public investment in farm preservation easements near the towns of Preston, Federalsburg, East New Market, and Trappe.

structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Conservation easements to protect prime farmland, stream corridors, and agricultural infrastructure

structured_extraction.program_description: The Maryland Schoolyard Forests Program is a Five Million Trees partnership initiative with the Maryland Association of Environmental & Outdoor Education that helps schools create and improve outdoor spaces that support student well-being, outdoor learning, and connections to nature. The program promotes healthier campus landscapes with access to nature benefits, develops partnerships with municipalities, schools, and students to increase tree canopy cover, create nature discovery pathways, and support local climate resiliency. It provides campus planning and technical support, hands-on training for staff and facilities teams, educational and student-centered activities, engagement and celebration events, youth career exploration experiences, microgrants, and classroom materials to help schools transform their grounds into healthier, more inviting environments — particularly for schools advancing toward Maryland Green School certification.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Schools may receive free services including: Teacher Workshops, Landscape Stewardship Manual, Specimen Tree Inventory & Mapping, Arbor Day & Earth Day Activities, Forest Health Assessments, Professional Development/Continuing Education, Hazard Tree Evaluation & Removal, Native Tree Planting, Edible Food Plots, and Summer Tree Maintenance. Additionally, campus planning and technical support, hands-on training for staff and facilities teams, educational and student-centered outdoor learning opportunities, engagement and celebration events, youth career exploration experiences, microgrants, and classroom support materials are available — particularly for schools advancing toward Maryland Green School certification or developing outdoor environmental literacy projects.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Maryland public schools of all types and sizes, with priority given to schools and communities with the greatest need. District-level facility teams and community partners working directly with school campuses are also eligible. Privately funded schools may participate, though resources are first directed toward public schools. The program serves students of all backgrounds.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Improving school outdoor spaces through campus planning, tree planting, native plantings, stewardship training, outdoor learning integration, environmental literacy projects, forest health assessments, hazard tree evaluation and removal, edible food plots, summer tree maintenance, and advancement toward Green School certification.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available to public schools statewide in Maryland.
requirements_list: Must be a Maryland school (public schools prioritized)
District-level facility teams and community partners working directly with school campuses are eligible
Privately funded schools may participate though resources are first directed toward public schools
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: A formal application process is being developed and will be linked from the program page once available. An online application link is currently provided on the page. Schools may also contact Veronica Guerra directly to discuss interest and initial questions.

structured_extraction.program_description: The Maryland Department of Natural Resources Chesapeake & Coastal Service (CCS) provides technical and financial assistance to waterfront property owners, non-profit organizations, community organizations, counties, and municipalities to fund living shoreline and erosion control projects along the Chesapeake Bay and its tributaries, as well as streambank restoration projects statewide. Formerly known as Shore Erosion Control (also referred to as Shoreline Conservation Service), the program was established in 1964 and offers technical assistance (site visit evaluations, problem assessments, and recommended solutions) and financial assistance in the form of 0% interest loans for the design and installation of shoreline stabilization and streambank restoration projects using nature-based techniques that maintain natural coastal processes. Structural solutions such as bulkheads and revetments are not funded. Loan funds are disbursed in portions as work is completed, and a county tax district or lien must be established to secure the loan.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Technical assistance includes site visit evaluations, problem assessments, recommended solutions, and design and installation support for shoreline stabilization and streambank restoration projects using living shoreline techniques. Financial assistance is provided as 0% interest loans ranging from 5 to 20 years in term depending on techniques used and their projected longevity. An upfront cash contribution is required for individuals and groups of homeowners for loans greater than $60,000. An administrative fee ranging from 3% to 10% based on project construction cost is included in each loan. Funds are disbursed for portions of completed work and distributed to the loan applicant upon proof of payment. A county-sponsored shore erosion control tax district (for community projects) or a shore erosion control lien (for private property projects) must be established.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Waterfront property owners (individuals or groups), non-profit organizations, community organizations, for-profit property owners, counties, and municipalities experiencing shoreline or streambank erosion along the Chesapeake Bay and its tributaries.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Living shoreline construction and erosion control projects using nature-based techniques (e.g., breakwaters, sills, groins, biologs, marsh plantings), as well as design and installation of shoreline stabilization and streambank restoration projects. Also covers site visits, problem assessments, and erosion control recommendations. Structural solutions such as bulkheads and revetments are not funded.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Available statewide in Maryland for properties along the Chesapeake Bay and its tributaries, as well as waterfront and streambank properties statewide.
requirements_list: Applicant must be an individual, group of homeowners, non-profit organization, community organization, for-profit property owner, county, or municipality
Individuals and groups of homeowners with loans greater than $60,000 must provide an upfront cash contribution
A county-sponsored shore erosion control tax district (community projects) or a shore erosion control lien (private property projects) must be established
Project must use nature-based living shoreline techniques; structural solutions such as bulkheads and revetments are not eligible
Must be a waterfront property owner experiencing shoreline or streambank erosion
Applicant must provide proof of payment to the department for disbursements
structured_extraction.application_process_overview: Apply through MD DNR Grants Gateway at mddnr.info/grantsgateway. Interested applicants can also fill out a technical assistance request form or submit the online form linked on the program page to request a site visit, or contact Wesley Gould at wesley.gould@maryland.gov or (410) 260-8812 to discuss technical assistance and funding opportunities. The department will assist with establishing the required tax district or lien.

structured_extraction.program_name: Special Rivers Chesapeake Bay Implementation Grant (Forestry Component)
structured_extraction.program_description: A watershed-based forestry initiative funded by the US EPA since 1983 to improve water quality in the Chesapeake Bay by supporting riparian forest buffer restoration, forest stewardship planning, and education and outreach in targeted Maryland watersheds.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Technical assistance for riparian forest buffer restoration, forest stewardship planning, watershed planning, and education and outreach on forest benefits for water quality and habitat.
structured_extraction.program_audience: Private and public landowners, local communities, and resource professionals in targeted Chesapeake Bay watersheds in Maryland.
structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Riparian forest buffer restoration and monitoring, forest stewardship plans, watershed-level planning, invasive species control, and education and outreach.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Four project areas: Susquehanna area (Cecil to Montgomery/Howard counties), Monocacy area, Anacostia/West Chesapeake (Prince George's, Montgomery, Anne Arundel counties), and Town Creek (Allegany County).

structured_extraction.program_description: Maryland's Waterway Improvement Fund (WIF) provides grants and/or loans to local governments, the Maryland Department of Natural Resources, and federal agencies for capital projects and services that benefit the boating public. Established in 1966, the fund supports projects that improve and promote recreational and commercial capabilities, conditions, and safety of Maryland's waterways for the benefit of the general boating public. Eligible projects include constructing or renovating boating access facilities, dredging high-use channels and harbors, marking channels and harbors, clearing debris from navigable waters, constructing jetties and breakwaters, marine sewage pump-out stations, bridge/drawbridge improvements, shore erosion control, boating information and education, and purchasing fire and rescue vessels in partnership with local fire companies. Since 1966, the fund has provided more than $429 million for over 4,900 projects at more than 400 public boating access sites. Revenues come primarily from a one-time 5% excise tax paid when a boat is purchased and titled in Maryland.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Grants and/or loans for capital projects benefiting the boating public. Grant types include 100% state-funded grants, 50/50 matching grants, small project grants (up to $25,000 for off-cycle minor construction and repair), and Matching Fund Fire & Rescue grants (up to $80,000 state share). Interest-free long-term loans (up to 25 years) are available for dredging projects. Funding is provided on a reimbursement basis (50% or 100% cost share options available). Eligible project costs include engineering, permitting, planning, construction, dredging, navigation aids, marine facility construction/renovation, pump-out stations, shore erosion control, marine firefighting/policing facilities and equipment, and boating education. Revenues come primarily from a one-time 5% excise tax paid when a boat is purchased and titled in Maryland. Since 1966, the fund has provided more than $429 million for over 4,900 projects at more than 400 public boating access sites. Applications are typically submitted between July and September for the following fiscal year's funding consideration.

For small off-cycle projects (up to $25,000), submit a completed WIF-application-25K form with project description, schedule, site plans/drawings/photographs, and bid tabulation. Reimbursement requests are submitted via email to the Regional Administrator with a transmittal letter on official letterhead, one Request for Reimbursement Form per project, copies of invoices with payment evidence, and supporting documentation.

structured_extraction.program_description: Maryland Department of Natural Resources offers free, self-guided (do-it-yourself) pheasant hunts on public lands for new and lapsed hunters. Participants are selected through a lottery and hunt stocked pheasants on designated Wildlife Management Areas or state forests across Maryland. Hunts take place on November 22-23, 2025. Only the lottery winner may carry and use a firearm, but friends or family may accompany them.
structured_extraction.assistance_description: Free access to stocked pheasant hunts on public lands on November 22-23, 2025. There is no cost to apply or participate. Selected participants receive a permit letter and map showing pheasant release areas. Only the lottery winner may carry and use a firearm, but friends or family may accompany them. Participants must supply their own gear and firearms.

structured_extraction.use_of_funds: Participation in free stocked pheasant hunts on public land across Maryland.
structured_extraction.geographic_eligibility: Hunts take place on public lands across Maryland (Wildlife Management Areas or state forests). Participants select their first, second, and third choice hunt area location from available options.
